We demonstrate that the change in helicity between the leptons and hadrons leads to an imbalance in the cosine of the relative angle between the hadron and the lepton flight directions. This phenomenon arises from the interaction between the helicity and spin-longitudinal components. Form form factor integration, we derive the expression for the cross-section and calculated the cosine imbalance in terms of the helicity dependence of the amplitude for $u\bar{u}$ and $d\bar{d}$ quark pairs. Furthermore, we illustrate how the cosine imbalance is affected by the kinematic variables and observes an interesting relationship with the helicity dependence of the amplitude.

In 1949, Arthur Coma and Leopold Infeld proposed a mathematical method for transforming any spacetime into its conformally equivalent version. Over time, this technique has become a standard tool in general relativity research. By applying this method, any spacetime can be transformed into a conformally equivalent version, known as the Weyl canonical form. Although originally proposed by Einstein and Pontryagin as an equivalent formulation of the Einstein field equations, it has since been recognized that this method has a more significant implication in the field of general relativity, relating to the conformal structure of black holes and white holes. Nonetheless, a similar transformation was previously unexplored within the context of de Sitter space. In this study, we transform the de Sitter space using the same method proposed by Coma and Infeld, and we demonstrate that the resulting spacetime corresponds to the inside of a hypersurface with a specific geometric property, which we term "maximally expansive." This property may provide clues for identifying black hole-rings within the de Sitter space.

We provide a detailed explanation of a novel technique for generating modified versions of symplectic manifolds. This new method can be viewed as an extension of the well-known technique for creating modified complex manifolds through changes in their K\"ahlerian structure. Employing our approach, we prove that if a symplectic manifold meets specific criteria, its symplectic structure can be transformed in a way that produces a K\"ahler manifold. Furthermore, we establish a connection between the original symplectic structure and its modified version, resulting in constraints on the allowable modifications. With the ability to generate modified structures comes the capacity to investigate original structures in the modified manifolds, enabling solutions to certain system of equations whose only given constraint is an inequality. As a result, we are able to prove that a particular class of closed symplectic manifolds contains an infinite number of distinct structure types.

The entity suggestion feature improves user experience by providing relevant entities for each search query, but effectively implementing this feature is a challenging task. Our novel approach, Diagram Embedding, tackles this issue by combining a sophisticated entity representation method called Graph Convolutional Neural Network and a straightforward sampling technique to efficiently generate suggestions from a large knowledge base graph. We also introduce a new evaluation metric called Precision at K Samples, which accurately assesses entity suggestions by considering the diversity of suggested entities. Our evaluation results demonstrate that our approach outperforms the existing state-of-the-art methods on both precision and diversity. Furthermore, our approach exhibits exceptional scalability by achieving a precision of 12.8% on the Wikipedia dataset, which consists of approximately 5 million entities connected by 217 million relationships.

The success of kidney transplantation is heavily dependent on the ideal matching of donor and recipient kidneys. Desirable pairings occur when the donor and recipient kidneys have the same "blood type" and when the donor and recipient have the same or similar "human leukocyte antigen" (HLA). Nevertheless, it is essential to note that having too similar HLA can lead to the rejection of the transplanted kidney by the recipient's immune system. While the exact risks of rejection for each HLA combination are not fully known, researchers do know that combinations with high risks of rejection should be avoided. In this research, a mathematical model is used to identify all combinations of kidneys that should be accepted or rejected in order to maximize the number of transplants performed. The study assumes that the only factor considered in kidney compatibility is the combination of blood types and HLA. It should be noted that this model is the basis for the current kidney matching algorithm used in the United States.

This analysis focuses on implicit connections in a sequential setting, specifically within a sequence-to-sequence model. Initially, we distinguish between two categories of implicit connections: contextual and semantic. We then explore three aspects of implicit connections in sequences. Firstly, we examine how contextual connections influence representation by investigating how contextual information affects both the overall sequence representation and individual sequence elements' representations. We find that each sequence element's representation is a combination of its own unique features and its position within the sequence. We develop the Multi-Head Linear Transformer model to demonstrate this interplay. Secondly, we analyze how semantic connections relate to sequence ordering. We identify that similar semantic concepts tend to appear in sequential order, enabling us to leverage pre-trained language models to learn ordered pairs of sequences with shared semantic meaning. We then create the Structured Semantic Reasoning model to capture this ordering by incorporating the sequential context into pre-trained transformer models through self-supervised learning. Finally, we explore how explicit connection representations are derived from implicit connections. We propose the Decomposed Sequence Decoding framework to decompose a sequence into individual elements based on both contextual and semantic connections, and then decode the sequence by combining these elements. This framework provides a framework for further research into the dynamics of implicit connections within sequences.

Our analysis reveals that current advanced word representations, including BERT, fail to accurately understand the language used in the Loughran-McDonald corpus, which is considered a standard for financial text analysis. We demonstrate that these representations are not inherently linked to the original sender's intentions but rather can be easily manipulated to align with various models' interpretations of the data. We propose a novel approach called Contrastive Learning for Financial Text (CFLT), which focuses on distinguishing between two similar but contrasting phrases expressed in a neutral tone. We utilized the CFLT framework to develop novel, interpretable word representations that directly capture the essence of the Loughran-McDonald corpus, including complex polarities such as antonyms, and showed its effectiveness in multiple financial text classification tasks.

This article proposes SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM based communication systems that achieve enhanced performance by combining spatial and frequency domain signal transmission. To optimize performance, a 5G New Radio (NR) compliant system is designed and tested. Results show that our proposed SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM based communication systems excel in terms of data transfer speed and overall efficiency. Furthermore, our research is set to contribute significantly to the development of future integrated data and power transfer systems. Due to copyright restrictions, we cannot freely disseminate the contents of this article. Nonetheless, we are happy to provide you with the complete article in its entirety.

This research introduces a novel approach to modeling the interaction of fluids with changing phases, combining level-set and embedded boundary methods to handle complex geometry changes. By leveraging the strengths of these techniques, we've developed a versatile strategy that easily adapts to various problem setups, from simple to highly intricate, allowing for efficient numerical solutions with minimal code modifications. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, we've applied it to solve three challenging problems: the melting of a solid due to external heat, the freezing of a supercooled liquid, and the interaction of these processes with moving boundaries. Our method exhibits desirable properties like second-order accuracy, monotonicity preservation, and minimal stretching or tearing, thanks to a non-distractive additional term that enhances stability. Our numerical findings match well with analytical solutions for the test cases, showcasing our approach's precision and highlighting its potential as a general framework for resolving a broad range of phase transformation problems.

Unary logical connectives, such as negation, in formal languages, have a profound impact when combined with negation's properties. The interplay between these connectives and the language's foundational rules can lead to intricate semantic assessments of formulas. A novel application of duality theory from quantum logic is proposed to enhance the language's expressiveness, offering a fresh perspective on unary connectives and their interactions. This incorporation of duality enriches the language's capacity for nuanced semantic analysis, enabling a more precise examination of the relationship between language and reality.

We propose a novel approach for resolving $n$-player normal form games when unique pure strategy equilibria exist, using a method that guarantees nearly optimal payoffs for all players through a simple algorithm. Our algorithm is designed for extensive form games as well, although it may lead to some players receiving negative expected values from their own actions. We also explore an alternative approach involving a mechanism that pays players their minimal rationalizable payoff or a fraction of their expected payoff, ensuring all players receive nonnegative expected payoff. Nonetheless, this alternative faces an unwieldy computational burden. Moreover, we demonstrate that no computationally efficient, multiplayer algorithm can guarantee each player a certain fraction of their maximal rationalizable payoff in every game with multiple equilibria.

An analysis of a stochastic SIR model is conducted, where individuals on a random graph connect to each other and disconnect (rewire) in response to an epidemic outbreak. The model is studied on various graph structures, including Erdos-Renyi graphs, scale-free networks, and small-world graphs. The ultimate goal is to identify the epidemic threshold, determined by the average degree of the graph and the rate at which individuals rewire it. The epidemic threshold is found to rely on both the average degree and rewiring rate, demonstrating an intriguing interplay between these factors. The impact of rewiring on the epidemic's spread is influenced by the graph's degree distribution. For certain degree distributions, a significant reduction in the epidemic threshold is achieved through rewiring, while in other cases, the threshold remains unchanged, and even increases with increased rewiring. A theoretical model is also presented, demonstrating that rewiring an epidemic network can significantly lower the threshold, while a numerical solution reveals that this effect increases with the variability of the graph's degree distribution.

In this study, we examine Cotton solitons within the context of nearly Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds. Initially, we establish the incompatibility of such solitons when the potential vector field is directly aligned with the Reeb vector field. Then, assuming the potential vector field is perpendicular to the Reeb vector field, we demonstrate that on non-Kenmotsu nearly Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds with the Reeb vector field being an eigen vector of the Ricci operator, a steady Cotton soliton emerges, characterizing a manifold that is locally identical in geometry to the warped product space $\mathbb{H}^2(-4) \times \mathbb{R}$.

This paper outlines the theoretical foundation for adjusting PDFs, focusing on fitting datasets within the context of the standard LHC proceedings. A detailed explanation of the underlying assumptions, the choice of fitness function, and the associated constraints is provided. Additionally, a concise overview of the implemented methods, along with relevant details on the specifics of our approach, is presented.

To accelerate training for deep reinforcement learning agents in complex, dynamic environments, experience replay has been a popular technique by allowing agents to learn from a stored record of past observations. Although effective, the standard approach of uniformly sampling episodes and episodes steps can lead to slow learning due to the retained variance in the rewards being replayed. As a result, we propose a new, adaptive method of sampling episodes based on the variance of the rewards, which selectively prioritizes episodes with the highest variance. Through thorough experimentation on various benchmark tasks, our variance-driven approach consistently shows the capacity to significantly speed up training convergence when compared to the uniformly-sampled method. Furthermore, we find that our approach is equally effective when combined with techniques like episodic policy optimization and latent variables. The code for our research is publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/hjdw3/RedER.
I'd like to introduce libcommute, a distinctive new programming language dedicated to managing polynomial operators that commute, along with a built-in function for precise diagonalization.

We employ an unconventional method of direct electronic architecture determination, utilizing scanning transmission electron microscopes with a coherently bright electron beam, to be on par with theoretical calculations for (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_{2}$As$_{2}$.  Our analysis of this material reveals the presence of a unique and well-ordered $d_{xz}$-$d_{yz}$ orbital configuration in (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_{2}$As$_{2}$.  This specific arrangement of electrons around the iron atoms is shown to contribute to the material's superconducting properties by facilitating the pairing of electrons through an exchange of virtual photons.  Our findings are further supported by calculations showing that this particular electronic structure gives rise to an unstable magnetic state, consistent with (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_{2}$As$_{2}$ not exhibiting magnetic ordering.  Additionally, we demonstrate that in (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_{2}$As$_{2}$, superconducting pairs are preferably aligned along the [001] direction, and that there is a distinction in the superconducting gap sizes between the $d_{xz}$ and $d_{yz}$ orbitals.  This knowledge gains significance in the broader context of understanding iron-based superconductors

A recently proposed equation for transforming any given bosonic quadratic operator into an equivalent form involving paired creation and annihilation operators has been compared to a modified version of the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation. Both transformations yield equivalent results, with distinct limits leading to the standard Hubbard-Stratonovich and a more recent superbosonization approach. Specifically, using a specific rotation matrix leads to a Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation, while using an arbitrary matrix results in the superbosonization equation. This distinction arises from requiring the matrix to be orthogonal in the latter case. Both equations have the same solutions and can lead to a closed algebraic system of equations. A key advantage of the superbosonization equation is its potential to create new interactions within a Hamiltonian. A comparison of the two equations also reveals that the superbosonization equation can be viewed as a transformation of the matrix into a similar form to the standard Hubbard-Stratonovich case, with implications for both theory and experiments.

At the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), top quark polarization is expected to be tiny, however estimating polarization from t-channel single top quark production is the aim of this study. By utilizing NNLO in gluon radiation (NNLO+NNLL), the theoretical prediction for polarization asymmetry has been calculated and shown to be accurate within 8% when compared to experimental data. Furthermore, the effect of varying experimental cuts on polarization asymmetry metrology has been investigated.

We have conducted an in-depth analysis of the metallic state in a LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattice using $^8$Li $\beta$-detected NMR in combination with TDPAC. Our findings reveal that the Korringa ratio varies depending on the number of LaNiO$_3$ layers, indicating differences in the spin density of conduction electrons across the LaAlO$_3$/LaNiO$_3$ interface. Moreover, our results demonstrate that the hyperfine interaction is influenced by the LaAlO$_3$ substrate, with the effect becoming more pronounced as the number of LaNiO$_3$ layers decreases. Furthermore, we have observed that the magnetic moment per Ni$^{2+}$ ion is 1.43 $\mu_B$, consistent with the presence of significant orbital moment contribution, likely resulting from the LaAlO$_3$ substrate-induced strain.

Current cutting-edge dialogue systems rely on single-neural-network architectures, which can't fully capture the complex structures of human conversations due to their limited contextual understanding. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel, highly-branching framework for dialogue generation, which complements existing approaches by enabling the processing of multiple contextual layers. In evaluations using both simple and complex datasets, our framework demonstrates superior performance compared to current state-of-the-art models. Furthermore, we introduce the MultiTalk dataset, comprising 13 distinct topics and featuring complex sentence branches, to facilitate the assessment of dialogue models with varying conversation pathways.

Our research is centered on enhancing the maximum achievable capacity in a wireless communication system, comprising multiple input and output antennas and a surface capable of intelligent signal reflection. To provide an accurate assessment, we take into consideration the impact of correlated signal weakening and a more precise method of representing phase shifting. By employing a mathematical approach that accounts for high-level phase shifts, we are able to determine the maximum achievable capacity in terms of a specific formula, eliminating the need for complex optimization techniques. We also explore how the performance of an IRS system compares to that of a system without the intelligent surface, specifically under certain conditions of correlation and phase shifting.

General modifications to gravity are often simplified using a pairwise approach, yet ultimately, n-body simulations are necessary to capture the complexity of real systems. Due to the computational expense of these simulations, researchers typically rely on theoretical models that approximates their behavior or distorts their trajectories in an idealized, simplified way. Despite this, accurate representations of generalized modified gravity models in n-body simulations remain unexploited for several reasons, including the high cost of conducting these simulations with multiple interacting objects. Recent advancements in computer processing technologies and our desire for more precise cosmic measurements now demand more realistic simulations of generalized modified gravity models. Specifically, we are now performing a thorough analysis of generalized modified gravity models using n-body simulations that maintain the original ratio between the gravitational force and the radius of of dark matter clusters up to the point of cluster formation and that alter the gravitational force in a way that accelerates or slows down the orbiting of stars within these clusters. These modifications are so subtle that they require highly accurate simulations, including a level of precision in time stepping, a technique used in computer processing to manage the flow of data, that is typically only needed for more precise simulations, among other technical challenges. We have successfully developed a reliable method for conducting these simulations and have found several key predictions, including specific patterns in the distribution of galaxy rotations, distinct features in the frequency of cosmic waves, and unique characteristics in the distribution of star speeds within clusters, that can be used to identify these modified gravity models. Furthermore, we believe

We discover a profound connection between the Gaussian free field and multiple Schramm-Loewner evolution, specifically when the target contours share common boundaries. To establish this link, we utilize the relationship between the Gaussian free field and the Laplacian of a random potential, which in turn is grounded in the joint work with A. Kupiainen and K. Khanin. Building upon this foundation, we prove that the Gaussian free field can be linked with multiple SLE evolution when the target domains do not overlap and are instead coarsely approximated as closely nestled circles. However, our central contribution extends beyond this scenario, as we demonstrate that multiple SLE evolution can be linked with a Gaussian free field in a more intricate setting, where the target domains are represented by highly intricate, randomly generated polygons, given that these polygons are finely approximated by analytic curves. Lastly, we provide a philosophical overview of our findings, emphasizing that our results showcase the intimate bond between random looney gas models and Gaussian free fields, which underpin our achievements.

MediaWiki-based platforms like Wikipedia have integral tools for seamless collaboration, ensuring transparency and auditability in user activities. By providing reliable navigation, a user-friendly API, and comprehensive contribution statistics, these tools are ideal for fostering cooperation in research and development. This combination of features makes MediaWiki an excellent framework for building tailored applications that promote collaborative work, and given its open-source and adaptable nature, this approach can be applied across various domains and industries. Here, we present WorkingWiki, a demonstration of the benefits of MediaWiki-based applications, where we explore ways to encourage collaboration and address common challenges faced by developers working together on open-source projects.

This research aims to analyze the interaction between a turbulent jet fire and a nearby structure influenced by acoustic waves. To simplify the complex problem, the active flame method is used to model the combustion process, focusing on localized flame areas within the turbulent jet. By applying acoustic excitation, the combustion process becomes unstable and switches between two different states - one excited and the other dormant. An analysis of the active flame method reveals that the excited state of the flame is stable while the dormant state is unstable. When the structure's acoustic excitation matches the natural frequency of the combustion process, a strong reaction between the jet fire and the structure's acoustic waves occurs, leading to increased heat and gas mass transfer between the two. However, when the structure's acoustic excitation exceeds the natural frequency of the combustion process, the reaction between the jet fire and the structure's acoustic waves decreases, resulting in a decline in heat and gas mass transfer between the two. Moreover, acoustic excitation is found to increase the temperature and change the direction of the gas velocity within the turbulent jet. It also causes oscillations in the mass transfer coefficient of the combustion process. In addition, acoustic excitation is shown to impact the curvature and shape of the combustion process, affecting the heat and gas mass transfer between the jet fire and the surrounding environment.

The study of seismic modes in stars is significantly advanced by employing a three-dimensional (3D) graphic user interface called GSTAR. This tool determines the exact frequencies of adiabatic oscillations, both in both linear and non-linear regimes, based on a given stellar model. Recently, researchers upgraded GSTAR to directly output the eigenfunctions of seismic modes, enabling a more in-depth analysis of seismic properties in stars. Specifically, this upgrade enables the identification of geometric modes, which occur when seismic waves within a star travel in a specific pattern across its surface, resembling those in anti-symmetric f-mode. Unlike the $l=2, n=0$ fluid mode, geometric modes are not affected by the star's composition and are therefore more robust against potential errors in stellar modeling.

We present a novel universal detection method for identifying traveling chimeras and synchronized groups within the spectrum of a given network, independent of specific parameters or driving forces. By analyzing the dynamics of a randomly initialized group of coupled neurons, our method detects the emergence of coherent patterns, such as group synchronizations and traveling wave patterns. This approach is universally applicable, allowing it to successfully detect coherent structures in various network configurations, including those previously unexplored, and even in settings where traditional approaches fail. Furthermore, we observe that the proposed detection method complements existing analytical techniques used to study traveling wave solutions.

In two-dimensional lattice fluids with adjacent site connections, a critical phenomenon occurs where a transition from an ordered state to a disordered state happens as the temperature increases. As temperature, molecular size, and next-neighbor interaction strength change, various patterns of bond formation and fluctuation develop, influencing the heat capacity and correlation lengths around the critical point, through both small and large angles. A detailed understanding of these temperature-dependent distributions is key to controlling the spontaneous curvature and cluster size near the critical point, and potentially resolving complex structures like biological membranes.

To explore the link between neutrinos and ultralight dark matter, a new formalism is implemented that directly ties the non-standard neutrino interactions to the dark matter field. This framework is then applied to two areas: first, a condition is identified that must be met for neutrinos' infinite lifetime, and it does not correspond to any combination of neutrino patterns that have been observed; second, the model is used to analyze how neutrinos interact with dark matter within dense environments, and it is found that it contradicts the observations made by satellite missions that study the large-scale universe, but it does fit with the results from laboratory experiments that study the internal structures of stars and planets.

Theoretical models predict that high-energy photons are produced when cosmic rays interact with the solar plasma. Specifically, it is anticipated that extremely high-energy photons will increase significantly above typical solar photon levels. These predictions need to be verified through experimental means, involving the study of solar flare data for possible correlations with aircraft and satellite observations. Currently available data does not display statistical significance for potential ultrahigh-energy photon streams. Further research is required to fully understand potential streams of ultra-high-energy photons from solar sources.

We start with a simplified version of the nonlocal gravity theory introduced in [1], based on a nonlocal modification of the Ricci tensor that satisfies the consistency condition. This model excludes nonlocal contributions from the Weyl tensor, implying that the metric $g_{\mu\nu}$ can be determined from a suitable choice of the constitutive connection $\nabla$. Consequently, we select a specific connection that allows for the separation of nonlocal modifications into intrinsic and extrinsic parts. This choice enables the formation of a four-dimensional manifold without additional nonlocal terms, allowing for solutions that conform to general relativity in large-scale environments.

Distributed systems with replicated data require a robust storage solution that ensures consistency across all replicas. We take a novel approach by focusing on a relatively unexplored area – consistency patterns that are both useful and uncommon. Our design, Eliminate-Win, is an consistency pattern framework that can be applied to various use cases and is easy to understand with just a basic knowledge of programming concepts. We invite you to delve into the details of our design and explore the unique aspects of our code examples together.

To integrate genomic data for 18 human traits, we used a vast dataset of 100,000 fully characterized genome-wide association studies and regulatory region datasets from multiple sources.  By unifying annotations from various sources, we employed the EnrichmentAnalysisR package to analyze genetic regions associated with the traits using regulatory region datasets.  Our analysis revealed significant connections between genetic regions and the traits based on functional characteristics such as gene expression, protein interaction, and tissue distribution.  Notably, we observed distinct patterns of associated genetic regions across different traits, with an average of 135 distinct functional characteristics linked to each trait.  Additionally, many of these associated genetic regions were found to be involved in protein interaction, with over 1,000 unique protein pairs connected to at least one trait.  Our research demonstrates the value of combining genomic data to gain insights into the complex functional characteristics of these associations.

This paper discusses the current status of searches for new, tiny particles at the Large Hadron Collider, specifically focusing on theories involving extra dimensions, dark matter, and axions. Advances in experimental searches are highlighted, along with impending searches that will see a significant boost in sensitivity, particularly in the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider era. Additionally, we examine the complementary capabilities of experimental and theoretical research in this field. Furthermore, we highlight the importance of beyond-the-Standard-Model physics in the LHC's ongoing and near-future research, which will help inform choices for future colliders.

A notable subset of neutron star binaries that exhibit X-ray activity, likely caused by accretion of material from a companion star, displays distinct patterns of activity that are linked to the orbital periods of these systems. However, the underlying connection between these patterns and the neutron stars' spins remains unclear and likely varies. Recent studies suggest that some galaxies host a population of dormant neutron star binaries at their centers, and understanding the dynamics of these systems is crucial. If the typical separation between systems that exhibit X-ray activity and those that remain dormant is linked to the largest possible orbital periods supported by these systems without causing the neutron star to over-spin, then a specific range of dormant system separations might also hold a key to the universe's overall gravitational physics. Analyzing the known Galactic Center neutron star binary candidates, we found that those exhibiting X-ray activity generally have smaller orbital periods, typically less than 65 days, and often less than 20 days. In contrast, the dormant systems with the longest possible major axes, indicating their actual orbital periods might be shorter, are still significantly larger than those with X-ray activity, further supporting a multi-modal distribution. If the characteristic that distinguishes exhibiting X-ray activity from dormancy is indeed linked to the largest possible spin period and considering how this relationship might affect systems with higher mass ratios, then a substantial fraction of the known Galactic Center candidates might indeed be dormantly active.

The binary test for gravity is renowned for its capability to discern between various theories of gravity. However, the proliferation of relativistic binary systems across different spectrums - including pulsar - has generated an overwhelming amount of data, which, when analyzed in totality, is better characterized as a multivariate test for gravity rather than a simple binary test. Nonetheless, the basic principles of the binary test remain integral in evaluating the parameters of pulsars, particularly in their spin down characteristics, which are largely consistent with the standard model, thereby ruling out any significant divergence from general relativity in the high-density phase. Although an anomalous spin down rate could potentially be indicative of an alternate theory of gravity, it is crucial to consider other possible explanations first. In fact, the simplicity and precision of pulsar systems make them ideal for searching for possible gravitational wave emissions, which could provide a direct means of distinguishing between different theories of gravity.

The properties of low-power radio galaxies depend on the aperture used, being affected by the size of the imaging frame. Previous studies that utilized large fields of view may have incorrectly represented the true characteristics of these sources. Our local source sample, consisting of 46 objects with a median redshift of 0.4, was selected for 1.4 GHz imaging with a smaller field of view (approximately 21 arcseconds). We compared our results with those from a larger-field study, finding a greater scatter in the radio power-velocity relationship and no significant correlation between velocity and size for sources on both large and small scales. Our findings also indicated a wider range in the ratio of large-scale to small-scale sizes and velocities, as well as a significant correlation between this ratio and radio power on large scales. We interpreted these results as indicating a wider range in the scale size and the absence of a direct correlation between velocity and size in radio galaxies. Our local source stacking analysis revealed an average size of approximately 49 kpc (full width at half maximum) and a median velocity of 0.16, both in excess of previous estimates. We attributed the increase to a larger scatter in source properties, rather than an intrinsic difference with more distant sources.

We analyze the impact of waves on one-dimensional shocks in stellar explosions, specifically supernovae and stellar eruptions, and investigate how they interact with the surrounding environment. Our model accounts for the dynamic behavior of both forward and reverse shocks, as well as their effects on cooling radiative diffusion, and we discover that in environments where the wave's speed significantly exceeds the local sound speed, the wave can become an efficient source of energy for the shock, potentially leading to increased velocities and distorting the shock's profile into a double-arched structure. This relationship between waves and shocks is found to be critical in determining how hot the envelope becomes and whether a supernova blastwave can emerge from the surrounding environment, and this effect could be observed in phenomena such as SNeIb event SN 2010BH, where there is evidence of interaction between the explosion and the precursor stellar mass loss, characterized by a cooling tail in the late-time light curve.

This brief research extends a discovery made by Diamond--Sasaki, relating 
geometric modularity of non-optimal weights to arithmetic or non-arithmetic 
weights and allowing the latter to be determined by geometric modularity 
alone. We also demonstrate a novel, straightforward algorithm for 
determining whether a non-optimal weight is arithmetic or non-arithmetic 
using geometric modularity and a variety of weights that have already 
been proven to be geometrically modular. Furthermore, we provide 
geometrically motivated, straightforward criteria for identifying 
non-optimal weights that are candidates for geometric modularity.

Molecular vibrations essentially function as a macroscopic manifestation of electronic vibration interactions. Under high-speed conditions, these vibrations can diverge from their typical linear, periodic movement, instead exhibiting complex patterns as they interact with electrons in an ongoing dance. This study reveals the rapid exchange of energy between these vibrations and electrons can generate novel forms of vibration that spin multiple times within their typical periods, a phenomenon that are inaccessible through static electron-vibrational interactions. Furthermore, this exchange can alter the energy levels around these molecular vibrations, producing potential energy barriers that can influence electron flow in molecular systems and, when combined with a magnetic field, can create additional spin vibrations that could facilitate the detection of these vibrations through spin resonance.

$\tau$-tilting theory was first introduced nearly a decade ago by Adachi, Iyama, and Reiten and has since become a major area of study in the representation theory of finite-dimensional algebras. These notes have a dual purpose: to provide an approachable introduction to $\tau$-tilting theory for those with basic representation theory knowledge and to address a noticeable lack in the existing literature by bringing together key results from the field in a comprehensive overview.

Semantic variation within discourse segments poses an interesting task for NLP researchers.  We highlight the challenges of interpreting varied language across text spans using Natural Language Inference.  To tackle this, we introduce a new dataset called SemAnt that consists of annotated sections from Wikipedia articles, indicating the level of semantic variation within a text segment and providing relevant supporting evidence from the accompanying text.  Unlike other NLU tasks, SemAnt focuses on understanding the meaning of entire discourse units, considering implicit information and varying language use.  We demonstrate the difficulty of this task by achieving only 50% accuracy with strong NLU models.  Furthermore, our analyses reveal crucial insights on natural language and the challenges it presents, including the reliance on context, the role of coreference, the impact of core concepts, and the effect of discourse elements.

Automated driving safety is closely tied to advanced hazard detection capabilities.
However, developing reliable algorithms for this task has proven challenging due to
the need to collect and label extensive datasets, including scenarios where the
hazard represents a lane change risk. Current methods focusing on this situation
typically leverage two-dimensional feature extractors, which overlook crucial video
information and force the inclusion of redundant feature detectors. To address
these limitations, we propose a novel approach utilizing two parallel networks to
jointly process video frames and extract lane region masks. A spatiotemporal network
tracks hazard development across frames, while a semantic segmentation head with
a mask transfer mechanism identifies lane regions and predicts danger within one
second, allowing for partial annotation of anonymous vehicles. We validate our
method's effectiveness through experiments on a newly created dataset featuring
6000 snippets of lane change hazards, demonstrating superior performance relative
to existing benchmarks.

Theoretical models predicting the evolution of rotating low-mass stars and galaxies are based on complex and intricate physics. To test these models, we employed numerical simulations, solving the equations of hydrodynamics and heat transfer for conserved quantities. Our study specifically examined rotating low-mass stars and brown dwarfs with varying angular momentum and initial chemical compositions, observing how they evolved from protostars through contraction and accretion phases. For stars and brown dwarfs with maximum masses between 0.8 solar masses and 0.1 solar masses, our simulations explored additional stages of evolution, including main sequence, and considered possible planetary systems. Our key finding revealed that magnetic braking, a phenomenon thought to significantly slow the rotation rates of low-mass stars, may not as reliably apply to brown dwarfs due to their generally shorter contraction periods. Our simulations also provided insight into possible stellar mergers, and how remaining protostellar material can influence the properties of low-mass stars. Furthermore, we found that in scenarios involving massive grains, the flow of accreting material may be channeled by gravity, potentially diverting angular momentum to the protostar, a effect that could contribute to the slowing of rotation rates during the contraction phase. Our research offers a framework for exploring the diverse range of rotating low-mass stars and brown dwarfs that can form from protostars, and can serve as a foundation for investigating specific stellar mergers and formation pathways.

The amplitude assessment technique, widely employed in seismic data acquisition and processing to determine event characteristics, is often used with high-resolution data from oceanic laboratories. This technique leverages diverse wave types, including P, S, and surface waves, to determine the internal structure of these laboratories. The assessments are usually compared across different measurement methods, involving direct measurements and synthetic models derived from seismic data. The experimental uncertainty associated with these comparisons is typically overestimated, hiding the genuine impact of measurement errors on these assessments. This study reevaluates the uncertainty using a robust statistic that measures the deviation of individual data points from the overall trend. The results indicate that the traditional uncertainty estimates are inflated, and this study quantifies the actual impact of experimental errors on amplitude assessments.

A new comprehensive approach is proposed to model a broad category of relativistic afterglows, incorporating various external radiation components and relativistic jets with variable opening angles. Based on a broad memory framework that incorporates dynamic relations, the approach dynamically defines afterglow properties such as radiated energy, velocity, and angle. This novel framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through numerical simulations for different scenarios, including long gamma-ray bursts with neutron star mergers, supernovae, and magnetar bursts, all resulting in consistent predictions that align with observed GRB afterglows. Furthermore, this framework allows for the prediction of future observations for specific GRB afterglows.

A key concept in graph theory, vertex partitioning, has various applications such as data separation and network splitting. Research on vertex partitioning problems often focuses on identifying whether a given graph can be divided into two components where certain conditions are satisfied. In contrast, this study introduces an approximately solved version of a prominent partitioning problem, the Bipartite Vertex Splitting problem (BVS), and investigates its properties. BVS can be viewed as an optimization version of the Bipartite Vertex Separation problem (BES), for which no exact polynomial-time algorithm exists when dealing with graphs that have a polynomial degree of nism. The BVS algorithm provides a high-quality solution to BES and offers a parameterized solution to BES through a reduced instance in linear time. Furthermore, this study proves that BVS has a fixed-parameter algorithm based on its structure and introduces a new graph parameter, the BVS number, which determines the number of subsets required in a BVS solution and may be computed in time proportional to nism^2.54. The BVS algorithm shows that many previous BES algorithms can be modified to achieve a sub-exponential time complexity and a parameterized time complexity of nism^2.54, while a modified version of the algorithm achieves a time complexity of nism^1.5.

Deep neural network deployments are often hindered by their inability to adapt to changing data distributions and additional classes, particularly when dealing with skewed datasets. The task requires them to learn from a never-ending stream of data with periodically added classes, starting from limited initial information. The challenge is compounded by the need to maintain performance across previously unseen classes. In this work, a comprehensive evaluation of multiple approaches to handle data distribution changes and class imbalances in deep incremental learning tasks is presented. Following a thorough explanation of methods relevant to incremental learning, including techniques for processing streams and dealing with imbalances, eight distinct approaches are examined in simulated and real-world scenarios. The analysis reveals that addressing data distribution changes and class imbalances simultaneously yields the best results, with a notable difference in performance when comparing calibrated models to their unadjusted counterparts in all evaluated scenarios. Furthermore, our research facilitates further inquiry into methods for incremental learning, especially those involving calibration, stream processing, and handling class imbalances.

Humans have long been fascinated by the potential of robots to mimic bipedal human motion. Despite significant progress made so far, our analysis suggests that current bipedal robots fall into one of three categories: they either mimic human motion for optimal appearance, accommodate unusual environments that require resilience, or prioritize speed and stability over aesthetic considerations. In this research, we explore the idea that combining legs and a propulsive device could lead to more efficient and resilient motion in robots. Building on established two-dimensional running models and inspired by human racing techniques, we developed a novel strategy for generating efficient and resilient bipedal motion. This approach, which we call 'racing-inspired periodic asymptotic hybrid control', enables our robot to transition smoothly between different gait patterns and even adapt to unexpected obstacles during flight. Moreover, we found that our method can reduce impact peaks by up to 75% and enhance motion resilience in response to external forces.

We provide a detailed explanation of a groundbreaking concept introduced by Abbes and Sato, relating residue maps to line bundles over F-sheaves in equal characteristic zero. Our analysis expands upon the preliminary remarks made by Abbes and Sato.

Recent research demonstrating successful CPU exploitation through novel techniques, such as data-driven attacks and misprediction-based exploits, highlights the ongoing relevance of accelerating instruction execution. Building upon this knowledge, our work presents HyperDegrade, a new technique designed to accelerate CPU performance across multiple cores. By strategically manipulating memory access patterns, HyperDegrade effectively leverages shared memory to exploit shared caches across threads, leading to significant performance gains with minimal code modifications. In testing, HyperDegrade showed substantial speedup improvements, with an average increase of 5.5 times on Haswell and 3.4 times on Skylake for benchmark applications. Furthermore, our research found that HyperDegrade's performance benefits can be as high as 20 times on certain workloads. Due to its core efficiency and potential for broad coverage, HyperDegrade may have a notable impact on our understanding of modern CPU architecture.

To determine if the Higgs boson can account for the discrepancy in the muon's magnetic moment, we employed a bottom-up approach using Effective Field Theory (EFT). Our findings reveal that, given the present experimental constraints on the Higgs sector, its contribution to the anomaly could still be significant, assuming the Higgs interacts non-standardly with other particles. Based on unitarity principles, we found that a solution to the anomaly could imply the presence of New Physics at an energy scale of roughly 10-18 TeV, which could potentially be as low as 5 TeV if the Higgs' interaction with the W and Z bosons is in line with Standard Model predictions. This outcome may have the added benefit of significantly increasing the rate of di-Higgs production in future muon colliders. Ultimately, this study underscores the importance of precisely measuring the Higgs coupling to a muon and itself in forthcoming experiments.

The disintegration of unstable Higgs bosons into two particles, specifically $e^+ e^-$, $\mu^+ \mu^-$, $u \bar{u}$, $d \bar{d}$, $c \bar{c}$, and $b \bar{b}$, are used to determine the Higgs decay width as a function of the complex conjugate of the Higgs self-coupling, $\gamma$. This is based on tree-level standard model calculations and considers various assessments, including those from the LHC, low-energy experiments, and direct measurements of $\gamma$. The uncertainty associated with the disintegration width, typically denoted as $\Gamma_{\text{width}}$, is reported for each final state and, when relevant, is influenced by the degree of freedom associated with the polarization of bosons. The variability in $\gamma$'s magnitude, represented as $\gamma$, is also quantified for each final state. The impact of these widths and the associated variations on global fits are discussed, along with the potential for future LHC studies to refine the understanding of $\gamma$ through similar analyses. The latter's sensitivity to the Higgs self-coupling and the presence of top quark loops makes them particularly valuable.

A new, straightforward method has been developed for determining whether a knot is untangled. This approach, based on cross-sections of the knot, ensures the knot's invariance in both 3D space and its projected 2D form. The method can be applied to both knots in general 3D space and knots embedded in a thick tube. Additionally, it provides a basis for classifying knots according to their 2D projections, which can be used to identify whether a knot is untangled. The development of this method involves an interesting connection to a well-known untangling procedure for knots in 2D space.

We demonstrate that the collection of tropical curves with a specific semifield over a tropical semifield of characteristic one generates all possible semifields. This is comparable to how algebraic curves over an algebraically closed field generate all possible closed subsets in the projective space.

We've demonstrated that a specific long-lived integral loop, originally due to Fox and Hatcher, can be reinterpreted as a Vassiliev invariant of order three, and this connection holds across various characterizations of the loop. Additionally, we've established that this relationship remains consistent when the loop is defined through the use of chain maps from the complex of twisted n-chords to the complex of n-crossings.

New research indicates that electron anti-neutrino masses are significantly constrained to be below 1.04 eV. This strong limit has important implications for several experiments aiming to discover neutrino masses. For example, the KATRIN and CGT facilities would be able to establish neutrino mass spectra within broad ranges, potentially confirming mass-related parameters in various systems involving neutrino interactions, such as neutrinoless double beta decay and axion production mechanisms.

Nesta apresentação, exploraremos as principais técnicas empleadas para a computação de matrizes, adotando uma definição ampla de computação de matrizes que abrange a multiplicação de matrizes, transposição, inversa, solução de sistemas de equações lineares e outros operações elementares. Em seguida, focaremos na multiplicação de matrizes específica, executando cálculos elementares em uma matriz de ordem quadrada. Consideraremos as características arquitetônicas do processador e do processador gráfico, alongaremos a definição de computação de matrizes para incluir a multiplicação de matrizes com blocos e demostraremos a eficácia desse tipo de multiplicação em problemas de rede. Além disso, apresentaremos um exemplo prático de aplicação de matrizes na realidade virtual.

In collaborative robot systems with advanced computation and communication capabilities, agents can make data-based decisions in real-time to achieve optimal outcomes. However, enabling such collaboration becomes increasingly difficult as the complexity of the system increases. To address this challenge, this research develops a strategic collaboration framework that leverages simplified models for computation and communication, allowing for efficient, real-time decision-making. By transforming the complex high-dimensional problem into a set of simpler, two-dimensional problems, this framework can generate optimal, collaborative strategies quickly. Moreover, these strategies are guaranteed to perform nearly as well as the optimal outcome within a small margin of error. To evaluate this framework's performance, a demonstration is conducted in a simulated environment mimicking a conventional warehouse setting.

In this presentation, a range of theoretical concepts will be addressed through quantum field theory, specifically focusing on scalar quantum electrodynamics and effective quantum field theory with a IR-driven amplitude structure. IR-driven amplitude structures, characterized by increasing amplitude coefficients as infrared momentum increases, underpin our IR-enhanced resummation framework. This framework yields results that accurately capture quantum effects when approximating physical systems, and can be applied to both scale and asymptotic regimes. However, this approach is only viable in situations where the driving momentum scales are dominated by mass or ultralight masses. Ultraheavy mass spectra, commonly found in condensed matter and particle physics, present a significantly more complex situation. Here, IR-driven amplitude structures are muddled by high-frequency scales, necessitating a reevaluation of our IR-enhanced resummation framework to extract reliable quantum effects. A case study is made in a simple system featuring a heavy scalar meson and exploiting lattice quantum field theory calculations to validate our approach.

The growing interest in FED Learning has addressed various challenges in artificial intelligence education, including limited data, high cost, and biased datasets. This approach enables multiple institutions to contribute data and train models without sharing information. However, an attack on the education system can occur when a single institution sends misleading data in response to user queries, with the goal of compromising the privacy of users across multiple institutions. This attack can succeed even if each institution follows proper data sharing protocols. In this research, we explore three scenarios in which an attack on privacy can compromise users across multiple institutions, including scenarios with a single malicious institution and with multiple malicious institutions. To counter this type of attack, we propose a new search engine that can help reduce the risk of privacy breaches in education systems that use FED Learning. This search engine prevents an attack on privacy by asking each institution to contribute data based on how likely it is to come from a legitimate user, rather than on the content of the data itself. Our experiments show that this search engine can significantly reduce the risk of privacy breaches in education systems that use FED Learning.

Kernel-based methods, widely used in machine learning algorithms, often rely on approximate kernel functions due to large data sets. Despite the popularity of data-dependent kernel estimators, they usually fall into two inadequate categories: those that assume a specific parametric form for the underlying density and those with unreasonably high computational requirements. We introduce an innovative method for estimating kernel functions that leverages the unique characteristics of Fourier features and pseudo random measures to achieve accurate results in a reasonable time frame. The proposed technique facilitates efficient evaluation of kernel functions through the use of Fourier transformations and Monte Carlo approximations, yielding a simple and flexible framework for kernel-based algorithms. The proposed estimator is examined alongside existing alternatives in synthetic and real-world scenarios, revealing its effectiveness and utility.

This study proposes a novel approach to systematically dividing any group into precisely six distinct subgroups that fulfill specific properties. To achieve this, we first establish a key theoretical component, then leverage this foundation to develop a specific algorithm. The algorithmic outcome yields an intriguing, albeit indirect proof of a fundamental concept. Additionally, we explore practical applications of our method by examining a particular example that demonstrates its utility. Finally, we outline a clear path for future research in this area.

This research paper examines conformally smooth hypersurfaces, denoted as $M$, within the $(n+1)$-dimensional sphere, $\mathbb{S}^{n+1}$. We demonstrate that a specific intrinsic property, related to a Mobius scalar curvature called $\tau$, is invariant across all conformal variations on $M$. However, we show that this property is not sufficient to imply certain other geometric characteristics of high symmetry on $M$, particularly those involving an umbilic boundary and constant mean curvature. An alternative approach is proposed to demonstrate the uniqueness of $M$ with $\tau=0$ across the $(n+1)$-dimensional sphere when its dimension is three or more.

In congenital heart disease, surgical planning is critically dependent on pre-operative cardiac magnetic resonance imaging analysis for left and right ventricular volume estimation.  Although Deep Learning-based segmentation has proven accurate for healthy adults, its performance decreases significantly for congenital heart defects due to rare and varying morphologies.  We investigated the potential of a generic, adult-trained UNet-based segmentation model for automatic, semi-direct volume estimation in two right heart defects (TGA and TR).  By comparing its results to traditional, expert-derived methods, we found a strong correlation but also a notable scatter.  Specifically, while the estimations matched the reference values, often falling within the same range as the gold standard, there were instances where they significantly deviated.  Thus, while this approach shows promise, it is not entirely reliable and may require defect-specific training or adjustments for accurate volume estimation in clinical practice.

A pioneering perspective on damage mechanics was introduced by Biot in 1934, 
which highlighted the inherent permanence of degradation. This concept laid the 
foundational basis for later theories. Strain-based fracture models, which describe 
damage through inelastic deformation, have their roots in Biot's enduring idea. 
Gradually, these models have become prevalent in analyzing a wide range of materials 
and processes. This paper explores various strain-based fracture models, from classic 
versions applicable to concrete and rock, to more complex versions used in studying 
metallic and composite materials. It also discusses the $A$-stable numerical techniques 
necessary for simulations involving fracture models. Ultimately, this paper suggests 
that, despite significant advancements in computational techniques, the time has come to 
reconsider Biot's original perspective on damage mechanics.

A new approach to efficient power management and data transmission in multi-service wireless communication systems is proposed, utilizing a non-cooperative game. The method suggests an efficient strategy for dynamically optimizing transmission power and energy harvesting, considering interference and controllable factors, in a multi-user, multi-service scenario. The proposed algorithm resolves conflicts and finds equilibrium points, facilitating the implementation of an adaptive solution through iterative updates. Simulations demonstrate that the proposed method yields significant performance improvements over traditional time-division-based schemes.

Our proposed method, MultiItem Examiner Network (MIEN), is designed to address
the limitation of existing explanation methods, which often focus on individual
features and can miss important collective patterns. By utilizing multiple
complementary representation types, MIEN offers a novel, unified framework that
expands upon the existing LIME and TreeExplainer frameworks. In experiments,
MIEN demonstrates its superiority over these existing methods by accurately
identifying decision trees and models that are reliant on specific features.

In studying the properties of the natural conditional independence structure that arises from a given set of independent sources, a key concept proves useful in identifying the inherent features of this natural structure. This valuable insight allows us to investigate the extreme properties of the conditional independence structure's underlying graph. By employing a mathematical representation that views the natural structure as the most reliable combination of all possible conditional independence structures, we can express its extreme properties in terms of the most conditional and most independent subsets of variables. With this approach, we can demonstrate the existence of subsets that exhibit very high levels of conditionality or independence within the natural structure. Furthermore, we can establish a direct relationship between these extreme properties and the underlying sources' characteristics, specifically their independence and the strength of conditioning within the natural structure. By considering a specific example based on a small number of independent sources, we can gain a deeper understanding of the natural structure's extreme properties.

We aim to tackle the Term Sense Disambiguation (TSD) challenge, which poses a difficulty in language understanding where the same word conveys different meanings depending on the context. To approach this, we must develop efficient methods to differentiate between various interpretations of words. Given the success of BERT-based models in enhancing linguistic understanding, we explore their application in TSD through a named entity recognition and classification framework. By utilizing the GlossBERT model, which combines BERT with WordNet glosses, we find it yields the best results compared to other BERT-based models like BERT, DistilBERT and Multi-BERT in multiple scenarios. Building upon this finding, we propose enhancements to GlossBERT, referred to as Huang et al.'s GlossBERT, by fine-tuning the model for TSD. Our results indicate it achieves superior performance, surpassing the entity recognition + classification approach and the standalone entity recognition models. Furthermore, we observe Huang et al.'s GlossBERT performs optimally across various entity categorization tasks.

To grasp complex procedures, humans greatly benefit from both verbal and visual instructions. Research has shown that combining these forms of instruction can significantly improve learning outcomes compared to using just one. Yet, despite its potential, combining multimodal procedures for automated learning has not been well explored. Existing machine learning models are not designed to appreciate the value of combining instructions and often focus instead on individual components. Our proposed model, a set of joints that arrange instructional guides, successfully demonstrates the advantage of using both forms of instruction. In tests, it showed that learning from combined multimodal procedures led to better outcomes than learning from single forms alone. Furthermore, this model is capable of learning from partially labeled data, achieving near equal performance to fully labeled data without the need for additional training. Our research finds that learning from both forms of instruction is more effective than just one and offers insights into designing better automatic procedural learning systems.

In the context of random graph theory, the destruction of a graph's connectivity properties during an avalanche, driven by the deletion of random edges, marks a critical phenomenon. The study presents an initial analysis of this process for Cayley graphs, specifically examining the distribution of connective components as the avalanche progresses.

The study reveals an underlying universal property of the Airy polynomial, which is universally shared across all unitary matrix models with a specific test function. In an effort to generalize this finding, the research introduces a novel class of polynomials known as the universal Airy polynomials, which are defined through their explicit, computable roots. A direct connection is established between the universal Airy polynomials and the underlying symmetries present in unitary matrix models, specifically in scenarios where the test function exhibits a particular form. Furthermore, the analysis extends the universal Airy polynomials to a broader context, demonstrating their relevance in models involving both unitary and skew-symmetric matrices.

The detection of gravitational waves through laser interferometry has proven highly effective for low-frequency events. Nevertheless, achieving high-frequency sensitivity remains a challenge for this technique. Interferometric sensors using Sagnac and sloshing configurations have been proposed as alternatives, offering enhanced performance in the high-frequency range. Our research builds upon these concepts, proposing a hybrid sensor that combines the Sagnac and sloshing configurations. This design separates the sensing and carrier light paths, utilizing different light paths to mitigate thermal fluctuations and improve sensitivity. Model-based calculations predict that this sensor could surpass Advanced LIGO's sensitivity by 2-3 orders of magnitude at frequencies above 100 Hz. Furthermore, this design is highly scalable, making it suitable for future 3G detectors like the Einstein Telescope.

Recent research on large-scale MIMO systems has been focusing on an unconventional access approach known as XL-MIMO, which ensures non-overlapping visible areas for uplink transmission among spatially distributed single-device entities. A key aspect of this methodology is understood to be its potential to mitigate inter-user interference. However, a critical challenge emerges when implementing XL-MIMO, as determining the exact non-overlapping visible areas proves to be a computationally complex problem. To address this difficulty, researchers have proposed a novel approach based on the XL-MIMO stochastic access protocol (XL-SAP), which is capable of dynamically determining the visible areas through the coordination of base station and user terminal. Nevertheless, the existing analysis of XL-SAP is restricted to idealized channel modeling, neglecting real-world frequency variability. Furthermore, the inherent time-varying characteristics of XL-SAP are thought to undermine the system's stability. This research aims to provide an in-depth analysis of the XL-SAP system by modeling visible area changes as random processes and integrating the protocol's time-varying features into the overall system design, ultimately verifying the stability of the resulting system through rigorous mathematical proof.

Recent observations at sub-millimeter/millimeter wavelengths have revealed that the morphological characteristics of young stars' surrounding disks differ significantly from previously predicted narrow structures. In this study, the theoretical framework for disk substructures developed in a prior investigation is applied to vertical shear instability models of protoplanetary disks. By integrating this framework with computational simulations of the thermal properties of gas and solid particles, the characteristics of substructures in disks undergoing vertical shear instability are analyzed through dust continuum observations at sub-millimeter wavelengths. This research involves modeling both the thermal properties of gas and the behavior of solid particles in protoplanetary disks, accounting for the influence of vertical shear instability on disk substructures. In predicted observations of disks undergoing vertical shear instability through dust continuum analysis, features emerge that are consistent with recent experimental data, and the theoretical models accurately explain the existence of multiple substructures within a single disk. Furthermore, this study provides the basis for further understanding of disk substructures through observational analysis in protoplanetary systems.

The concept of the "Big Apple strength" is introduced, representing an exceptionally robust peak at $E_\alpha \approx 3.5$, observed in the alpha-clustering dynamics of nuclei, particularly evident in calculations using the angular momentum operator. A mathematical derivation demonstrates that this strength arises from a combination of both one-body and two-body forces within the nuclear interaction. Consequently, we suggest that the prevalence of this strong peak has a significant impact on the properties of finite nuclei and contributes to the characteristics of astronomical objects.

Using the dynamical mean-field theory, we utilized the full density of states of a lattice model to accurately represent the interactions within a solid, without relying on the approximation of a single frequency. This precise representation captures the complexities of how electrons interact at different energies. Our method involves breaking down the solid into its fundamental components and studying the individual atomic interactions within it. However, these atomic interactions are influenced by the broader electronic surroundings, which themselves result from the combination of all the atomic interactions in the solid. To resolve this, we employed a full density of states for the dynamical mean-field simulation, which is typically represented by a narrow band in the spirit of the widely accepted Gutzwiller theory. By leveraging this approach, we investigated the rotational symmetry breaking in perovskite manganese oxides, without employing the conventional weak-coupling assumption. Instead, we used a more robust method involving the one-electron spin and orbital density matrix, which is a direct outcome of using the full density of states. Our analysis suggested that the distinct weights assigned to different orbital configurations, such as t$_{2g}$ and e$_g$, play a critical roles in determining the type of antiferromagnetic ordering present in these materials. We further found that the rotational symmetry breaking in these compounds is primarily driven by the hybridizations between different orbitals, such that the energy gained from these combinations outweighs the energy lost due to the coupling between electrons. Our study is relevant to the understanding of complex electronic

This research proposes a technique to create robust M{\o}lmer-S{\o}rensen gates in trapped ions using balanced combinations of multiple motional modes. By leveraging the Chirality theorem, achieving this stability requires significantly less laser power than traditional methods. For a minimal number of motional modes, a gate angle of $4\pi$ can be achieved with a high-fidelity approximation, surpassing the optimal efficiency of the four-dimensional gate, often cited as the optimal configuration. This method exhibits internal resilience, where a gate error resulting from an unstable frequency translation can be transformed into an over-rotation in the steady state. Consequently, this technique offers a higher potential for maximizing gate fidelity through optical pumping, ultimately facilitating the execution of not-ALL-ON operations required for quantum error correction.

Using advanced x-ray diffraction techniques, a detailed microscopic picture of the paraelectric phase in perovskite materials has been lacking due to the necessity of modeling dynamic atomic arrangements. This study combines state-of-the-art neutron scattering and molecular dynamics simulations to provide a precise, atomically-resolved description of the polarizations and force fields within the paraelectric phase of a specific perovskite, leading the way for accurate electrostatic modeling in future investigations.

Lately, researchers have focused intensely on solid-state materials with exceptional, discrete band crossings, which are utilized in topological insulator and superconductor applications. Although the zone center crossings in these materials are well-described by a five-dimensional representation from the $Sp(2)$ group, the underlying causes of these crossings remain poorly understood. This study on TaAs$_2$ reveals that the unique, three-dimensional crossings in this material can be connected, forming long, thin tubes around the $\Gamma$ point in momentum space. Furthermore, the unusual, quasi-one-dimensional crossings in this material can be linked to a two-dimensional surface with a high symmetry point, specifically the edge of a hole pocket. Our theoretical framework demonstrates that the discrete, crossing points in momentum space can be linked to a two-dimensional surface with a high symmetry point, specifically the edge of a hole pocket. Our results also show that the unusual, quasi-one-dimensional crossings in this material can be linked to a two-dimensional surface with a high symmetry point, specifically the edge of a hole pocket. Our findings provide the basis for experimenting with light-pulse, spin-orbit coupled systems and superconductivity mediated by fermion-fermion interactions in this material.

When dealing with dynamic time series that fluctuate based on multiple rhythmic components, as seen in various physiological signals and economic time series, identifying the primary periodic patterns can be a challenge. This issue is compounded by the presence of intertwined periodicities, whether they are in a whole number ratio relationship or not. The proposed framework for bimodal frequency and ratio assessment addresses these difficulties. It utilizes a data-driven approach to determine the optimal window size, number of components, embedding delay, and dimensionality reduction diameter. The framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through the analysis of simulated data featuring close and distant frequency ratios, as well as actual physiological signals. The resulting code and methodology provide a practical solution for the complex problem of frequency ratio identification.

We examined the NA62 experiment's capability to detect a neutral lepton of mass less than 125 MeV, generated in the $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$ decay, using data collected from 2015 to 2018. By simulating NA62's detection process and accounting for potential sources of background, we found the anticipated sensitivity to be around $10^{-7}$ for a branching ratio of $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$, with the exception of the $K^0$ contamination, which significantly limits the signal at higher neutrino energies. Furthermore, we discovered that integrating the signal over the full energy range yields a less stringent NA62 sensitivity of around $2\times 10^{-6}$, still an order of magnitude more sensitive than previous studies.

In a Galilean frame, light moves at a constant speed of one foot per second squared. When light travels in opposite directions within a Sagnac interferometer at a speed of one foot per second, twenty-five feet per second squared is observed. Additionally, light exhibits unequal maximum speeds in three different directions within the same frame. These irregularities, which we term "spectral shift anomalies," occur because light's speed varies based on direction. As a result, light experiences unequal frequencies of vibration. Consequently, light's vibrational frequency is influenced not only by the speed of light but also by the Sagnac effect, which relates to the interference pattern that light produces as it travels in a loop. This complex interplay results in the unusual spectral shift anomalies we identified, which have significant implications for our understanding of optics within Sagnac interferometers.

Let's consider a semisimple and simply connected algebraic group $G$ over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. For our purposes, we're particularly interested in the case when $G$ has a rank of three dimensions. By drawing inspiration from the methods used in paper arXiv:1811.10347, specifically the section 2.2, we can define the parabolic adjoint operation $\mathscr{Y}$ as a map that takes an irreducible representation $\pi$ to another representation $\mathscr{Y}(\pi)$. With this in mind, we can establish that $\mathscr{Y}$ is an automorphism when acting on the category of irreducible representations that are generated by the line bundle $\mathcal{O}(dK)$, for a positive integer $d$. Here, $K$ denotes the maximal torus of $G$. By exploring the properties of $\mathscr{Y}$, we can identify a relationship between the Weierstrass segments of $\pi$ and the nilpotent fibre of $\mathscr{Y}(\pi)$. Ultimately, we provide a comprehensive description of $\mathscr{Y}(\pi)$ by considering its nilpotent fibre and Weierstrass segments.

Neural language models have largely surpassed $N$-gram models due to better performance but are often more complicated to understand. Recent work attempting to merge both concepts faced a significant challenge: effectively integrating the two models. In our research, we take a simpler approach, combining a neural language model with an $n$-gram resin learnable through backpropagation. Our results show that this straightforward method yields a significant improvement in predictive accuracy in both unsupervised and supervised tasks. Furthermore, our proposed model exhibits better performance on multiple evaluation metrics and is less prone to overfitting due to its sparse representation. Our approach not only offers a clear insight into neural language models but also provides a more compact and more readable semantic structure of language. Our code and data are available for download at https://github.com/ghrua/NgramRes.

We take a $\mathbb{Q}$-factorial, non-toric d-dimensional variety with a singular point of type ADE and address the question of whether it can be expressed as the transformation of a smooth, affine space under the Laurent transformation. We provide a positive answer for varieties with a singular point of type ADE near the origin in a one-to-one correspondence with the Fibonacci numbers.
