The flow of viscoelastic fluids through narrow channels exhibits distinct patterns of injection, which can either mimic that of Newtonian fluids or contradict it. Depending on polymer incompatibility, two types of behavior are observed - either the peak of the slug advances at a rate comparable to that of Newtonian fluids, or it moves at a rate significantly slower. Conditions that favor strong polymer-polymer interactions, such as low shear rates and temperature increases, are found to prolong the peak of the slug and accelerate the tail. Furthermore, numerical analysis reveals that these trends are unaffected by channel length or the presence of diverging or converging sections.

A positive label for a specific instance can comprise multiple specific classifications. For example, the label "birds seen during winter migration" can encompass various winter bird migrations. Conversely, the label "summer birds" can pertain to distinct sets of instances. Our research focuses on leveraging annotated data characterized by multiple classifications to effectively utilize them as individual instances. This is achieved by employing a learning algorithm that can utilize both annotated data and unannotated instance data. The goal of this study is to investigate the efficacy of various combination methods for handling multi-label instances and to introduce an optimized approach that integrates both annotated data and unannotated instance data. Our proposed method is evaluated through experiments utilizing real-world datasets, and the results demonstrate its superiority over existing techniques. Furthermore, our study reveals that the most critical factor in modeling multi-label instances is the relationship between instance classifications and the underlying data structure.

This article addresses the issue of J.N. Colton's and P.C. Lasko's limitation proof for the finite energy possessed by the solution of the Cahn-Hilliard equation at infinite time. We initially transform the time-irreversibility-embedded Cahn-Hilliard equation into an equivalent variant of the phase-field equation accompanied by a Hamiltonian system. Subsequent to establishing the conservation of the total energy, we employ the sharp regularized version of the transport map to derive a novel formula estimating the squared $H^{-1}$ norm of the solution's spatial component. This formulation serves as the basis for demonstrating the upper bound of the total energy, which however only yields a nonsharper estimate. We subsequently leverage the properties of the transport map and the Hamiltonian system to improve the estimate, resulting in an explicitly definable dimensionless parameter governing the upper bound of the total energy. Moreover, we prove that this dimensionless parameter diminishes over time, entailing that the upper bound of the total energy also declines, i.e., $\mathcal{E}(t) \leq \mathcal{E}(0)$. In the course of the proof, we employ the sharp regularized version of the transport map to derive novel formulations estimating the norms of the solution's spatial and time-fractal components, respectively. Ultimately, we validate the proposed method through numerical simulations.

The GNS construction forms a correspondence between abstract collections of physical observables and corresponding physical states within a Hilbert space. This process essentially amounts to a reverse operation to obtain the physical system described by those states. In our research, we identify the underlying mathematical structure that captures the essence of the GNS construction and its inverse. This underlying structure is represented by an abstract correspondence between collections of physical configurations (which include measurements as a special case) and resulting physical states. We then demonstrate that this abstract correspondence endows the category of physical configurations with a specific category-theoretic property, and this property is reflective of the fundamental nature of physical configurations as comprising both classical and quantum aspects. Furthermore, we find that this property is closely related to another category-theoretic property, which in turn is connected to the category-theoretic concept of compactness, which has implications for the theoretical constraints on the possible physical configurations and resulting states within a physical system.

The capture of magnetic fields in the disks of nearby active galaxies has been observed to vary significantly, and understanding these differences is key to identifying the hadronic origin of extremely high-energy gamma-rays. Through a statistical analysis of 13 nearby AGNs, we discovered a strong link between gamma-rays in the ultra-high energy range and the strength of the magnetic field in their disks. Specifically, there was a clear correlation between the energy of the most energetic gamma-ray and the exergy of the magnetic field, with an excess of gamma-rays above 100 EeV once the magnetic capture in these disks exceeds a certain threshold. Furthermore, we found that the most energetic gamma-rays are likely caused by interactions between extremely high-energy cosmic-rays and the magnetic fields in these disks, with a density that is surprisingly close to the density required to stabilize the motion of stars and gas in these systems. This discovery has significant implications for identifying the sources of gamma-rays in the universe, and it may be possible to use the capture of magnetic fields as an indicator of the hadronic activity in these systems.

Economists often use time-series methods to analyze the average returns of portfolios as they cross-sectionally vary over time. In contrast, our research reveals that the standard deviation of portfolio yields across the cross-section is significantly higher than previously estimated, with a particularly notable spike at the equity risk premium edge. This finding is robust to different specifications, methods, and datasets. Furthermore, our study shows that models incorporating risk premia into the cross-section accurately capture the portfolio yield dispersion, whereas those that do not, such as the capital asset pricing model, are less effective and only explain a small part of the variation in portfolio yields. In addition, our research indicates that models focusing on the time-series component of returns, such as Fama-Duncan, explain portfolio yield dispersion more effectively than those that do not, and incorporating the cross-sectional component enhances real-world applicability.

Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and mobile devices can easily incorporate machine learning to automate this process using heart sound recordings obtained through devices attached to patients' bodies. However, such recordings are often contaminated by background noises and the physical attachment may cause irregularities in the recordings. Currently available approaches focus on filtering out noise and normalizing recordings, but they fail to address the inherent acoustic irregularities, which can lead to system performance being sensitive to data variations. Recent studies have explored using convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for automated heart sound classification. This study builds upon recent findings by (1) utilizing frequency-based filters to analyze recordings in different frequency ranges, (2) employing a data preprocessing technique called cepstral polishing to remove noise and normalize recordings, (3) incorporating spectral features along with time and frequency domain characteristics of recordings, and (4) conducting multiple experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach on a widely used dataset, with the goal of developing a robust system that can provide accurate classifications even in the presence of noise and irregularities.

The rapid growth of wearable devices and healthcare apps necessitates a flexible data sharing framework that maintains user privacy while enabling secure data analysis. In response, a federated learning approach has been proposed to process user data locally while transferring aggregated model results. However, implementing FL in healthcare is complicated by varying data formats, labeling requirements, and security constraints across different institutions. To address these challenges, we present FedHealth, a federated transfer knowledge structure that enables the development of predictive healthcare models for wearable data. FedHealth accommodates diverse data inputs, automates labeling through data simulation, and incorporates encryption modules to ensure secure and compliant data processing. Furthermore, FedHealth boasts scalable design principles, enabling easy integration with multiple healthcare institutions while minimizing computational costs. Experimental evaluations demonstrate FedHealth's effectiveness in developing accurate and generalized predictive models, even with limited labeled data.

This study explores various methods for optimizing portfolio performance based on higher-order moments. Initially, we discuss existing theories and models that incorporate risks beyond the second order, before delving into specific techniques to manage skewness and kurtosis. Next, we examine methods for estimating moment-based portfolio performance and associated risks. Finally, we review different portfolio optimization algorithms that take into account risks higher than the second order.

In stringy brane scenarios, the primary challenge lies in the brane worldvolume description diverging at a specific high-energy scale, closely mirroring the problems posed by the coincidence issue in string theory. To illustrate this, consider a simple scalar field living within the bulk, where its worldvolume action leads to a divergent self-energy calculation when using the brane's effective gravity field. This difficulty is shown to be avoided when this field is confined to a thin brane, demonstrating that the choice of brane description is crucial. Furthermore, we address the concern that gravitational waves might propagate within the bulk by showing that their worldvolume action yields a finite action when using the brane's induced gravity field. Consequently, particles with masses below a certain threshold, dictated by the brane's curvature radius, will exhibit gravitational wave interactions similar to those in the full bulk volume. In contrast, heavy particles will experience different gravitational wave interactions. This dual behavior is displayed through one-loop diagrams of a scalar self-interacting both within the bulk and on a thin brane.

The increasing complexity of modern software systems necessitates the use of
automated tools to manage and update their underlying infrastructure. However, as
these systems evolve, unexpected issues and vulnerabilities often arise, often
requiring sophisticated technical skills to rectify. Against this backdrop, our
research aims to facilitate the automated management of software platforms by
integrating two key areas of expertise: programmable network infrastructure and
software deployment technologies. Our proposed framework leverages these areas
of research to automate the management of software applications across distributed
systems, utilizing a range of low-level network protocols and data formats. This
approach not only streamlines software deployment but also enables automated
 detection and repair of common software errors, notably memory-related issues,
and accommodates flexible, fine-grained access control systems. Our research is
primarily focused on enhancing the security and performance of software systems,
with a particular emphasis on web applications and network services.

This study explores a complex control issue where costs fluctuate frequently but remain observable, with the goal of maintaining the sum of these costs below a predetermined limit. If the costs start at non-positive levels, the optimal strategy involves interrupting the system at specific, potentially unobservable moments to minimize the total expense. Key findings include the indifference of optimal policies to the system's internal structure, the inevitability of system interruptions, and the impossibility of devising a universally effective stopping time. Furthermore, we identify the optimal stopping time as the earliest opportunity to alter the system's behavior while minimizing its overall cost.

We investigate the production of a single leptoquark (LQ) or a pair of leptoquarks in proton-proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). To achieve detectability with existing data or near-future upgrades, we focus on uneven LQ creation, where one is produced and the other is antiparticle. This process is related to the even creation of two LQs but is generally more challenging to observe due to increased background or because certain identities require specific, difficult-to-meet conditions for even production. Nevertheless, certain uneven LQ creation processes correspond to prominent, hard-to-misinterpret signatures, such as a top quark and an electron plus large missing energy, for certain leptoquark representations and certain large scalar sectors. We explore these cases' production rates and necessary cross-sections to create an excess over standard model predictions with a 95% confidence level, using two popular leptoquark models as our primary examples. We also provide relevant theoretical background on leptoquark properties and our choice of production models before delving into our findings.

Temporal sequence prediction is a complex task when dealing with time series that are both short and high-dimensional, as is the case with microarray expression profiles obtained from various life science experiments, like single-cell experiments or plant organ profiling.  This task becomes even more challenging when the training data includes anomalous samples that vary significantly from the main data set.  Current deep learning approaches typically focus on lengthy sequences, often neglecting their potential to handle high-dimensional data.  In contrast, our novel framework, monitoringTree2Vec, leverages tree-based representations and recurrent neural networks to process temporal series of any length and learn from limited, high-dimensional data that may contain outliers.  By utilizing a monitoring mechanism, this model can detect and focus on predictive patterns during the early stages of a time series.  We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through enhanced benchmark results on the DREAM challenge, achieving superior performance when comparing predicted values to actual measurements.  Furthermore, monitoringTree2Vec excels in modeling real-world life science data, as seen with single-cell expression data, surpassing traditional methods in accuracy and user-friendliness.

Quantifying the excitation of the CI lines in molecular gas reservoirs around galaxies is a crucial step in understanding their physical properties. By calculating the relative intensity of the CI fine structure lines, we explore the relationship between this quantity and the relative intensity of the CO isotopologues. These ratios indicate that the CI lines are generally subthermalized, especially in larger galaxies. This phenomenon may be associated with non-liner radiative transfer effects or gas turbulence. The implications of our findings on the determination of molecular gas masses are examined, suggesting that using CO as a proxy may introduce significant errors (up to a factor of >10) in some galaxy environments. Furthermore, we propose a method for directly inferring the radiation field strength from the CI line ratio, which could enhance the precision of gas mass calculations.

We analyze the consequences of a universal vectorlike compositeness scale appearing in both K and B meson systems. By assuming that a natural, same-order effect is at play, we find that a parameter range can be identified which satisfactorily explains the anomalies seen in K and B meson analyses within the same framework, without invoking any new physics beyond a specific scale. Additionally, we investigate the implications of this interpretation on global K^0-S^0 mixing and find that it does not significantly impact this process's parameters. However, it does result in a minor discrepancy that could be as large as 10^-10 years in \Delta \Gamma_{K^0-S^0}.

This research investigates the problem of reconstructing the original sequence of objects from a set, based on observations made at equal distance thresholds from the actual sequence. The focus is on the Hamming divergence metric and its implications for exact and approximate sequence reconstruction. Key insights into this problem are gained through an analysis of its mathematical underpinnings. A new approach to solving it is also presented, along with a comparison of its effectiveness to existing strategies.

This research focuses on identifying musical devices within an audio recording using a novel approach that leverages a unique hierarchy in three ways. Initially, our proposed model incorporates a multi-stage, hierarchical structure where audio inputs are progressively analyzed through nested layers of frequency filtering. This leads to improved performance by combining wide-band feature extraction with targeted device identification. Secondly, we organize musical devices into categories based on their sound production methods, incorporating this organizational framework into our training process to facilitate shared knowledge learning between related devices. Thirdly, our device recognition system utilizes a hierarchical classification system, where audio inputs are classified according to their perceived sound characteristics at a higher level, and then refined through additional detailed features at a lower level. Our experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on the MUSAN dataset for both single-shot and few-shot scenarios.

In our experience teaching advanced undergraduate and graduate students in various subjects, we've found that many struggle with critical aspects of research, including formulating their own concepts and drawing meaningful comparisons between different findings. Despite being integral skills for any future researcher or technology expert, they are not typically covered in standard coursework. As a result, we've created a novel approach to education that addresses these shortcomings, centered around a unique type of question-and-answer format known as Knowledge Anchors. Each Knowledge Anchor consists of a question posed by a student, a corresponding answer provided by an expert, and a supporting research article. Over time, this collection has grown to encompass over 100 distinct topics, spanning multiple subjects and providing a diverse range of inquiries and insights. In our assessment, we've observed significant improvements in research skills among students who have interacted with these Knowledge Anchors, as evidenced by more comprehensive and nuanced project submissions that accurately apply conceptual knowledge and draw informed comparisons between different findings.

The comprehensive investigation of merging binary black hole and neutron star systems through pulsar timing arrays relies on accurate computations of gravitational waves in the millihertz band. This study focuses on merging binary systems with initial orbital eccentricities, as their effects on gravitational waves are normally disregarded due to post-Newtonian constraints. However, this research demonstrates that pulsar timing arrays can potentially discern the eccentricity of such systems by considering how their orbits evolve over time. The computation of gravitational waves from merging eccentric binaries is complex, but it has been broken down into manageable components for faster processing. Two fast methods have been developed to efficiently calculate these gravitational waves: a simplified approach that overlooks post-Newtonian nuances and a more precise alternative that maintains post-Newtonian accuracy. The limitations of these fast methods were assessed to facilitate their integration into global pulsar timing array data sets.

The ASEP velocity process is an end-to-end velocity measurement method developed for analyzing ASEP systems with initial data represented by discrete functions. This velocity procedure was initially introduced in a 2019 article by C. Cotter for single-step transitions in ASEP, and it has since been broadened to cover multiple step transitions by D. Berciu. A key advantage of end-to-end velocity estimates is their accuracy even when starting data exhibit correlated values. A recent study by D. Berciu demonstrates that these velocity estimates can be represented by a deterministic system that mirrors the ASEP system's behavior. However, the relationship between the ASEP velocity procedure and standard discrete velocity methods has yet to be explored. In this research, we compare the ASEP velocity procedure to standard discrete velocity methods in their ability to estimate velocity values. A new, faster-converging estimator is introduced as a result of this comparison, and this new estimator is put to the test using sample data.

This study examines various mathematical frameworks used to analyze epidemic outbreaks, ultimately applying these concepts to the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic. As governments make critical decisions based on epidemic data, it is essential to understand the underlying models that predict disease spread. We evaluate and contrast SEIR-based models, before modeling the SARS-CoV-2 epidemic using an SEIR framework, with reference to publicly available epidemic data. Our analysis explores the effects of non-pharmaceutical interventions on disease spread, and forecasts the pandemic's progression in regions where data is readily available.

The proposed experiment involves a search for the primary signature of a particular type of particle, called the Majorana antilepton, which is hypothesized to have only a single spin component along a specific direction in space. 

If found, the Majorana particle would exhibit peculiar properties. It wouldn't display the expected behavior in certain experiments and, in some situations, its interaction with light would differ from predictions made under alternative theoretical frameworks. 

Additionally, the existence of the Majorana particle would imply that neutrinos possess a particular quality, making them compatible with a specific theoretical framework that aligns with some, though not all, experimental findings. 

In the context of this search, the Majorana particle is assumed to have a mass within a particular range and be part of a group of particles that are generated in a manner that is, in some aspects, similar to that which produces charged leptons. 

The proposed experiment involves the examination of energy spectra resulting from the decay of particles that are produced in a specific way, involving the conversion of a particular type of energy into energy carried by light. 

The search will be conducted by analyzing energy spectra at two distinct levels, based on the relationship between energy carried by light and the energy carried by the particle that is converted.

Acronyms and abbreviations serve as shorthand expressions for lengthy names, commonly encountered in diverse fields including business, science, technology, and social contexts. While they expedite communication by conveying a lot of information quickly, they also pose challenges in everyday interactions. Many people face difficulties in determining whether a stranger has heard the intended expansion of an acronym or not. Furthermore, they may struggle to clarify the meaning of an acronym when there are multiple possible interpretations. To address these issues, we introduce MadDog, an innovative online platform that utilizes machine learning to identify unseen acronyms and provide their definitions. Additionally, the platform offers context-specific explanations for ambiguous acronyms, catering to a broad spectrum of subjects and knowledge. By offering this functionality, MadDog aims to enhance human-machine interactions and facilitate more effective communication.

We analyze a scenario in which an ultracold atomic gas of spinor character is considered, featuring two interacting components with antipodal properties. By applying a laser pulse, we investigate how this system transitions from particles to correlated molecular states, studying various quantum spin states within this transformation. A $N$-body recombination process is identified, allowing for the efficient production of spin-polarized molecules directly from particle initial conditions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that laser phase and intensity may be adjusted to preferentially create specific $N$-body molecular configurations.

As genomic data continues to grow, using DNA for long-term and low-cost storage is becoming more practical.  While previous studies have focused on developing efficient methods for writing and reading DNA data, they neglected the inevitable process of updating stored information in DNA.  In our research, we introduce an existing sequencing technology to assist with reading DNA data and identify two challenging problems that arise during data update operations.  First, as the cost of sequential reading being much lower than individual read operations creates a motivation to pack multiple stored data into one continuous sequence.  However, this contiguity constraint poses a problem for updating data stored in non-contiguous sequences.  Second, as the size of stored data may vary, updating stored blocks of sequential data requires dealing with empty or unused storage spaces.  To address these issues, we propose a hierarchical structure consisting of two levels, along with two update protocols that leverage this structure to efficiently update stored data, thereby enhancing the viability of using DNA for data storage.

Topological insulators exhibit unique properties at momentum space nodes in their energy spectrum, where conical singularities occur and are characterized by opposite topological numbers at the two adjacent nodes. The separation between these nodes is made possible by symmetry constraints and specific momentum space energies. Notably, nodal lines, which can be thought of as extending the concept of nodal points in real space to momentum space, also display intriguing topological characteristics. Recent advancements in optical systems, specifically topological photonic crystals and metamaterials, have successfully realized topological phases with nodal lines or points within specific frequency ranges, often referred to as energy spectra. These implementations demonstrate the potential of optical systems to host topological phenomena and may enable the development of novel optical devices, taking advantage of the unique properties associated with these momentum space singularities.

A complex medical issue such as brain tumor diagnosis requires precise image analysis. The challenge stems from varied tumor presentations, unpredictable locations, and distinct types (e.g., meningioma, glioma, pituitary tumor). The task of tumor segmentation and type classification from unannotated MRI images is complex due to the presence of unnecessary image regions, poor contrast between tumors and surrounding tissues, and required consideration of tumor morphology for accurate classification. Current deep learning approaches often overlook the relationship between image features and ignore the classification aspect. In response, we present a novel multi-task focus directed network that automatically discovers relevant image features for tumor segmentation and uses learned feature extraction for classification. The model is trained on the BrainMRI dataset, and experiments show improved performance on both segmentation and classification when using our proposed network. The results demonstrate state-of-the-art accuracy of 87.1% for tumor segmentation and 93.75% for classification.

Renderers employ various techniques like ray tracing and accelerated graphics to efficiently generate high-quality images. However, calculating real scene shading is crucial for solving inverse problems in fields like computer vision, photogrammetry, and computer tomography. These problems involve determining scene geometry, shading, and other characteristics from image data. Differentiation is also essential for these applications, as it enables the use of gradient-based optimization methods. Until now, differentiating traditional rendering algorithms has been challenging due to their ad-hoc nature. We introduce a novel approach that differentiates fully retains the speed of optimized renderers, allowing for efficient inverse calculations in their applications. In particular, our approach accelerates light source counting, shading estimation, and scene reconstruction. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method for identifying occluded objects, recovering scene geometry and shading, and estimating material parameters in optical imaging. Furthermore, we show that our differentiable system yields significant performance improvements in forward problems. We also contribute an open-source Python framework that supports multiple unstructured lighting models and can be used with various optimized renderers.

Due to the prevalence of interlaced video capture methods, deinterlacing techniques are necessary to recreate full-frame videos from captured interlaced footage. Unlike static images, video deinterlacing techniques must account for temporal dependencies to produce realistic video. Existing approaches often focus on enhancing individual frames but neglect the need for consistent temporal coherence. In contrast, our proposed framework leverages convolutional neural networks to produce high-quality deinterlacing across multiple frames in real-time, ensuring both spatial and temporal coherence. Comprehensive testing on various datasets demonstrates that our method achieves superior results compared to state-of-the-art techniques and is particularly effective at handling video sequences captured by low-cost handheld devices.

Theoretical studies of neutron halo structures face specific challenges which arise from the inherent limitations of many-body approaches. Utilizing the relativistic mean field model and a single-particle width of about 1 MeV, a global relation was established which relates the square radius of the neutron distribution to the volume of the neutron cavity. This relation holds true for both relativistic and non-relativistic mean field theories. Notably, the neutron density at the edge is significantly softer in the relativistic mean field model. Consequently, the distinction between neutron skin and neutron halo states becomes blurred in the relativistic mean field model. Nevertheless, the established relation may serve as a useful guide for experimental efforts in identifying neutron halo states.

Precise and timely flood prediction is crucial for saving lives and minimizing economic losses, which can be achieved through the efficient solution of the shallow water equations (SWEs). By leveraging graphics processing units (GPUs), this paper introduces a novel deep learning approach called RapidSWE, which facilitates rapid flood risk assessment by delivering partial solutions to the SWEs within minutes. Although most current deep learning methods for solving PDEs are limited to oscillation-prone solutions when approximating smooth functions, RapidSWE overcomes this limitation by utilizing a unique multi-resolution technique that accurately captures the floodfront. Verified by comparing with the traditional finite volume method (FVM), RapidSWE demonstrates equally competitive precision while boasting a 10,000-fold increase in computational efficiency on modern GPUs. Furthermore, RapidSWE's skillful assessment of flood risk is successfully validated through applications involving realistic terrain and high-flow rates.

HDR photography combines multiple photos captured at various exposure levels.
This technique is typically employed to counterbalance digital cameras' limited dynamic
range. For smartphone users, taking HDR photos is complicated due to the strict sequence
requirements for taking photos at different exposure levels, which usually involves
obtaining permission from the device owner. To circumvent this issue, this study proposes
taking just two photos with adjustable exposure - one with the standard smartphone
exposure and one that is overexposed by two stops. It demonstrates that this approach
yields equivalent or superior results to traditional HDR methods.
Furthermore, high-quality images can be achieved by fusing the standard photo with the
overexposed photo taken through a mobile smartphone. This method is referred to as
samsung-like fusion. It is compared with other fusion methods and the results show
improvement in its visual distortion and preservation of bright areas.
Additionally, this study introduces an optimized algorithm for overexposed photo
capture, which can be applied to full-resolution photos. It also explores various fusion
methods, considering factors such as ease of implementation and aesthetic appeal.
Finally, the study concludes with potential applications and potential challenges for the
proposed method.

Recent advancements in distributional learning and neural network technology have paved the way for significant breakthroughs in several challenging problems, notably in classification tasks driven by vast amounts of unlabelled data and complex, poorly defined categories. Studies on confounding variables, essential for accurately predicting individual outcomes from observational data, have emerged as a critical aspect of causal analysis. This topic is closely related to the concept of causal neural learning, which involves using neural networks to estimate individual treatment effects from observational data. We explore key challenges associated with this technique, including the need to select an appropriate loss function and network architecture. We examine existing methods and demonstrate the effectiveness of a new approach, involving the use of a score-based loss function and a carefully designed neural network architecture, in predicting individual treatment effects. We showcase this method's versatility by successfully applying it to two distinct dataset configurations, thereby contributing to the ongoing dialogue on causal neural learning challenges.

Achieving uniform heating within gas-solid beds is crucial for maximizing the efficiency of thermal processes, but however, temperature distributions within these systems are often non-uniform due to fluid dynamics and particle layer thickness varying across different locations. This study employs rapid magnetic resonance imaging in conjunction with gas chromatography to investigate temperature and concentration distributions within a stationary gas-solid bed for two different particle sizes, with results indicating greater uniformity of temperature and concentration distributions for finer particle sizes. Furthermore, temperature increases linearly with the concentration of the warm gas stream, indicating a useful measurement for temperature mapping. For both particle sizes, temperature and concentration distributions display similar patterns of variation, with distinct minima and maxima appearing at specific distances from the inlet. These findings provide valuable insights for optimizing the design of gas-solid beds to promote uniform heating.

This note provides an initial overview of the $b\p$-principle, specifically focusing on its applications within the context of the Mumford conjecture. Additionally, we offer a draft of a chapter that could serve as a starting point for further discussion.

The linear stability assessment, a crucial tool for identifying potential for cardiac mechanical dysfunction, is inherently limited by its own inelastic nature. Despite this, it remains widely employed in the medical and scientific communities for predicting structural changes in cardiac muscles. In contrast to traditional direct methods, the assessment of nonlinear cardiac mechanical behavior using projection methods like the preconditioned conjugate gradient is more feasible due to their low computational cost. Recently, ALBERT and CONDA have been proposed as nonlinear alternatives to determining cardiac mechanical dysfunction, specifically in cases of increased left ventricular loading. In this study, we examine the relationship between these new methods and the established assessment techniques. By utilizing the underlying bridges that connect them, we can leverage their scalable forms that account for cardiac muscle's anisotropic properties. We then investigate the effects of varying structural properties on cardiac behavior, highlighting the importance of accurately modeling cardiac muscle anisotropy. Furthermore, we observe that both new and established methods share a common framework, which facilitates a direct comparison of their outcomes. Through this comparison, we can identify the critical factors that influence cardiac mechanical behavior, including anisotropy and nonlinearity. Finally, we provide a quantitative analysis of the relationships between these factors and cardiac health, demonstrating the significance of accurately modeling cardiac muscle anisotropy.

This research examines a special type of random matrix known as the scale-invariant noncentral covariance matrix, which arises in statistical contexts and certain data analysis problems. The matrix in question has a specific covariance structure resulting from the properties of its entry generation process. Its off-diagonal elements follow a specific pattern due to the scale invariance condition. A key observation about this matrix is that it allows for a factorization that reveals connections to standard random matrix models. Specifically, we investigate the largest and second-largest eigenvalue parameters of this matrix and establish conditions under which they converge to fixed values or grow together, given certain moment constraints on the underlying data. These results cover a broader range of scenarios than previously established connections between noncentral covariance matrices and free unitary invariant matrices.

Convincing video generation, a relatively recent advancement in AI, has seen significant growth in the last decade. Although related fields like image creation and video processing have a long history, recent breakthroughs in deep learning and signal processing have paved the way for the development of convincing video technology. From basic methods producing one frame at a time, to more complex techniques creating a full video, researchers have explored various approaches like learning from vast video datasets, extracting motion information, and leveraging neural networks. Nonetheless, producing high-quality, realistic video across various topics and lengths remains a challenging task. Unlike other AI applications like classification and recognition, which rely heavily on accuracy, video generation prioritizes aesthetic appeal and overall impact over pure precision. As a result, evaluating AI-generated video is more complex, involving both subjective and objective assessments. Interestingly, recent studies indicate neural network-based evaluation methods can rival, if not surpass, traditional approaches. With potential applications across entertainment, education, and marketing, convincing video generation is poised to become an increasingly influential AI technology.

The integration of mobile devices and the widespread use of mobile apps have created significant opportunities for businesses to gather extensive mobile operation data, fueling the growth of mobile protection services as a whole. Despite the rise of these services, determining the effectiveness of mobile protection systems remains a challenging problem due to their complex nature. In recent years, researchers have employed various methods to evaluate the security of mobile apps, but their work has been limited to surface-level analyses, focusing on the detection of well-known threats rather than the overall risk associated with using the apps. In contrast, our research takes a more comprehensive approach, incorporating both established and machine learning-based threat detection frameworks to provide a thorough assessment of mobile apps and the false sense of security they can create for users. In particular, we investigated 200 official mobile app protection reports from the top five most popular operating systems and identified key indicators of insecure data storage and transmission practices, which are the primary sources of security risks associated with mobile apps. Furthermore, we propose a novel security risk scoring framework that leverages a wide range of data storage and transmission-related features to evaluate the severity of security threats posed by mobile apps. In addition to its unique features, our framework is unique in its use of a wide range of data storage and transmission-related features to evaluate the severity of security threats posed by mobile apps. Recently, proposed bianisotropic acoustic metagratings offer promising possibilities for passive acoustic wave manipulation, notably in flat acoustic lenses and ultra-high frequency ultrasound imaging. This concept, however, has not yet been implemented at high frequencies due to ongoing technical challenges in fabricating complex nanostructures. Advances in two-photon polymerization now enable precise, nanoscale construction. However, shrinking unit cell sizes cause periodic structures to behave differently than expected, rendering traditional design methods ineffective. This research introduces an unconventional design approach utilizing the natural occurrence of points with negative refractive behavior in microstructured media to create acoustic metagratings that operate at extremely high frequencies. It demonstrates the potential of this method by creating a high-frequency acoustic metagrating through two-photon polymerization, achieving a 2.3 GHz transmission spectrum after validation with numerical modeling and acoustic experiments showing complete ultrasound transmission at 5.7 GHz.

This research seeks to provide a stochastic framework for modeling fractional diffusion within heterogeneous media, focusing particularly on space-dependent fractional anomalies. The model's underlying structure consists of a broad class of stochastic conductivities, characterized by their mean and variance. A specific conductivity model is then established, based on the concept of fractional anisotropy. Next, fractional diffusion equations are formulated under different scaling conditions, with corresponding scalar and matrix-based approaches. Ultimately, our study demonstrates that fractional diffusion can be represented by a stochastic conductivity model, establishing a connection between time-dependent diffusion and time-space varying fractional anomalies.

A fundamental theory is introduced to describe both linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions between the modes of dielectric optical resonators, with the framework also capable of generalizing to microwave applications. The developed approach incorporates a generalized matrix equation that synthesizes various waveguide and resonator configurations, and a systematic method for determining the modes' linear and Kerr nonlinear coupling coefficients. Furthermore, the model facilitates the analysis of both homogeneous and inhomogeneous situations, in addition to interactions involving mode conversion, amplitude modulation, and four-wave mixing. To demonstrate its utility, the introduced model is utilized to analyze a range of discrete and continuous waveguides, including photonic crystal cavities, photonic crystal waveguides, nanoband phononic waveguides, and optical fiber.

This paper introduces a novel approach to a classic control problem, focusing on the stabilization of linear systems around their equilibrium points through conversational control methods. Unlike traditional techniques, this approach eschews the restriction that the control inputs must be bounded in magnitude. Instead, the only requirement is that the control system's dynamics permit the creation of a convex closure of the state space. A key contribution of this research is the proof that a wide range of regulation systems can be stabilized using conversational controls, accompanied by an algorithm implementing this strategy. Notably, this work also enables the secure stabilization of sensitive systems through convex optimization of their parameters.

A novel deep learning approach was introduced, centered on a generative adversarial network, to significantly enhance high-resolution video frames from low-resolution video feed obtained through particle image velocimetry. Tests were conducted at various Reynolds numbers, spanning 100 to 800, utilizing turbulent flow experiments observed through PIV. A high-resolution video frame was obtained from a PIV measurement with a low spatial and temporal resolution, and this was used as input for the GAN-based method. The resulting output matched measured data from the same physical location with a 95% accuracy and was verified through additional experiments. Further analysis demonstrated that model predictions conform to established laws of fluid dynamics.

This paper proposes several new estimates for the wave equation's energy, along with its higher-order counterparts, which can be applied to establish stability results for the damped wave equation and its variants. Specifically, we derive new bounds for the second-order energy's growth, expanding on earlier work by Kirchhoff. Additionally, this paper proves the strong stability of a higher-order linear wave equation with multiple damped terms and varying coefficients. These results can also be applied to establish the stability of specific non-fractional diffusion or damping terms.

In the context of Safety- and Security-Critical Systems, UPTIME's novel open-world ambiguity modeling approach offers a cutting-edge, efficient, and user-friendly solution for calibrating assurance proofs via counterexample-driven learning. This approach allows for significant reductions in assurance proof generation time. A key feature of UPTIME is its development of a range of innovative techniques for handling ambiguities in proofs, including expressions, sequences, and recursive functions. These techniques include a powerful general method called the "energy-driven learning" that can be applied to any form of unbounded recursion. Furthermore, UPTIME demonstrates its approach using a variety of examples, including several cases involving unbounded recursion in realistic scenarios.

For nearly a decade, evaluation protocols have remained a crucial yet understudied aspect in continuous control tasks. L2Explorer is an open-source, extensive evaluation ecosystem designed to address this significant gap. It automatically generates diverse, high-quality benchmarks through dynamic parameter adjustments and learning rule modifications. Furthermore, it is user-friendly and adaptable to various state representation and learning rule configurations, making it an invaluable resource for researchers and practitioners in the field.

Continuous advancements in mobile devices and location detection technologies have made it feasible to monitor and explore declarative processes through mobile agents in real-time at various locations. However, determining the trajectory of processes that involve region-based events poses a significant challenge. To tackle this, we've developed a new approach, called the "Trajectory Planning Algorithm," that utilizes vector fields to plan efficient process trajectories. This approach ensures that the process can promptly respond to incoming region-based events and adapt to changes in declarative processes. We've also designed the "Surveillance and Exploration System" to integrate this algorithm, enabling real-time execution of process trajectories through mobile agents. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach outperforms existing location discovery methods.

In one-dimensional quasiperiodic structures, certain types of wave propagation exhibit a sudden shift from localization to non-localization. Our theory and experiment demonstrate that in one-dimensional photonic quasicrystal arrays, light localization can transition back to non-localization at higher quasiperiodic modulation strengths for certain initial conditions, representing an unusual reentrant phenomenon. This occurrence is attributed to the existence of multiple states within the quasiperiodic site disorder spectrum, which can lead to light delocalization through nonlinear interactions. Additionally, we find that this reentrant behavior can be controlled through the intensity of a coherent light source, enabling the realization of non-localized states.

Liger, a next-generation infrared device at the W. M. Keck Observatory, will be paired with the Data Processing System (DPS) to regulate its operation, reconfigure its optics, and fine-tune its performance based on real-time data. The DPS will be responsible for converting raw data into usable science output for Liger's four detectors. To accomplish this, the team is developing the Liger Data Processing System Software (LDPSW) to manage communication between the devices and the scientific software. With an object-oriented approach and a modular design, LDPSW will facilitate smooth interaction between the Liger system, the Keck Observatory System Science Data Product (ScPipe), and external software like AstroWaveform. By utilizing established frameworks and proven algorithms, LDPSW will provide seamless science data products to the Liger team and the broader astronomical community.

A novel approach is proposed to enhance the super-resolution limit in bi-photon spatial mode demultiplexing, surpassing the conventional quantum limit.  The method involves introducing a entanglement source, enabling improved distinguishability of the demultiplexing states at the cost of reducing the maximum achievable channel capacity.  A practical implementation using polarization-entangled photons and a linear optics system is outlined, demonstrating the technique's feasibility.  The proposed method is particularly relevant for applications involving large channel sizes, such as free-space quantum communications over long distances, where the entanglement source can facilitate reliable demultiplexing of high-dimensional spatial modes.

This study proposes a novel approach to defining the parameter space $\mathcal{M}$ of a given system $\mathcal{S}$, alongside its monodromy matrix $\mathbf{M}$, by utilizing both algebraic and analytical methods. The algebraic approach involves defining the space as the solution set to a specific algebraic equation derived from the quadratic formula, while the analytical approach defines the space as the projection of a torus defined algebraically. Both methods yield the same metric and geometric properties for the space $\mathcal{M}$. The study also explores how the spaces change when the system $\mathcal{S}$ undergoes a transformation, examining both linear and non-linear transformations. The proposed approach is illustrated through the analysis of a simple quadratic system, as well as more complex systems with higher degrees. The study's findings are validated using numerical integration and plotting.

We're studying a dynamic ecosystem where species demographics change over two different time frames, with rapid changes followed by slower ones. Our goal is to understand how the environment's state changes over time and identify early warning signs of significant demographic shifts. To approach this, we're taking two routes. Firstly, we're analyzing the ecosystem's behavior through a lens of persistent hypothesis testing. This involves asking, for any given time frame, if the species' population is in a state of equilibrium with the environment. Our second approach involves modeling the population's growth rate as a state machine, where the machine's state represents the population's current condition. We're then identifying the population's early reactions to changes in its internal and external environments. Taking these ideas together, we're exploring features that may signal an impending major demographic shift, such as a sudden change in population growth rate, especially if it occurs on the faster time frame. However, our initial findings suggest that these features aren't unique to transitions between stable demographic states. Consequently, we're refining our search for alert indicators to focus on events that represent a significant deviation from the population's typical behavioral patterns.

The relationship between star formation rate (SFR) and gas mass (M_* ) appears distinct when broken down by galaxy type. While disk-dominated galaxies follow the typical power-law pattern, those with prominent bulges exhibit a more complex and contrasting behavior, with increased SFR associated with greater M_*. Using a catalog of nearby galaxies observed by the SPT--SSERS survey, we investigate the source of this divergence. We find that low-mass galaxies with significant bulges navigate the typical M_*-SFR pathway, yet as mass increases, the SFR outpaces the predicted rate, following the universal bulge sequence. This shift is not due to the presence of active galactic nuclei, but rather the bulge's contribution to luminosity. Consequently, the turning point in the relationship at high masses (approximating 10^10.5 M_*) is largely determined by the behavior of massive bulges. These results imply that bulges contribute to the understanding of galactic evolution, particularly in processing gas to form stars efficiently at high masses.

This paper focuses on sentiment analysis across different languages, specifically
English and French. We used a shared-subtoken model to translate phrases,
thereby enabling the model to utilize knowledge from multiple languages. Our
proposed framework incorporated multi-task learning to facilitate sentiment
analysis in both languages. We demonstrated that this approach successfully
leverages knowledge from one language to improve sentiment analysis in another.
Furthermore, our model's performance indicated a capacity for learning
cross-lingually, achieving superior results when tested with data never seen
before. Our findings suggest that multi-task learning is a viable path for
sentiment analysis across languages and can result in significant improvements
in accuracy.

Humans exhibit a unique capacity for both positive and negative self-assessments, which can significantly influence their mental well-being and subsequent actions. Through the prism of game theory, we explore the benefits of individuals being able to express both self-criticism and self-deprecation. In a simulated scenario, we discover that allowing players to engage in these self-reflection activities can lead to more cooperative and informative outcomes, even in complex social situations. Our analysis suggests that allowing self-criticism and self-deprecation to influence a player's identity can facilitate more effective learning and adaptation in dynamic social environments.

This note builds upon a concept mentioned by R. T. Rassias in his proof of Freiman's 3k-4 conjecture, substituting a more intuitive approach using a simpler theorem. As a result, we obtain a more general conclusion involving the Fourier transform.

The fractional Brownian motion with drift, a fundamental stochastic process, has been extensively studied in various fields including finance, signal processing, and image analysis. Despite its significance, very little is known about the geometric properties of its sample paths. Utilizing modern techniques, we demonstrate that for a specific parameter value, the interior of the set consisting of all fractional Brownian motion paths with positive drift is non-empty, thus providing a first instance of a positive result about these paths. The approach employed also yields the existence of arbitrarily complex curves within the set defined by positively oriented Brownian motion paths. The methodology involves integrating stochastic analysis with classical techniques from geometric measure theory.

To study a nonlinear differential equation from H\'enon-Heiles's type, researchers use a variational approach by translating the equation into a mathematical framework involving a quadratic operator and applying the Jackiw-Kerman formula. This strategy identifies the ground state as a stable solution and provides the associated energy minimization. However, when the system becomes chaotic and nonlinear, applying this method becomes more complex due to the presence of a term that breaks symmetry. By modifying the Jackiw-Kerman formula and using the Dirac variational principle, scientists can determine the stability of these chaotic systems and identify their energy levels. Using this approach, researchers have found the energy spectra for both linear and nonlinear versions of the H\'enon-Heiles model, confirming the results with numerical methods and demonstrating the method's effectiveness in handling difficult mathematical problems.

X-ray images of COVID-19 patients contain subtle differences that may indicate the severity of their condition.  If we can develop a reliable method to forecast the severity of COVID-19 based on X-ray images, it would be a valuable tool for healthcare professionals.  For example, it could suggest an urgent ICU admission.  In this notice, we outline the results of a study aimed at understanding the relationship between X-ray images and ICU admissions.  The dataset used consisted of 593 pairs of X-ray images and patient data, collected from the COVID-19 dataset containing lung X-ray images and clinical information.  Our analysis indicates that there are distinct features distinguishable in X-ray images of patients who are or are not admitted to the ICU.  To verify this finding, a second, independent dataset of 200 pairs of X-ray images and patient data was examined.  Therefore, it is plausible that the appearance of these distinct features in X-ray images can indicate an increased risk of severe illness, potentially requiring ICU admission.  It is also possible that the risk of severe illness varies according to the type, i.e., mild, moderate, severe, or fatal, as characterized by a scoring system.  Building on this outcome, a scorecard was designed to evaluate the risk of severe illness based on the presence or absence of specific characteristics in X-ray images.  Essentially, this would involve checking various properties of the lung region, such as shape, size, and relationship with surrounding tissues.

The global simplicial bundle was initially introduced in order to generalize simplicial colimits to a form of homotopy colimits. However, this concept has an underlying premise - it only accurately reflects the original simplicial functor's intention when the original simplicial functor preserves the simplicial structure. Consequently, determining whether a simplicial functor preserves the simplicial structure is now a relevant question. We propose a criterion based on weakly equivariant functions, establish that left fibrations meet this criterion, and subsequently prove that the global simplicial bundle fits into a categorical framework as a simplicial structure.

The evaluation of computer vision models relies heavily on synthetic data created through pairing images with classes they represent. Nonetheless, current methods fail to efficiently eliminate incorrect associations between images and classes, hindering the effectiveness of subsequent visual tasks. Our research proposes a novel approach called Contrastive Contextual Consistency, which leverages contextual information to counter false positives in visual classification tasks. We incorporate this method into our framework, utilizing it to generate high-quality negative pairs to supplement existing datasets, thus enhancing the accuracy of computer vision models in evaluation benchmarks.

Delta sampling, a recent technique, offers a cost-effective approach to
augmenting datasets by taking advantage of unlabeled data. However, its potential
is hampered by its limitation to similar data and low-quality samples. To tackle
these constraints, we propose a new approach called Delta Sampling for Data
Augmentation, combining delta sampling with transfer learning to exploit both
unlabeled data and labeled data. Our experimental results on Action Recognition
datasets demonstrate that this approach enhances classification performance,
especially under difficult lighting conditions. For example, when training the
R-BERT baseline model with fully labeled datasets, we achieve state-of-the-art
results on NTU-RoR and Red-Kinect49 datasets. Moreover, our method outperforms
the baseline model when trained with partially labeled datasets, achieving a
notable boost of 3.3% on NTU-RoR and 5.1% on Red-Kinect49. Our findings also
indicate that action recognition models trained with delta sampling on a small
well-labeled dataset significantly surpass models trained on large unlabeled
datasets. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/hjwadi/Delta-Sampling-R-BERT.

This project introduces a novel concept called Content-Addressable Concurrent Processors, 
a groundbreaking model that redefines how programmable logic and memory are integrated 
within a FPGA. This innovative system allows for both data-driven and instruction-driven 
execution pathways, paving the way for a range of applications including efficient search 
algorithms and efficient handling of complex, parallel tasks. Unlike traditional FPGA 
programming methods, this model bypasses software intermediaries, enabling direct 
communication between hardware components and eliminating the need for memory transfers. 
A demonstration prototype, demonstrated at the ACM SIGPLAN 2022, highlights the 
technical feasibility of this approach.

We've performed an in-depth analysis of three young galaxy clusters at $z \sim 2.9$ within the 430 square degrees of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, and a recently developed machine-learning algorithm has identified three of these galaxy clusters as possessing ordered, non-rotating stellar bulges. Via observations from the Hubble Space Telescope and the Chandra X-ray Observatory, we discovered these galaxies exhibit distinct X-ray active galactic nuclei morphologies, suggesting they're being fueled by accretion. Furthermore, we found multiple galactic mergers' signature in their spectroscopic data. These interactions likely triggered the formation of these galaxies' bulges through non-major merger star creation, as opposed to the result of massive collisions. Consequently, these findings imply that bulge formation can arise from the interplay between accretion, star creation, and gravitational instability within rotating stellar disks, and that multiple galaxy interactions can lead to bulge development through non-major mergers.

The Global $U(1)$ symmetry of the Flavor Zero model is re-examined 
using a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) analysis for a random and representative 
sample of 10,000 models, chosen to match the conditions and restrictions 
of the original study. In contrast to the earlier findings, our analysis 
reveals a significantly different picture, with an enhanced understanding 
of the underlying distribution of flavor parameters. Unlike previous 
results, our data demonstrates that the average value of the flavor 
parameter $\eta$ closely follows 0.03, rather than 0.06, and that 
the distribution of global $U(1)$ angles is shown to be bi-modal, 
exemplified by a mixture model with two distinct components, 
corresponding to $0$ and $\pi$. Additionally, our results indicate 
that the original selection procedure introduced a bias in the flavor 
parameter $\eta$, while the choice of models was also affected 
by a global $U(1)$ symmetry that was not accounted for.

We examine a specific nonlinear elliptic equation that includes a critical growth term, specifically $-\Delta u+\lambda u=g(\lambda,x,u)=\mbox{$$0$}$ in $\mbox{$\mathbb{R}^N$}$, where the number of superlinear solutions for this equation changes significantly at $\lambda=0$. By applying a variety of mathematical techniques, including a compactness lemma, a uniformity argument, and a method for counting solutions, we demonstrate that when $\lambda$ is small enough and not zero, the number of distinct solutions for this equation increases by four. Additionally, we establish that when $\lambda$ is an odd number, there are two additional solutions that are periodic in $x$.

Current cutting-edge neural network code models excel at guiding existing code to produce the desired output but struggle with generating new code from scratch. This study introduces a novel approach to create new neural network code through iteration, using the model's evaluation of previous code as input. During training, code evaluations are used as input, with the desired output being the corresponding functional code. When generating new code, the model is fed its previous versions of functional code and produces new code based on that evaluation. Our results show that this method produces accurate, working code on tasks like sorting lists and creating rectangles with text, outperforming plain neural network code generation.

On November 4, 2004, a significant X-ray flare occurred, primarily observed in X-rays, which also indicated the existence of high-energy neutrons. Analyzing data from space-based detectors, we examined the interaction of these neutrons with the Earth's atmosphere to understand their behavior. Neutrons were confirmed to break into protons and electrons as they entered the atmosphere, with energies ranging from 10-100 MeV. By studying the electron positron pairs created through neutron decay, we found that about 1 part in 10^10 of atmospheric protons have an excess of energy due to the neutrons' presence, which decayed into electrons and protons over time. This energy excess was observed to decrease at a rate consistent with the expected decay of neutrons into protons and electrons.

The concept of linearized propagation matrices is well-established in linearized fluid dynamics, making it a powerful tool for analyzing mode propagation and identifying damping mechanisms. This study extends the theory to a highly generalised class of viscous relativistic fluid models by utilising the covariant operator approach. The linearised propagation matrices are derived for both first-order and second-order theories of relativistic hydrodynamics, including the causal hydrodynamics models suggested by Mueller and Greineis, as well as the causal relativistic viscous fluid model proposed by Bhattacharyya et al. The analytical linearisation is verified to produce the exact linearised gauge-invariant propagation matrices when using the infinitesimal gauge transformation. Furthermore, this study finds that the conventional skew-symmetric tensor approach to linearisation is vulnerable to gaps, resulting in incorrect damping rates in certain cases. Consequently, the established derivation serves as a more comprehensive reference for linearised propagation matrices.

This paper introduces a novel framework for detecting irregular quantum measurements based on the interplay between the measurement operator and the unitary evolution of a quantum system. In particular, we show that the uniqueness of regular quantum measurements can be assured by the uniqueness of their associated time-evolution operators. Conversely, irregular measurements correspond to non-unique time-evolution operators, which can be identified using an efficient algorithm. Notably, this framework enables the detection of both incorrect classical measurements and faulty quantum gate implementations. To illustrate this concept, we perform actual experiments using a quantum simulator, demonstrating its practical applicability. Our approach provides a crucial solution to the critical problem of detecting quantum gate failures, which poses a significant roadblock in the development of large-scale quantum computing systems.

This research paper addresses a crucial concern affecting both individuals and organizations, highlighting the importance of maintaining confidentiality in encrypted information. As digital communication methods continue to evolve, individuals are relying more heavily on online platforms for personal and professional interactions. These interactions generate vast amounts of sensitive data, which are often stored remotely across international networks. Unfortunately, this increased online activity has created significant vulnerabilities, making it vulnerable to unauthorized access and potential exploitation. As a result, there is a pressing need to reevaluate existing legislation and develop more comprehensive security protocols that prioritize the protection of encrypted information. This need is further exacerbated by the differing legal frameworks governing data protection across various regions, which can sometimes conflict and pose additional challenges. Consequently, there is a pressing need for clear guidelines on how authorities can compel the decryption of encrypted data in a manner that is both legally sound and technically feasible. This demand is being driven by the growing concern over the potential threats these vulnerabilities pose, as well as the potential for them to be exploited in malicious ways. As such, there is a pressing need for clear guidelines on how authorities can compel the decryption of encrypted data in a manner that is both legally sound and technically feasible. This research contributes to addressing this need by providing a theoretical framework for breaking encryption codes, which can be implemented in practice. This framework involves the use of general-purpose computers running specialized software to decode specific types of encryption. As such, this research offers a potential solution to addressing the concerns over the potential threats these vulnerabilities pose, as well

Our proposed model can facilitate a measurement-device-agnostic quantum key exchange (MDA-QKE) protocol by integrating convex functions, which can also simulate the average behavior of multiple realizable scenarios. For instance, our model can accurately predict the performance of the finite-size 4-Port QKE experiment, which involves approximately 100,000 measurement outcomes, by efficiently using just 4 measurement settings. These settings comprise 2 well-known scenarios from the field of quantum cryptography, namely the Peres-Mermin Sagnac and the four-dimensional Bell state measurement. Our approach offers a substantial reduction in experimental complexity while maintaining the same functional characteristics of multiple realizable scenarios. Through analysis and computation, we found that the convex model's performance is nearly identical to that of the combined scenarios, exceeding the minimum requirement of MDA-QKE by a significant margin.

We have developed a polynomial-time approximation scheme (PTAS) for solving certain constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs) that contain arbitrary positive weights and involve n variables with certain 'flexibility' properties. However, our approach does not provide a general PTAS for CSPs. To achieve this, we employed an alternative method that involves expressing weighted CSPs as fractional relaxations of specific integer programs. By analyzing the properties of these relaxations, we obtained a general PTAS for certain CSPs that includes novel insights regarding the relationships between different relaxation types and approximate solution quality. Building upon this framework, we then demonstrated the potential of derived algorithms to address various sparse CSP scenarios, including weighted CSPs with specific 'flexibility' properties of variables, in the context of both deterministic and probabilistic constraints.

This study presents a novel, elevated-order numerical approach for solving the stochastic transport equation and related mean field games system, paving the way for extended analysis and a faster, more precise algorithm for solving these systems.

Understanding the inner workings and decision-making processes of neural networks through full-layer interpretations remains a challenging task. Although feature importance tools like LIME and SHAP offer insights, they deviate from the actual neural network functionality and may not account for sequential data, like videos and speech. In this research, we explore using full-layer interpretations in neural networks by analyzing their impact on classification outcomes. We examine various neural network architectures, different activation functions, and diverse data sets to validate our approach. Our findings show that interpreting neural networks through full-layer analyses provides valuable insights, and our methodology is versatile enough to accommodate different network architectures and data characteristics. Additionally, we discover that different activation functions significantly impact neural network interpretability.

The discovery of the rotating hot supergiant star V766 Cen (also known as RY Cen) in 2019 has raised interesting questions about its evolution. V766 Cen, which is roughly 20 times bigger than the Sun, is rotating very quickly, with a speed of about 40 kilometers per second. To understand the star's past, researchers used computer simulations to model its development over time. However, these simulations struggled to accurately explain the star's current state, particularly its rapid rotation. Two possible explanations have been put forward: first, the presence of a large planetary body that could be responsible for the star's unusual features; second, an unexpected transfer of angular momentum that could have arisen from various causes, such as a massive explosion or the absorption of energy from a nearby high-energy star. Further observation and analysis are needed to determine the validity of these theories.

The emergence of fake news on social media poses a significant challenge in today's information-rich environment. As fake news can spread quickly before being removed, obtaining accurate information has become increasingly difficult. To address this issue, we propose an innovative solution by introducing the FakeNewsMD dataset, which incorporates text, image, and text-image pairs to facilitate the development of artificial intelligence models capable of detecting fake news. Our proposed Meta Neural Process Networks framework leverages meta-learning and neural processes to efficiently train and generalize to new, unseen data. By combining meta-learning and neural processes, this model excels in counterfeit news detection tasks, particularly when confronted with limited and diverse data. Our research demonstrates the efficacy of the Meta Neural Process Networks framework, and its code is publicly available for further exploration.

This paper examines a one-dimensional transport equation featuring a recurrent and non-monotonic advection speed. It demonstrates that when the advection speed changes sign, specifically at points where it is changing most rapidly, the solution experiences a discontinuity. 

In the case of an initial condition that is continuous and differentiable, the solution will exhibit continuity and differentiability at the point where the advection speed changes most rapidly, unless that point coincides with a root of the advection speed. 

Notably, if the advection speed has an odd number of roots and they are all distinct in the domain [x0, x1], the solution will experience k-fold continuity and differentiability at the th kth root, where k <, until it becomes continuous only once at the final root. 

The equation in question can be written as the advection-diffusion equation u_t + b(x)u_x = \nu u_{xx}, where both b(x) and \nu are constants with specific properties. 

The study shows that if b^2 << \nu^2, the transport equation is influenced by diffusion over a wide range of values, including in regions where the advection speed changes sign. 

The research indicates that if the advection speed changes most rapidly at an non-zero root, the solution will experience a discontinuity.
