This paper proposes an independent perception framework for swarms of unmanned aerial vehicles to operate in complex environments. The pilot application of this concept is demonstrated through a collaboration of three RVs, each equipped with separate on-board computers using a Coarse-to-Fine algorithm. The effectiveness of this approach is verified through realistic flight simulations, showing that independently perceiving situations allows for improved scalability and more robust swarm behavior.

Dynamic processes on networks exhibit diverse behaviors on different structures, which can sometimes lead to isolated occurrences of a desired phenomenon within the larger network. The task of identifying suitable network features that concentrate the desired behavior is particularly challenging due to the intricate relationship between network architecture and dynamic behavior. Instead of searching for specific network features, our proposed method focuses on determining the locations within the network where the desired phenomenon occurs, once the network architecture is known. By applying this approach to the example of localized synchronization in complex networks, we show that the assigned labels can be used to construct the regions where the desired phenomenon occurs, which in this case is localized synchronization. The constructed regions can be expressed mathematically as the intersection of two implicitly defined network substructures. The proposed method is then tested on a set of sample networks, demonstrating its effectiveness. Furthermore, one of the assigned labels is found to correlate strongly with a recently defined measure of network connectivity, providing valuable insight into localized synchronization events.

The success of sports teams is often influenced by various factors including home field advantage, team valuation, and defensive strategies. To gain a deeper understanding of UEFA European Football Championships, we conducted a geographical analysis of football data from the 2020 and 2022 tournaments. By developing a statistical model that values teams and estimates their defensive chances of scoring, we identified patterns in team performance in relation to their location. Our findings show that European and Asian teams generally perform better than those from Africa and South America. Countries with high GDP per capita, such as those in Western Europe, tend to produce more valuable teams. In contrast, teams from low-GDP per capita countries have a greater advantage when playing at home. We also observed that teams from warmer climates have an easier time defending against colder climate teams. Furthermore, we found that teams from countries with better infrastructure values perform better, and those from countries with more supportive fans also exhibit improved performance.

This study presents a novel approach to automatically analyzing forms without a template, a common challenge encountered by everyday users in their daily lives. Our method leverages convolutional neural networks (CNN) to recognize and extract crucial information from unstructured forms, overcoming the limitations of traditional template-based methods that are often inflexible and require time-consuming setup. To evaluate our approach, we introduced the FormAnalysis Benchmark, a comprehensive and challenging dataset consisting of 1,000 images representing 25 distinct form types. Our experiments demonstrated that our proposed design outperforms a state-of-the-art baseline, achieving a remarkable 92% accuracy rate. To further demonstrate the practical applicability of our method, we incorporated it into a real-world scenario, showcasing its effectiveness in automating invoice processing.

In the development of control systems and signal processing algorithms, a significant limitation of conventional state space models exists, as they require full access to a system's underlying dynamics parameters. Unfortunately, these parameters are often partially or fully concealed, hindering the effective use of state space approaches. To address this challenge, a novel recurrent state space framework has been devised, capable of accommodating partial concealment of parameters and flexible observation and action functions. The framework's novelty lies in its incorporation of hidden neural network layers, allowing for the exploration of diverse dynamic scenarios through sequential state transformations. To optimize this complex system, a data-driven training protocol has been established, involving the simultaneous learning of system dynamics, action and observation functions, all from raw time series data. The efficacy of this approach is demonstrated through its application to control tasks involving complex, self-interacting systems, and the results show that recurrent state spaces can efficiently tackle a wide range of challenging scenarios.

In our previous work with A. Kostyuchenko, we established the concept of free independence of degree 2 for arbitrary polynomials in the non-commutative *-algebra $M_n(\mathbb{C})$, and corresponding applications to random matrices and matrix-valued random variables. Here, we expand this idea by showing its connection to conditional independence concepts, including the free version of the de Finetti theorem.

We provide a detailed description of the theta characteristics of a degree-3 cover of a genus-1 curve, specifically expressing them in terms of the original curve's properties. Furthermore, we establish that this relationship gives rise to a connection between the theta characteristics and a product of the curve's invariant and a value derived from the Fano matrix of the curve. This discovery enables us to identify the variety associated with these theta characteristics as a subvariety of the Jacobian of a genus-2 curve, whose defining equation can be determined directly from the Fano matrix.

Social networks are frequently analyzed to understand the dispersion of opinions among users, the influence of propaganda, and the spread of misinformation. Researchers often study these phenomena by examining and interpreting complex graphs containing opinion expressions from various social media platforms. To facilitate comparison across distinct data sets and sampling time frames, this paper introduces a novel statistical approach to evaluating the dispersion of opinions. This method involves conducting random opinion-expression experiments on randomly formed graphs and utilizing the results to derive meaningful statistical measures to describe the dispersion of opinions. The proposed approach is applied to three popular social network data sets, and the results demonstrate improved clarity and consistency when comparing the dispersion of opinions using these data sets. Furthermore, this research introduces three distinct methods for validating the opinions expressed on these graphs, addressing key challenges in the field with increased rigor and transparency.

The concept of solution propagation was recently introduced, representing a solution where all network oscillators, except one, are synchronized to a common target. This work builds upon the foundation laid by Gaba, LeBeau, and Röst (2022), which identified essential and sufficient conditions for solution propagation on monolayer networks. In contrast, the condition for solution propagation on multilayer networks remains unknown. Here, we establish a key condition for solution propagation on multilayer networks by determining the condition for solution propagation on a single interface between two connected nodes. Interestingly, this condition is more restrictive than its monolayer counterpart, demonstrating that the analysis of multilayer networks requires consideration of interlayer connections. Additionally, we demonstrate solution propagation on multilayer networks using a simple example, and the results are shown to align with those obtained using a multilayer phase oscillator model. Furthermore, we explore the dynamic transmission of solutions on multilayer networks, revealing that solutions can only transmit in one direction on some networks. Finally, we examine the relationship between solution propagation and the concept of drive-response symmetry in multilayer networks.

The classical concept of the stress tensor has been redefined using the Airy stress function, which replaces the direct determination of the individual components of the stress tensor with the solution of a complex scalar function. This approach was further enhanced by the formulation of the Beltrami-Mitchell theorem, which utilizes the Airy stress function to describe two-dimensional equilibrium states. Nonetheless, the application of this method is limited by the requirement for a fully explicit representation of the stress tensor. This study investigates the possibility of a non-explicit, implicit definition of the stress tensor, which could offer a more flexible use of the stress function. The proposed new framework implicitly defines the stress tensor through its relationship with the rotation of the displacement field. This implicit definition is equivalent to the traditional explicit definition, thereby retaining the same finite-element method solutions. Nonetheless, it now allows for the incorporation of geometric constraints on the stress tensor. To demonstrate its effectiveness, the new framework is employed in conjunction with the finite-element method to model a crack subject to mixed boundary conditions. The obtained results are compared with those generated by the original explicit definition, yielding a precise match.

In the context of safe-by-design learning for dynamic systems, understanding why programs are incorrect is crucial to preventing harmful behaviors. By leveraging empirical observations and intuitive grasps of correctness through visualization, we develop a new hypothesis explaining the benefits of using learned geometric models in analyzing program executions. We test this hypothesis by creating and evaluating the effectiveness of two new metrics in gauging the complexity of dynamic system programs. The results show that these metrics correlate strongly with the difficulty of analyzing the programs, both on their own and in conjunction with the underlying system dynamics. Furthermore, we find that they offer significant improvements over existing methods of 10-30% in predicting the accuracy of models, without relying on explicit specifications of correctness. We conclude by outlining potential paths for exploring dynamic system programs in greater detail.

Our proposal, HyperPrompt, aims to enhance the task-conditioning capabilities of transformer architectures in models like BART and T5. To achieve this, HyperPrompt structures task conditions as hypergraphs and defines a new method for generating prompt sequences that can be combined with the model's internal hypergraph structure. This results in better performance when compared to basic prompting methods across various tasks included in the SuperGLUE and MultiGLUE benchmarks. Furthermore, HyperPrompt's creative prompting approach can be easily integrated with existing self-supervised learning objectives, leading to additional enhancements in robustness and generalization.

Let $\mathfrak{g}$ be a semisimple Lie algebra and $\mathfrak{h}$ a Cartan subalgebra, from which we derive the associated root system $\Delta$. Let $\mathfrak{g}_{\mathbb{C}} = \mathfrak{n}^- \oplus \mathfrak{h} \oplus \mathfrak{n}^+$ be the complexification of $\mathfrak{g}$, where $\mathfrak{n}^-$ and $\mathfrak{n}^+$ are nilpotent subalgebras corresponding to the positive and negative roots in $\Delta$. For any $\alpha \in \Delta$, we define the Canselo vector fields $e_\alpha$ and $f_\alpha$ as follows: for any $X \in \mathfrak{g}_{\mathbb{C}}$, the derivative of the trajectory $e_\alpha(t)X$ at $t=0$ is equal to the coefficient of the $e_\alpha$ term in the expansion of the eigenvalue $1$ representation of the Heisenberg Lie algebra with generator $e_\alpha$, while the derivative of the trajectory $f_\alpha(t)X$ at $t=0$ is equal to the coefficient of the $f_\alpha$ term in the expansion of the eigenvalue $1$ representation of the Heisenberg Lie algebra with generator $f_\alpha$.

In the context of quantum field theory, parity symmetry plays a significant role in the emission of scalar and fermion bundles within the SU(Nc) gauge theory. This study demonstrates that the parity symmetry characteristic of asymptotic states leads to the distinction between bosonic and fermionic parities, resulting in distinct spectrum patterns for both. Furthermore, our findings indicate that non-zero quark masses disrupt the parity symmetry, giving rise to unstable states of mixed parity and shifting mass thresholds for stable parity-symmetric states. These developments offer the theoretical basis for interpreting LHC data in light of parity symmetry, while also implying that the formation of parity-breaking vacua could be signaled by asymmetries in particle lepton number and baryon number.

The development of scalable and efficient distributed learning algorithms is crucial for future artificial intelligence systems. Given the significant impact of edge devices on machine learning model accuracy, it's essential to account for the graph topology of the underlying network when estimating node values. However, the challenge lies in constructing a reliable estimator that converges quickly. In this paper, a novel estimator is introduced, which achieves a time complexity of O(dT) by utilizing gradient information and establishing a connection between the GMM parameters and the network degrees. The proposed estimator demonstrates robust performance in the presence of corrupted data and can be integrated with existing algorithms to accelerate convergence. Through theoretical and experimental analysis, the benefits of the new estimator, particularly its enhanced convergence rate and reduced time complexity, are highlighted. The results show that the estimator's robust time complexity outperforms non-robust methods by a factor of T^0.4 when facing large amounts of corrupted data. Furthermore, the study finds that a significant portion of the time complexity is due to the network's small-world properties rather than its large diameter. To further improve the estimator's performance, a modified version is proposed, and its benefits are verified through extensive experiments.

The growing use of intelligent transportation systems (ITS) and increasing complexity of urban traffic networks create significant challenges for traffic management agencies to make informed decisions. One crucial decision is adjusting signal timing to minimize congestion and improve the flow of traffic. Currently, decision-makers rely heavily on historical data, which can be outdated, or conventional methods that are expensive and time-consuming to set up. In response to these limitations, this research introduces a novel, low-cost technique for estimating real-time queue lengths at intersections. The approach leverages existing inductive loop sensors and a new signal timing system called the traffic signal control system (TSCS) to collect probe vehicle data, which are used in a new combinatorial method called the reduced permutation method (RPM). The RPM reduces the dimensionality of the data by identifying the most influential signal intervals and assigns a score to each interval based on the presence of a probe vehicle's position in the queue. The score indicates the likelihood of a vehicle being in the queue during that interval. The results showed that the RPM's accuracy was higher than other methods, especially in scenarios with limited data, achieving an average accuracy of 85.5%. The study also found that the most influential signal intervals varied depending on the approach used, such as the approach used, the intersection type, and the queue size. The findings demonstrated that the RPM's performance improved with more data, but also identified sources of inefficiency, such as checking all possible permutations, that could be optimized further. Numerical simulations in relativistic gravity face a fundamental limitation when solving the Einstein field equations due to the constraints imposed by the theory's algebraic properties, specifically the vanishing of the Weyngarten tensor. This study presents a non-standard formulation of the Einstein field equations that allows for the introduction of arbitrary three-dimensional geometries through the relaxation of certain constraints. As a result, this new approach enables the inclusion of complex matter sources that are inherently linked to these geometries. Consequently, this formulation facilitates the use of highly detailed physical configurations as initial conditions for numerical simulations of gravitational interactions. Furthermore, this approach is compatible with the application of advanced techniques such as the Cauchy-Characteristic approach.

The search for rare decays of strange and beauty mesons enables physicists to
understand how nature's smallest particles behave when interacting with each other.
The LHCb experiment at CERN's Large Hadron Collider has discovered the decay
$\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$, which occurs only once in every $10^{5}$ decays
of $\Sigma^+$ mesons. To confirm this finding, we utilized a statistical
approach, combining data from 2015 and 2016, resulting in 4 observed events
after applying necessary safeguards, compared to a predicted occurrence of 0.06
events. These results demonstrate the significance of LHCb's capabilities in
identifying rare phenomena.

We detect an abnormally large and persistent Nernst effect in Mn$_3$NiN thin layers, which endures up to 30 K beyond the Néel point in an external magnetic field. The anomalous Nernst coefficient shows an inverse correlation with the spin Hall conductivity in the normal state. The unusual Nernst phenomenon is linked to the chiral magnetic structure and anomalous Hall response in this material.

Multi-instructor labeled distillation has gained significant attention in recent years due to its efficiency in training neural networks with limited annotated data. Nonetheless, the default synthesis method for combining the results of multiple instructors is a simple weighted average, which doesn't fully leverage the information produced during inference. To address this, we propose Pairwise Iterative Logits Coalition (PILE), an advanced synthesis method that builds upon these results through iterative comparisons and adjustments. PILE initiates the process by comparing each pair of instructors and using an energy-based model to prioritize their combinations based on the likelihood of corresponding labels being correct. It then employs a self-modulating mechanism, where the probability of each label being correct is calculated by examining both the likelihood of each instructor's logit being the correct answer and the likelihood of the other instructor's logit being the wrong answer. We demonstrate the effectiveness of PILE by conducting multiple experiments under different multi-instructor labeling scenarios. Compared to the default average combination method, PILE achieves notable improvements in the experiments we've conducted to date, with an average enhancement of 2.21% in accuracy.

This document explains the dynamics of beam and beam-reduction processes in circular accelerators, including both general and specific applications, covering transverse and longitudinal beam interactions, as well as examples of beam sharing and fast beam rejection systems.

The surge in mobile device usage and growth of mobile data transmission has generated increased interest in developing fast and scalable signal processing techniques. To address this need, a significant amount of research is now focusing on applying machine learning principles to analyze and process mobile device data. However, existing approaches have limitations when dealing with complex data from multiple sources, particularly in large-scale settings requiring intensive processing power. In an effort to overcome these challenges, we present novel deep learning schemes capable of efficiently processing large volumes of mobile data while minimizing latency and data storage requirements. These models can be easily trained on relatively small datasets and can effectively analyze a wide range of measurement types with high accuracy, outperforming traditional methods. Moreover, our proposed framework facilitates distributed processing and reduces computational costs, eliminating the need for centralized control and data aggregation: it achieves this by leveraging a cutting-edge optimization method known as federated learning. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach by applying our models to analyze mobile measurement data in an actual scenario.

This article examines the solutions to a specific class of barrier problems, where the original equation exhibits subquadratic growth terms and is influenced by discontinuous and non-compact forcing terms that vary over time. Despite these conditions, our findings indicate that a unique solution exists and is constant across time, meeting specific uniformity criteria. Furthermore, when the original equation exhibits quadratic growth, we demonstrate the existence of a minimal solution when certain monotonicity constraints are met.

This work investigates the impact of a temperature gradient on gas bubble modes, specifically focusing on how it affects the normalized growth rate of these instabilities and their characteristic spatial structure. Our linear analysis applies to a tokamak with a circular plasma and considers the temperature difference varying both radially and vertically. As a result, a condition is identified that must be met for these modes to exist to to. Furthermore, our research reveals that a temperature gradient can either increase or decrease the growth rate of these modes, ultimately determining their stability. Additionally, certain current and magnetic field configurations may even cause these modes to become more unstable.

A promising technique known as quantum annealing has been proposed for efficiently solving combinatorial optimization problems embedded in the Ising Hamiltonian's ground state. This approach involves two distinct types of Hamiltonians: a driver Hamiltonian and a problem Hamiltonian, whose gradual transformation from driver to problem form allows researchers to find the target ground state. Including non-stoquastic terms in the driver Hamiltonian is thought to enhance QA's performance, but a major obstacle in achieving this is the presence of unwanted excitations generated during the annealing process. These excitations prevent the successful application of quantum annealing. A recent theoretical finding suggests that incorporating environmental decoherence throughout the annealing schedule can successfully mitigate this issue, enabling the successful use of non-stoquastic driver Hamiltonians in quantum annealing. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that, in the presence of decoherence, the optimal performance of quantum annealing is dependent on the decoherence rate and number of annealing steps, with potential advantages arising from using quantum annealing over classical methods such as simulated annealing.

This essay explores the development of the Kapteyn Astronomical Institute in Holland from 1921 to 1946 under the direction of Pieter Johannes van Rhijn, who succeeded the institute's founder, Jacobus Cornelius Kapteyn. When van Rhijn took over, the institute was on the brink of bankruptcy due to Kapteyn's lavish spending and questionable financial management. Despite initial difficulties under his leadership, van Rhijn established a systematic approach to research at the institute, allowing it to thrive in the mid-1930s. His plans included dividing the sky into 1-degree squares, which were to be studied in depth, a project first conceived by Kapteyn. Van Rhijn graduated numerous students during his tenure and rebuilt the institute's library, which had been nearly destroyed in World War II. His commitment to his goals remained strong even in the face of significant challenges.

We provide a straightforward explanation for a recent discovery made by
  Barnet-Lamb, Bernais, and Tsimerman and independently by
  Le~Huang and by Y.~S. Li, involving the application of Kummer theory to
  the Serre weights problem for GL_2. Specifically, we demonstrate how the
  strategy of Brueckner, Guitart, and Venkatesh, along with the earlier
  work of Diamond and Sasaki, Guo, and Ye, can be combined to show the
  density of non-trivial characters in base change cases, thereby obtaining
  a clear proof of the density of the Serre weights conjecture in such
  situations. Furthermore, this involves an interesting connection between
  the conjecture and the distribution of isogenies within isogeny networks,
  as initially observed by Diamond and Sasaki.

We establish a precise result for optimal sets minimizing the perimeter under an area constraint within a larger area. This result involves analyzing the structure of sets that nearly minimize perimeter under an area constraint and deriving a smoothness criterion for surfaces with nonzero mean curvature outside a small-scale regime.

Modern neural networks are characterized by their simplicity and low depth, which may not fully leverage the potential of modern computers. Given the scalability limitations of large models, researchers have been exploring model-parallel learning techniques. These methods distribute the neural network's computations across multiple machines, enabling training on profound models. However, synchronizing parallel synapses introduces additional memory and communication costs, which can hinder performance gains. Despite this challenge, model-parallel learning offers a promising pathway to processing advanced neural networks. To address this issue, we introduce a novel regional evaluator architecture that reduces parallel synapse interactions and minimizes memory costs. This innovative design is then incorporated into a training framework, which utilizes a customized optimizer to boost evaluation region accuracy. The proposed method is experimentally evaluated and shows substantial gains in computational efficiency, without a notable decrease in classification accuracy.

A self-sensing harmonic contour detection method is proposed for composite materials, utilizing a non-invasive electrical impedance tomography technique in conjunction with a physically motivated forward model and a data-driven inverse solver based on evolutionary algorithms. The proposed approach is experimentally validated and demonstrates accuracy in identifying harmonic contours within self-sensing composite materials without the need for a reference configuration.

Humanity's most renowned leaders throughout history have frequently been praised for their exceptional abilities in politics, warfare, and social interactions, which in turn have enabled them to assemble skilled teams of advisors and generate groundbreaking intellectual pursuits. In contrast, many celebrated innovators and scientists have often been lauded for their unique intellectual characteristics, which in some instances have led their counterparts to view them with suspicion. It has been commonly believed that the most effective organizations, whether they are nations or scientific collaborations, are those that combine individuals with both exceptional intellectual abilities and a lack of ego. However, the actual relationship between cognitive characteristics and intellectual advancements is not as straightforward as it seems, and there are diverse perspectives on this topic. Here, we examine the interplay between cognitive profiles and innovative achievements in various domains, including the development of theoretical physics, biology, chemistry, mathematics, astronomy, geography, economics, social sciences, engineering, medicine, and Earth sciences.

By integrating physical simulations and video recordings, we create a comprehensive dataset consisting of text descriptions and images for various humanoid robot skills. A novel data-driven approach is then developed to train a state representation, action selector and reward predictor as a single entity using this dataset. The proposed framework leverages limited high-fidelity simulation data and an abundance of low-fidelity rendered images to train these components. To achieve this, we employ two distinct state representations: one based on 3D kinematic features and another on 2D image coordinates. The former is utilized in conjunction with simulation data, while the latter is combined with an abundance of video recordings. The resulting state representation is a hybrid of these descriptors. The proposed system is subsequently trained to execute numerous humanoid robot skills in simulation and on an actual robot. Notably, it achieves successful landings, swims, walks and flies with the robot, despite never having seen it in action during training.

This work introduces a tensor representation of Euclidean spaces, drawing on Finsler geometry principles. Specifically, we utilize a method from non-Euclidean geometry that generalizes the concept of distance in Euclidean spaces. The resulting tensor representation facilitates the computation of center of mass and other geometric averages. However, standard calculations in Euclidean spaces are simplified when comparing the computational complexity of using tensor representation versus the classic formulas for these calculations. Nevertheless, this approach may provide the basis for future generalizations of computational methods to non-Euclidean spaces.

If a light boson with zero charge and a modest mass exists, it may interact with other particles in a peculiar way, allowing it to transition between two distinct states. This phenomenon could make it very durable, potentially affecting its role in the universe. The most straightforward instance of this situation would require the boson's mass to be nearly, but not quite, identical to that of the neutral Higgs boson. If the boson's mass is significantly greater than that of the Higgs boson, its impact on the universe might be very different. Either of these scenarios could lead to unusual flavor-permutations that persist for a remarkably long time and could be triggered by the movement of neutrinos through rock, potentially resulting in the misperception of the neutrino's magnetic moment as it interacts with other particles. The durability of these flavor-permutations could allow them to travel considerable distances, potentially leading to the misperception of the neutrino's non-zero mass. The conditions necessary for these fleeting interactions to occur could be identified using existing and upcoming experiments, particularly those that investigate the movement of neutrinos through long paths. The most straightforward instance of this situation may require the boson's mass to be very close to, but not quite, identical to that of the Higgs boson, either because it makes the flavor-permutations last too long or because it makes them too common. The Higgs boson's mass is particularly significant in this context because it affects how easily the light boson

This investigation seeks to separate the distinct impacts of remote education on students' ability to maintain schedule during the pandemic, taking into account various combinations of online learning setting, student characteristics, and teacher characteristics. To achieve this, we used a nationwide online course usage dataset from 2020, coupled with results from a nationally representative K-12 learning capacity survey conducted in 2021. Our research design leverages natural experiments and propensity scoring to account for the self-selection biases inherent in observers' reports. Our analysis employs a linear regression model, controlled for pandemic-related factors and controlled for student and teacher characteristics. The results show that, overall, remote education has a negative impact on students' ability to maintain schedule. However, this effect is significantly more pronounced for students who experienced full online learning, with no significant differences found for students who experienced blended or traditional learning. Moreover, certain student and teacher characteristics, such as gender, race, age, and level of education, influence the effect of remote education on maintaining schedule, with distinct outcomes evident for elementary, middle school, and high school learners. During online learning, girls demonstrated a greater capacity to maintain schedule compared to boys, while blended learning significantly improved the capacity of white students, boys, and younger teachers' capacity to maintain schedule. In contrast, full online learning led to a decreased capacity in black students, and the ability of boys to maintain schedule was enhanced with blended learning. This paper provides an explicit proof of a set of conserved charges existing within the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal quantum field theory. Those charges, derived from Ward identities, allow us to determine the spectrum of the theory's excitations. Furthermore, they enable the formulation of third-order differential equations in the source variable, which can be used to solve for the correlation functions of the Toda field itself. Those solutions, in turn, allow us to compute two-point and three-point correlation functions of the Toda field.
We demonstrate that Coxeter groups possess biautomatic properties, resulting from which we derive that uniform lattices within isometry groups of buildings also exhibit biautomatic structures.

In this research, the first and second laws of thermodynamics are established for a class of Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black holes through the use of a scalar field. Specifically, this study demonstrates the conditions under which the first law holds true for these black holes and identifies the specific temperature and chemical potential that satisfy the second law. Furthermore, this research offers a preliminary analysis of the thermodynamic instability of these black holes and investigates the validity of the weak cosmic censorship hypothesis in their development.

In 1913, Ernst Zermelo formulated the axioms that underpin modern set theory, which he subsequently refined in 1930 with the assistance of Abraham Fraenkel and Thoralf Skolem. Over time, mathematicians have developed a range of models describing the principles underlying sets, from the basic axioms of Zermelo-Fraenkel (ZF) to the expanded ZFC with choice principles. Nonetheless, the fundamental ZF framework has consistently served as the foundation for which these models are derived. We contend that incorporating a paraconsistent or paracomplete logic within the foundational axioms of set theory yields a more versatile and coherent framework, one which can accommodate various intuitionistic and constructive mathematical constructs. By introducing a contrary or void connectives into the ZF axioms, we derive a robust theory that surpasses the capabilities of classical logic-based set theory. Our proposal is underpinned by the use of a dialetheistic or void logic, which facilitates the development of a consistent theory covering all combinations of instances and their negations, thereby providing a cohesive framework for set theory.

Long-term, detailed information about a patient's ambulatory state is crucial for optimizing treatment and making informed decisions in neurology and psychiatry. Currently, assessments are primarily conducted using standardized clinical evaluation tools, but these have significant drawbacks, including being time-consuming, expensive, and subject to significant scoring variability. Recent advances in machine learning hold the potential to significantly improve the efficient and accurate capture of ambulatory states. Building upon a previous study that successfully classified 10-min intervals into one of three categories (sedentary, walking, or highly active), the current research extends the model's capabilities by incorporating additional features and achieving more precise results (above 90% accuracy) across multiple test subjects. The optimized model can accurately predict walking patterns (above 95% accuracy) and overall activity levels (above 85% accuracy). Furthermore, the study demonstrates the feasibility of long-term, real-world applications of the model, with one subject wearing the EEG device for over 27 hours. The perfected model demonstrates a high level of generalizability, successfully classifying over 75% of 10-min intervals in the long-term data set.

This paper proposes a new statistical approach to calculate the entropy of various probability distributions using nested sampling. Initially, the basic concept of nested sampling is outlined, followed by an explanation of the method's application to estimating Bayesian model evidence and parameters. The paper then demonstrates the relevance of nested sampling to calculating the maximum likelihood and Bayes estimates of model parameters, as well as Bayesian model selection. Furthermore, it showcases the method's use in computing divergent factors, mean values, and standard deviations of parameters. The proposed algorithm is tested on a simple cosmic void model, involving multiple free parameters in a likelihood function that has an intricate shape.

The paper explores how right-angled Artin groups are divided into subgroups, specifically focusing on the situation where the graph underlying the group has no isolated vertices. It demonstrates that if a subgroup intersects the group's core in a non-trivial way, it must do so in an connected component. Conversely, every connected component of the graph's vertices corresponds to a subgroup that intersects the core in a maximal way. Additionally, two subgroups corresponding to distinct connected components will never intersect in a topologically finitely generated way.

In previous work, the proposed AutoTemporalGraph method effectively identified
interdependencies between variables through time series data. However, it had two
significant limitations: it only worked for binary classification problems and was
not suitable for high-dimensional data due to its linear scalability. To address
these challenges, we have developed a new algorithm, seamlessly integrating
optimization and graph construction into a single deep learning process called
Deep Temporal Graph, that significantly outperforms the existing solution for
real-world datasets like Wikipedia usage and airline passenger numbers in both
classification and dimensionality reduction tasks.

Phylogenetic networks serve as a consolidation of multiple trees, capturing the evolution history of various species, and have become an essential tool in computational biology. Researchers often develop and utilize various methods for creating and analyzing these networks. This study compares the underlying graph structures of multiple phylogenetic network construction algorithms, focusing on three main categories: bidirectional algorithms, single-directional algorithms, and those with mixed directionality. By examining the created networks using a random tree model, the study reveals significant differences in graph structures, highlighting the importance of considering both tree edges and reticulations when analyzing phylogenetic networks. Furthermore, our findings suggest that many current algorithms produce networks with impractically large reticulations, underscoring the need for more realistic models that integrate taxon labels and generation mechanisms.

Animal locomotion research benefits greatly from advanced technology, including high-speed cameras and computer software, to study living organisms in controlled environments and from multiple perspectives. However, analyzing video recordings obtained in such setups can be a time-consuming and impractical approach for repeated observations due to their size. A proposed algorithm takes in video recordings from various angles and system settings before producing a streamlined, easily comparable output of movement data. This method was tested on fish movements studied from three different camera angles, with the results showing it can effectively process and analyze such data, even in complex lighting conditions.

The iterative matrix inversion methods are the foundation for various advanced order techniques in dynamic systems, including their application in control engineering. However, these methods can be computationally expensive when dealing with a large number of state variables. We present a generalized framework that utilizes sparse matrix data structures to accelerate iterative matrix inversion, taking full advantage of the capabilities of GPU acceleration. The framework employs an optimized memory layout that minimizes data transfer during matrix operations, thereby boosting performance. The use of sparse matrices enables the inclusion of nonlinear state and input constraints within the iterative predictive control algorithm, paving the way for its integration with complex systems featuring a large number of state variables. Successful testing of the proposed method is shown with a case study involving a large-scale wind farm simulation.

In quantum scattering theory, a crucial concept has been introduced, 
representing a hypothetical device that perfectly measures a system's energy 
without modification. This measurement device is modelled as a perfect 
energy-resolving sieve, associated with a scattering matrix that characterizes 
its operational principles. A fundamental aspect of such a device's functioning 
is defined as energy absorption eigenchannels, which determine how the system 
absorbs energy based on its operational principles and structural composition. 
This study establishes a key mathematical relationship, known as the sum rule, 
which links energy absorption eigenchannels to system properties and provides a 
universal formula that can be applied to any energy spectrum. Additionally, 
we derive specific formulas for key scenarios, such as continuous spectra and 
discrete spectrum with distinct eigenvalues. Our research also explores the 
role of time-reversal symmetry in determining energy absorption eigenchannels, 
finding that this symmetry solely affects the scattering matrix's conjugate, 
not the matrix itself.

Inspired by the topological Anderson insulator proposed by Li et al., we examine a model where a binary random potential is applied uniformly in a range to the on-site orbitals of a two-dimensional square lattice, excluding the site where the disorder is strongest. We investigate the topological properties of this model using numerical methods and explore the effects of various disorder strengths on the topological phase transition. Our results indicate that, beyond a certain disorder strength, the topological phase cannot be achieved due to the absence of a gap in the spectrum at the Fermi level. We develop an analytical model to explain the underlying mechanism and find that the topological phase can be achieved when the disorder strength is less than half the energy difference between the highest and lowest on-site energies. We validate our findings using the Kubo formula and demonstrate that the anomalous Hall conductivity shows a peak at the phase transition point. Furthermore, we investigate the spatial distribution of edge states in real and momentum spaces and observe that the localization length of edge states increases with increasing disorder strength.

This study focuses on a specific class of protocols known as Trimming Protocols, which form a core component of many recent works incorporating the Isogeny-Based Protocol framework. Trimming Protocols essentially facilitate the reduction of a given degree-$d$ polynomial to a linear form through a series of degree-$2$ transformations. We have established the theoretical foundation for these protocols and demonstrated their efficacy in particular scenarios. Furthermore, we have developed an integrated system leveraging TPS, which we found to be essentially equivalent to previous proposals using the Isogeny-Based Protocol framework but with improved performance.

Within the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model, the presence of a natural electroweak symmetry breaking requires a specific mass scale for the Higgs boson and the lightest Higgs particle's mass. This paper delves into the phenomenology of the on-shell Higgs sector in the MSSM, focusing on scenarios where the stop quark's mass parameters are disparate. As a result of the stop quark's split mass parameters, the lightest Higgs boson's mass can naturally reach approximately 125 GeV. However, this leads to a fine-tuned relationship between the stop quark's familiar and unknown components, which becomes distorted in the face of supersymmetry breaking. Consequently, the lightest Higgs boson's mass is instead dominated by the stop quark's unfamiliar component, which is directly linked to the top quark's contribution. As the stop quark's mass parameters become increasingly disjoint, the lightest Higgs boson's mass is instead governed by the natural parameter scale, which is around 5-10 TeV. Nevertheless, this has a surprising effect on the heavy Higgs bosons' masses, which are instead dominated by the top quark's contribution through the stop quark's familiar component, thus displaying an unusual mass parameter scale that is disjoint from the supersymmetry breaking sector. Moreover, the coupling between the lightest Higgs boson and the smallest mass difference between the two neutral Higgs bosons, which is approximately 125

Network autoregressive models have recently been the focus of interest due to their ability to seamlessly integrate dependency information into regression analysis, especially in cases with complex connections. However, the linearity assumption within these models has yet to be thoroughly assessed, particularly in regards to their ability to model conditional expectations. A new linearity test has been developed for high-dimensional, sparse networks, along with a simulation-based method to estimate precision for each model parameter. This proposed test significantly outperforms existing options when evaluated across a variety of scenarios. Furthermore, the new linearity test is found to be highly effective even in very small samples, offering insights into the optimal design of network score tests. Moreover, our research demonstrates the importance of accounting for network structures when conducting linearity tests, as this leads to a substantially more efficient use of data. The benefits of the proposed method extend to modeling conditional means through network regression, which is illustrated through real-world applications.

In this work, we build upon the foundation laid by Zhang and Chen and expand the Issue Framework, initially proposed by Levesque, Shanks, and Diaz, to incorporate negation rules. We then apply this expanded framework to two scenarios, utilizing the WebEval platform, and demonstrate its effectiveness in guiding a deep neural network towards accurate question answer pairs. Additionally, our model is capable of learning from feedback provided in the form of declarative sentences.

A recently proposed framework for modeling single cells that change location and protein positions on their surface has significant potential for studying dynamic cellular behavior in flow environments. This flow-cell framework can be applied across various species, providing insights into biological processes affected by fluid forces, such as the distribution of flagella, adhesion sites, and chemosensory molecules on surfaces that are subject to external fluid influences.

The underlying technology behind cryptocurrencies is transforming the way we perceive and interact with technology. Through smart contracts, the integrity of programs can be ensured, and their efficiency can be measured by the sequence of transactions they generate. Our research focuses on identifying suspicious activity within cryptocurrency transactions. By analyzing temporal patterns of transaction occurrence, we separate normal behavior from suspicious activity. Utilizing statistical methods, we predict the temporal patterns of transaction times. Our investigation centers on the Steem social networking cryptocurrency, which allows users to post content and vote on others' postings. The underlying technology behind Steem includes industrial-scale servers, known as "full nodes," that maintain the blockchain and direct the flow of transactions. These full nodes are located across the globe, as is the user base of the social networking application. The temporal patterns of transaction occurrence in Steem can be categorized into ten distinct groups, representing the actions taken by users on the network. Our research reveals the currency paths associated with suspicious activity, and reveals that users who engage in questionable behavior tend to have a distinct history of transaction times. Moreover, transactions related to suspicious activity tend to occur in a currency path that is uncommon in the blockchain.

By integrating reinforcement learning with coding theory, we've developed encoders and decoders that can correct errors occurring during quantum computations. This code-recover framework learns from trial-and-error interactions with simulated quantum processes, allowing it to efficiently correct various types and patterns of quantum errors. We've investigated several self-correcting quantum systems that can be accurately represented in this coding framework. Utilizing this representation, we've training a range of quantum error-correcting codes, including the five-qubit code, Shor code, and hexagonal code, among having the capability to correctly encode and decode codes with up to 11 qubits. Additionally, we've explored a novel decoding approach that can correct errors occurring within any subspace of a high-dimensional Hilbert space. This research has the potential to advance the development of reliable quantum computers through the efficient recovery of quantum errors.

Quantum metrology enhances precision by leveraging the principles of quantum physics. This is particularly evident in a double-cavity network, a complex system consisting of two interconnected cavities, where applications of quantum chemistry and biology are being explored. A recent study by a research coalition led by J. M. Brown from the University of Oxford, S. H. Mousa from the University of Cairo, and M. M. Godikkelung from the University of Oslo suggests that quantum overlaps in double-cavity networks can significantly increase precision in measurements, a phenomenon known as quantum leap metrology. In an experiment involving the interaction of two coupled cavities, each linked to separate, semi-isolated environments, the coalition obtained evidence of quantum leap metrology. The associated paper describes the theoretical basis of this phenomenon, providing an overview of double-cavity networks and deriving the quantum dynamics in a good-isolations limit. The findings indicate that quantum leap metrology can occur when there is minimal interaction between the two cavities, allowing for precise measurement of various physical properties within the system. The study also explores potential applications of quantum leap metrology in the measurement of chemical bonds and biological processes.

The data collected by the PHENIX Collaboration at Brookhaven National Laboratory between the years 2006 and 2007 constitutes a comprehensive dataset for jet-medium interactions in Au$+$Au and $d$$+$Au collisions at 200 GeV. Our simulations incorporate the PYTHIA 6.2 generator, accounting for differences in $d$$+$Au and Au$+$Au collisions, including an expanded medium in the latter case. By comparing theoretical predictions to experimental data from the PHENIA experiment, specifically direct photon-hadron correlation results, we can determine the properties of this medium and assess jet-medium interactions. Our analysis yields the medium's temperature at approximately 1 GeV, a lapse rate of 0.01 in temperature variation across the medium, and a scattering length of around 1.4 fm. Notably, we find that assumptions regarding the medium's initial state, as well as details of jet formation and the choice of parton fragmentation function, have a negligible impact on our findings. Furthermore, direct photon-hadron correlations emerge as a powerful tool for investigating jet-medium interactions and the properties of quark-gluon plasmas in experimental studies.

This paper examines a universal property claimed for the Smarandache's sequence, which is based on a hypothetical, all-digital arithmetic expansion concept. We demonstrate that the claimed universal property is inaccurate and offer a counterexample in the form of a specific sequence. Furthermore, we propose a novel term, "universal $k$-digit property," and prove that it is applicable to a broad category of sequences that meet specific criteria. Additionally, we provide a theoretical framework for determining the $1$-digit property in a general sequence context.

Cloud providers promote the use of their proprietary network technologies for optimal performance and efficiency within their data centers.  However, despite their recommendations, utilizing in-house cloud networks leads to substantial costs.  This research investigates the effectiveness of leveraging outside network resources for cloud-based applications, considering factors like latency, bandwidth, and the distribution of data.  Our findings indicate that certain high-performance computing applications can achieve better scalability and cost-efficiency by tapping into external network resources rather than relying on cloud providers' proprietary networks.  This study is based on a collaboration between two universities in the United States.

In large-scale systems with numerous agents, cooperation often requires sharing sensitive information about their environment, which can be problematic due to the need for mutual understanding. We examine a new scenario for cooperative learning where agents must learn in an unknown environment using a limited number of observations and must make decisions that optimize their own rewards as well as the overall reward of the system. We establish a key result that allows us to develop an effective approach, which involves creating personalized policies based on local observations and optimizing a shared structure through the exchange of bandit feedback. When the environment satisfies certain conditions, our approach achieves the same performance as if the agents shared their setting. We also demonstrate the efficacy of our approach by applying it to a scenario involving the management of a large network of sensors.

The widespread adoption of remote working in Scrum project management remains understudied despite growing popularity. This trend was not altered by the global COVID-19 pandemic, which further emphasized the necessity of considering remote working in Scrum. Prior research has shown mixed results on the effectiveness of remote Scrum implementation, resulting in our desire to conduct a thorough examination from multiple perspectives. A systematic review of existing research was followed by a survey of Scrum practitioners, after which we conducted in-depth interviews with Scrum professionals. These approaches revealed that remote working can have both positive and negative effects on Scrum project success. Successful implementation of remote Scrum requires clear communication, trust among team members, and established boundaries. However, remote Scrum is vulnerable to distraction, performance disparities, and leadership challenges. Finally, we highlight four key areas that influence remote Scrum: performance, safety, trust, and adaptability, suggesting that future research should explore the role of trust in remote Scrum.

We appreciate the discussion opportunity facilitated by editors and valuable input from discussants. Our work is influenced by the inspiring research of Kallus (2020), who leverages the empirical risk minimization principle to develop a context-free method for identifying treatment policies that yield optimal average performance across diverse contexts. In contrast, our research focuses on developing a simple framework for evaluating and learning context-sensitive individualized treatment guidelines based on comparative effectiveness estimates. This framework can be applied to both observed and generated data. In the observed data setting, we introduce a new objective function named distributionally strong risk that unifies existing concepts such as strong regularization, robust optimization, and efficient utilization of diverse data. We prove the consistency of our estimator and propose a blockwise coordinate descent algorithm for computing the minimum distributionally strong risk. Moreover, we show that this estimator achieves a better risk than other strong regularization methods under certain conditions. In the generated data setting, we propose a new neural network architecture named Contextconditioned Average Comparative Efficacy estimator (CACHE), which can efficiently learn context-sensitive individualized treatment guidelines based on comparative effectiveness estimates. Our theoretical findings guarantee the consistency of our neural network estimator. We also design a blockwise coordinate descent algorithm for which we prove the explicit stability risk and show it matches the minimax risk up to a constant factor.

Our study offers a comprehensive analysis of elliptic flow's underlying causes, focusing on initial conditions and constituent particle interactions within the medium. We utilize the Jülich Kaiserslautern Microscopic Transport Model, a multi-phase transport model that simulates collisions at the lead-lead collision scale with 2.76 TeV center-of-mass energy. In our research, we investigate elliptic flow's coefficient, $v_2$, in three distinct forms: particle-specific, integrated, and event-shaped. Our findings demonstrate that event-shaped $v_2$ reveals collaborative particle movements and is closely linked to initial energy distributions. Furthermore, our study finds that $v_2$ differentiation stems primarily from variations in initial energy patterns rather than differences in constituent particle interactions.

This paper proposes the Quaternion Linear Canonical Stockwell Transform as a derivative of the Linear Canonical Transform, and proves related properties including uniqueness and stability. A discrete implementation and two inverse methods are also defined.

This work verifies numerically the theoretical prediction from a previous study, 
which posits that the extremal sum rate of first order approximation of generalized 
Dobkin's theorem for an $K$ user interference channel increases proportionally 
to $\sqrt{K}$. Additionally, our findings indicate that the sum rate of binary 
power control can be as much as twice the sum rate of optimal power control, 
with this disparity widening as the number of users increases. Furthermore, 
our research extends previous findings by showing that the difference between these 
two approaches can surpass the square root of $K$ when considering the four user 
ERISI-4 dataset, an extension of the well-studied ERISI-3 dataset which consists 
of three users.

In particle-resolved simulations, interaction models are often simplified for efficient computation, with the aim of restoring accuracy through larger time steps. However, this strategy is compromised when simulating complex flows with high Reynolds numbers due to the short duration of particle collisions. As a result, time steps are often limited by the need to accurately capture these short events, leading to significant computational costs. A new multi-time-step integration method has been developed to tackle this issue by explicitly modeling different time scales of fluid flow and particle collisions. The method involves separating fluid flow and particle interactions, with the former being solved over longer time steps and the latter over shorter steps that reflect the duration of particle collisions. The proposed method demonstrates improved accuracy and increased computational efficiency in modeling sedimenting suspensions of polystyrene particles, with an overall efficiency that is 5-10 times greater than current methods.

This paper investigates number theory by examining the diagonal quadratic form $a^2+ab+b^2$, specifically focusing on whole number solutions to the equation $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$. Initially, we leverage Euler's approach and the use of congruences to establish constraints on possible values of $n$. Subsequently, we employ a methodical approach, incorporating parameterization and congruences within different base systems (mod 4 and mod 9), to derive conditions under which solutions exist for all non-negative integers $n$. Furthermore, we demonstrate a method to derive and validate a range of values within those conditions.

A leaping monopod made of a deformable material jumps onto a soft surface, and we want to improve its performance. To understand this, we create a simulation that considers the monopod's movements and the surface's impact, then use this to identify factors affecting its stability. By applying this knowledge, we design and test a more stable monopod configuration through physical and computational testing methods.

This paper proposes modifying the standard hydrodynamic model to account for
the spin of mesons. This modification yields an expanded form of the
hydrodynamic model, which encompasses both the standard model and the new
spin-related mechanism. However, our analysis indicates that the standard
hydrodynamic model is already capable of accurately capturing the observed
behavior of mesons. Nonetheless, we do establish that the new model can
better describe data related to the production of K-zero mesons. Furthermore,
our analysis reveals that the new model's additional components do not
substantially alter the established parameters of the standard hydrodynamic
model.

Our research reveals the previously unreported phenomenon of droplet electrohydrodynamic fan patterns when a non-conductive surface is placed across from a conductor soaked in an electrically conductive liquid, specifically in the presence of air. When the conductor is negatively charged in relation to the surface, a distinctive pattern of conductive liquid filaments emerges from the conductor, extending towards the surface at a set angle. Conversely, a pattern of less dense liquid filaments emerges when the conductor is positively charged. The angle at which these filaments occur can be calculated using the liquid's surface tension and the electric field strength. When air is introduced, the patterns evolve into circular fan shapes. The force propelling these patterns can be influenced by the air's movement, with potential applications including the prevention of biological contaminants from sticking to non-conductive surfaces in aerodynamic environments.

Effective communication relies on understanding the nuances of language, including the implications of negation. Despite being a fundamental aspect of language, research on the topic has been limited until now. We introduce CONDAQA, a pioneering dataset that requires users to accurately interpret the meaning of sentences containing negation. This dataset distinguishes itself from other interpretive datasets through its focus on negation and extensive coverage of written texts. We also present NegAction, a cutting-edge model capable of interpreting the implications of negation. In tests, NegAction outperforms existing models while utilizing significantly fewer parameters, indicating progress in this underexplored area of research. However, a notable gap remains between NegAction's performance and that of the human brain. We anticipate that CONDAQA and NegAction will guide the development of more effective models for interpreting the consequences of negation.

This research proposes an innovative approach to addressing the challenge of
maintaining updated information about the organizational structure in complex
systems. As the system size grows, traditional hierarchical modeling loses its
effectiveness, and there's a need for a more efficient method to handle frequent
changes. To address this issue, we've developed a new theory of expandable
models, which can adapt to modifications and provide the system's updated
organizational structure. This new framework can be applied to develop scalable
algorithms for solving common problems, such as identifying the shortest path, the
minimum spanning tree, and the transitive closure in a changing information
system.

Quantum annealing and quenching are both used to find equilibrium states in complex systems, but they differ significantly in their underlying principles and resulting outcomes. While quantum annealing is a gradual process for reaching a ground state, quenching involves an abrupt change, often resulting in non-equilibrium behavior. In this study, we examine the precise cover problem, a task that represents exact cover over a specific set with additional constraints. This problem can be formulated through an Ising Hamiltonian on a complete graph, and we investigate the effectiveness of both quantum annealing and quenching in finding a cover cycle. Our findings indicate that quenching yields better performance than quantum annealing, and interestingly, small variations in the quench parameter can lead to increased coverage rates. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that a fixed-size quantum annealing interval can guarantee a solution with cover cycle, and this interval is directly proportional to the number of available items. In contrast, the required duration for quantum annealing varies greatly depending on the specific instance.

A process workflow produces a series of events represented as traces, which are compared against a predefined standard, or reference model also composed of events that form traces. The reference model is divided into individual parts, or segments, and we explore how these parts can be used to validate the process workflow against the standard model. Our approach requires the use of event attributes and allows for partial matching of the workflow against the reference model, even in cases where certain events do not have corresponding elements. We demonstrate our method with a practical example, focusing on how it can be applied using a technique called postfix alignments. Additionally, we show the method can be reinterpreted using another technique called infix alignments, although this offers no practical advantages.

We present a theoretical dual-band model for the infinite-layer nickelate, which is capable of exhibiting superconductivity via electron pairing. This model, originating from a $d$-orbital only consideration, is grounded in the physics of transition metal compounds. To accurately capture the nickelate's behavior, we employ a combination of 3d orbital basins and a medium-range hoppings framework. Our analysis takes into account the strong on-site Coulomb repulsion and medium-range electron pairing terms. By applying a mean-field approximation, we simulate an infinite layer nickelate and demonstrate that the resulting Hamiltonian mimics a multi-orbital Hubbard model. Ultimately, we utilize this model to investigate the electronic properties of infinite-layer nickelate compounds and demonstrate that electron pairing driven by the metal's medium-range interactions can lead to the phenomenon of superconductivity.

This research investigates the long-term behavior of the one-dimensional Boltzmann equation under non-cutoff collisions on an infinite space. Specifically, initial conditions are examined where low velocity collisions lead to negligible particle interactions, while higher velocity collisions result in significant interactions that affect the particle distribution in a notable way. The impact of these interactions on the particle distribution is compared to a more limited class of collisions. The study demonstrates that in a infinite range of collisions, the particle distribution over time is influenced by a blend of the two classes of collisions, leading to a mixed diffusion rate. However, if the range of collisions is restricted to a semi-infinite range, the particle distribution over time is instead influenced by a combined effect of a blend of the two classes of collisions, resulting in a mixed diffusion rate, but only if the time of at least one infinite time frame has elapsed.

We utilize radiance data from space to evaluate the performance of two wave-crest height estimation techniques previously developed by Cox and Munk. To minimize biases, we utilize direct radiance measurements from the Spinning Enhanced Visible and Infrared Imager (SEVIIR) are matched with adjacent Infrared Atmospheric Sounding Interferometer (IASI) scenes. Since SEVIIR and IASI have distinct spatial and temporal characteristics, we incorporate a weight function to reduce the impact of SEVIIR's spatial response on its measured crests. Furthermore, we account for the bias in IASI's wave-crest measurements by utilizing a linear transformation, and our results show a significant improvement in the validation of our technique with a root mean square error of 0.32 meters. We also investigate factors that influence the performance of the Cox and Munk method, such as wind speed, wave age, and coastal effects, and find that it yields accurate results for medium to high wind speeds, but wave ages less than 1.5 are detrimental to its effectiveness and may lead to a 100% increase in error.

The growing complexity of software systems calls for thorough testing to identify defects during their development phase. The choice of test data has a direct impact on the effectiveness of subsequent tests, influencing the quality of the software in the end. Nonetheless, determining optimal test data is a challenging problem due to the sheer number of possible configurations arising from increasing parameterization. This problem is further exacerbated by the growing trend of parallel processing in both hardware and software. To efficiently identify optimal test configurations, a multi-dimensional algorithm is proposed that leverages the power of parallel processing to quickly filter potential configurations and focus on more promising areas. By incorporating a singular value decomposition technique, the algorithm's performance is optimized, allowing it to handle a broader range of system parameters with ease. The results show that the proposed algorithm outperforms existing methods by achieving a significant reduction in evaluation time with the same level of accuracy.

The COVID-19 pandemic's rapid spread demanded immediate action from worldwide leaders, resulting in widespread lockdowns and a significant shift to remote work. People turned to social media for emotional support during this time of isolation, with microblogging becoming a key source for understanding public emotions. In this research, sentiment analysis of Twitter posts was performed to gauge the emotions of users throughout the pandemic. Our experiments indicated that a machine learning model comprising LSTM and Bi-LSTM components achieved the most accurate emotion predictions, with an overall classification accuracy of 83.84%. Furthermore, our analysis pinpointed the most influential language features associated with each emotion and characterized the pandemic's emotional trajectory through a combination of public sentiment and topic extraction methods.

In cuprate materials, conduction occurs across layers despite a large insulating barrier between them. Typically, this conduction is explained by two models: interlayer tunneling and Coulomb interaction, or electron transfer mechanisms. Normally, these models are examined separately, but normally, cuprate materials exhibit additional electronic properties such as orbital symmetry and charge density oscillations that could offer greater insight into this phenomenon. This study shows that an expanded version of the electron transfer model is capable of predicting the same results as the tunneling-Coulomb model. Furthermore, this prediction remains valid for materials with charge density oscillations, as demonstrated using a variational wavefunction and a constraint variational approach. These findings suggest that both electron transfer and tunneling-Coulomb models share a common underlying physics.

The characteristics of dense stellar matter within strange and dense stars are intricately tied to the complex relationship between baryon density and sound speed. Research into the adiabatic index of dense matter is, however, hampered by the constraints placed on theoretical models by relativistic stellar structure requirements, which limit possible values to 2-4/3 for the adiabatic index at high density thresholds. In order to bypass this theoretical limitation, researchers have implemented the sound speed versus density relation model, which can be used in 1.1 - 1.4 solar mass stellar structure analyses. Utilizing this approach with a range of density relations spanning polypolytropic structures, our study finds that sound speed values at high density thresholds can exceed the conformal limit, with little to no distinct features distinguishable in oscillation mode spectra. Our analysis also reveals that high frequency quasi-normal modes can serve as stellar compactness indicators, with an estimated mass-radius relation that deviates from the standard 1.4 solar mass expectation.

The counter Tai mapping is a newly described labeling concept for arborizations, closely related to the Tai mapping. While Tai mappings have been extensively studied and characterized through various equivalent definitions in the context of graph theory, counter Tai mappings lack a clear understanding. Our research focuses on identifying the criteria that distinguish counter Tai mappings from Tai mappings, building on existing knowledge of these labelings. We present a preliminary analysis of counter Tai mappings and explore potential relationships with other labelings, but our findings do not directly contribute to the solution of the underlying problem. Instead, we establish connections between the problem statements and existing research questions in the domain.

We investigate a proposed experiment using a quantum-optical version of the scattering theory to create a coherent state superposition across multiple modes. This involves placing a partially transparent beam splitter at the intersection of two mirrorless cavies, with one side further obstructed by a photon-absorbing medium. Our analysis shows that even a small change in this setup can significantly impact the state of the photon field. To better understand this system, we're developing a user-friendly tool using Python that can model and visualize the physics behind it.

A phenomenon known as vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in protoplanetary disk systems requiring quick cooling of gases, potentially influencing how particles form and grow in these areas. While the formation of dust is generally well-mapped in inner regions of protoplanetary disks, its development in outer regions is not as clear. Using computational modeling for gas and dust combinations, we examined how dust formation affects VSI in protoplanetary disks, particularly in their outer regions. The algorithm accounted for the development of particles through accretion of gas, their impact on energy release and the absorption of stellar light. When dust develops freely, it becomes embedded within gas streams and takes on their orientations. Analyzing this algorithm's outcomes for protoplanetary disks with Visco-resistive cores, we discovered that full dust development actually hinders the conditions necessary for VSI, potentially providing a scientific explanation for VSI's rarity in such systems.

This research focuses on confirming a key theorem regarding continuous, changing volume functions under specific Ricci dimension conditions, specifically when the dimension is constant, a condition known as RCD-(K,N) with N equal to the sum of one and the logarithm base e of pi over two. In simpler terms, our study verifies a fundamental conjecture first proposed by the notable mathematician J. Shanmugam. Our work also highlights the implications of this verification for a broader conjecture known as the RCD-Conjecture.

Deep learning-based single-image super-resolution (SR) models have achieved great success in recent years. However, the traditional fully convolutional approach has a significant drawback: it relies on undetermined upsampling factors, resulting in unnecessary computation and memory usage. To rectify this, we propose a novel dynamic entrance module with global mean pooling to select relevant low-frequency information from the input image, thereby enhancing SR performance. By integrating this module into each scale branch of a deep cascaded darknet (DCDN) network, we achieve state-of-the-art SR results on several benchmarks, including the widely used DIV2K dataset. Notably, our model produces superior results with significantly reduced parameters (-43.6%) and operations (-46.1%) compared to the state-of-the-art DCN paper, while achieving comparable PSNR and SSIM values.

High-accuracy astronomical measurements are modeled using general relativity, considering post-Newtonian corrections. This research analyzes how uncertainties in a specific post-Newtonian parameter, $\gamma$, affect measurements made through astrometry. By analyzing multiple combinations of general relativity and post-Newtonian models, researchers demonstrated that $\gamma$ uncertainties are inherently linked to parallax measurements. For Gaia-like missions, this relationship results in a significant impact on parallax determinations. Ultimately, the accuracy of these measurements will be limited by the $\gamma$ uncertainty, and therefore, the four-fold reduction in uncertainty for Gaia+LSS parallaxes is solely the outcome of this $\gamma$ model.

We have developed an efficient approach for a rapid, precise model reduction method that can be applied across various complex systems. This approach leverages limited, high-fidelity data to determine a compact, simplified model that accurately captures the original system's dynamics. The proposed technique combines the use of dynamic mode decomposition for initial condition-based snapshot generation and residual networks to create a concise, high-accuracy model. The residual network's complexity is directly tied to the level of model complexity desired, allowing for a seamless balance between precision and computational efficiency. Moreover, our method includes an adaptive evaluation of the desired model complexity by comparing predicted outcomes to actual data, ensuring that the simplified model effectively reflects the underlying physics of the system.
