When training the model to utilize density and velocity information, it reveals that velocity fields have a significant impact when combined with density maps. Furthermore, by assessing the contribution of velocity and density components, it shows that velocity's impact is marginal when incorporated into density maps that have already been processed through a non-linear transformation. This suggests that the relationship between velocity and density is linear, and the same scalar coefficient applies across different scales. In turn, this means that the connection between velocity and density is independent of the formation history of the universe, and is instead determined by the physics of structure formation.

Historical audio recordings containing speech and music have long been analyzed, 
but recordings of instrumental music with a keyboard remain underexplored. 
This paper introduces a semi-supervised technique using low-rank matrix factorization 
to automatically generate accurate transcriptions for a specific keyboard part 
within a broader musical context. Convolutive Nonnegative Matrix Factorization 
(BNMF) is a proven method for single-instrument extraction, yet its limited 
generalization to recognize specific notes within a broader audio spectrum poses 
a significant challenge. To address this, we introduce a semi-supervised BNMF 
model that leverages limited expert annotations to influence factorization results, 
enabling the model to recognize distinct notes within an audio spectrum. 
Implementation details, including the use of convolutional BNMF and auxiliary 
models to enhance performance, are also explained. Notably, our proposed approach 
outperformed conventional supervised and unsupervised learning strategies in our 
test cases.

We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving convergence in simulations of rotating stars under the theory of general relativity.  Our method deviates from traditional schemes that solve the conservation of momentum through the use of first-order integrals.  Instead, we integrate the conservation of momentum directly, taking into consideration the effects of rotation.  A particular challenge arises when simulating stars that rotate rapidly, as their shape differs significantly from that of spherical stars.  In such cases, the conservation of mass becomes a complex equation that cannot be solved analytically and must be numerically resolved through integration.  However, our approach involves a straightforward algebraic solution for mass distribution.  We have successfully demonstrated our new scheme by modeling several well-known pulsar stars and found that our results accurately match those obtained through other methods.  We have also used this approach to investigate the properties of rotating stars in rapid rotation regimes, where significant deviations from spherical shapes occur.

A major hindrance to scaling state-of-the-art document extraction platforms, which heavily rely on visual inspection for annotation, is the time-consuming and costly process of manual labeling. The traditional approach involving one annotator per target field has a significant drawback: it can handle only a limited number of annotations per second, largely unmoved by advancements in computing power. In contrast, our novel annotation method allows a single annotator to efficiently label an entire document at once by focusing on content as a whole rather than individual fields. This new approach takes advantage of human eyes' ability to process visual layouts in an instant. Compared to conventional annotation methods, it speeds up annotation by 3-4 times and reduces costs by 75%. Furthermore, we've built an end-to-end document extraction platform that utilizes this accelerated annotation process, thereby enabling the seamless integration of machine learning-based document understanding into real-world applications. This platform demonstrates a cost-effective annotation method that can process up to 1,000 documents per day with a single annotator, achieving a remarkable feat of combining high accuracy with incredibly low costs ($0.20 per document).

The observations of neutron star-black hole (NS-BH) coalescences made by the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO) from 2017 to 2020 have yielded a diverse range of data that can be leveraged for advanced purposes. By employing a deep learning approach, we have developed a method to identify and classify GW events resulting from the merger of neutron stars and black holes. Our neural network-based model excels at distinguishing between the two event types, demonstrating a 0.94 accuracy rate when compared to a dataset that includes the complete set of approved LIGO observations. Furthermore, our approach allows for the extraction of key features from raw gravitational wave data, providing insights that can aid scientists in subsequent analyses. By combining feature engineering with machine learning, we have discovered new indicators with enhanced sensitivity, that can aid in identifying the spin parameters of neutron stars and improving existing searches for binary mergers in LIGO's data.

The determinants of health are made up of numerous social factors that influence an individual's physical and mental well-being, affecting different population groups in varying ways. Understanding these intricate social connections is vital for developing effective healthcare policies and tailored interventions. While extensive research has been conducted on analyzing health data, combining it with social data to identify the intricate determinants of health poses a significant challenge. To address this, we present a token-based neural network framework that can be used for both single-label and multi-label classification tasks, allowing for the accurate identification of various social factors influencing an individual's health. Our approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art models in multiple datasets, showcasing its potential to selectively focus on relevant medical information and accurately predict associated social factors. Our research finds that pre-trained neural networks can generalize medical information effectively, and our proposed multi-label model provides a valuable resource for healthcare professionals and researchers by enabling the prediction of multiple social factors from a single analysis of medical notes.

This study is centered on a model describing the rhythmic swimming movement of a scallop, which can switch between two opposing jet velocities to achieve forward and reverse locomotion. We examine three primary configurations: when the body and the jet are aligned with the water's surface, when the body is perpendicular to the water's surface, and when there's an angular displacement between the body and the jet. For each scenario, we use Pontryagin's Maximum Principle to identify the optimal jet velocity profile. Nonetheless, obtaining analytical solutions proves challenging; hence, we focus on numerical solutions instead. When the body and the jet are aligned, we employ linearization to derive an approach for determining optimal trajectories. In the other scenarios, we use the optimal solution in the first configuration as a basis and observe that the optimal velocity outside of this initial range is divided into two distinct components. We also investigate how changing the water's resistance or the scallop's mass affects the optimal movement in the aligned body-jet configuration.

The COVID-19 pandemic led to widespread substitutions of home-based social interactions for online connections.  Analyzing a vast online dataset before and during the pandemic allowed researchers to measure the structural changes in urban residents' interactions.  Statistical modeling indicated a significant increase in online social connections among lower-income urban dwellers during this time, in contrast to a decline in face-to-face connections.  Conversely, higher-income city residents maintained their pre-pandemic online social connections but increased their in-person interactions.  As a result, the disparity in urban social interactions shifted from online to offline during the pandemic.

The formation of massive stars is subject to a longstanding mystery: how are massive young objects accumulated or merged without disruption to form massive stars?  It is commonly accepted that massive stars require a significant mass accumulation in a short period of time.  While previous research has primarily focused on protostar-mass spectra, our analysis takes a unique approach, using computational modeling to track the growth of massive protostars and surrounding disks within a high-density molecular core.  This method allows for a more realistic representation of grain growth, evaporation of particles, and viscous disk development.  Through this process, we observe that in optimal environments, the disk can supply up to 10 times the protostar's mass, with an average of 5-6 times the protostar's mass.  However, in cases where the disk breaks apart due to gravitational forces, it can still contribute 2-3 times the protostar's mass.  Furthermore, our findings indicate that in approximately 20-30% of ideal conditions, two massive protostars can merge into a single star with a mass equivalent to or greater than 10 M_.  This research offers a more comprehensive understanding of massive star formation, emphasizing the potential role of protostar mergers in the development of massive stars.

Buchholz established a practical approach to understanding massless two-dimensional scattering theories. Within this approach, we've demonstrated that the algebraic structure underlying these theories can be resolved into a wedge-local network of integrable systems. Furthermore, we've found that this decomposition arises from the application of the input algebra's universal, unitary endomorphisms to its conformal algebras, which define the scattering theories. Specifically, these endomorphisms generate the chiral CFT algebras associated with integrable systems through their global, multiplicative extensions. As a result, we've derived a comprehensive description of the basic properties for wedge-local networks of observables, including their von Neumann algebras, as well as their integral and semi-integral system components.

Recent studies claiming a link between 5G technology and the COVID-19 pandemic have prompted concerns worldwide. As a result, various countries have suspended or slowed down 5G deployments until factual evidence is presented. Contrary to these scientific findings, we have observed the lack of practical measurements and real-world data in this context. Consequently, we designed and executed a comprehensive measurement campaign to investigate 5G cellular exposure in various locations, including schools and medical facilities. Our custom-built, portable, and low-cost measurement device collected detailed information on 5G signal strength, frequency, and polarity at more than 1,000 locations across three different cities. Our analysis reveals the insignificant levels of 5G exposure in these environments, often below the limit of detection in our measurements. Interestingly, our findings indicate that 5G signal strength can vary based on the orientation of nearby antennas, which has important implications for ongoing debates. Furthermore, our study highlights the challenges and limitations associated with conducting this type of research, which we hope will facilitate a more collaborative and open-minded approach. Given the widespread adoption of 5G technology, it is essential to address these concerns and prioritize the validation of scientific findings with practical data.

This research focuses on modulated long-wave train existence within a two-dimensional, incompressible flow that includes uniform vorticity, and it proves that a Hamiltonian-formulated Dysthe equation represents the leading order of the problem's solution.

This paper proposes a novel approach to differentiating higher-degree functions on an archimedean locally finite polytopal surface in three-dimensional space. By leveraging a set of predetermined differential forms, we demonstrate the validity of the Stokes theorem. Additionally, this approach can be applied to simplify and generalize renowned formulas, including those from surface area measures and curvature variance formulas.

This project involves integrating real-time sonar sensors with a mobile robot's navigation controller to facilitate safe and efficient movement across non-level surfaces, specifically in environments with varying water levels and obstacles. A key challenge in this area is accounting for undetectable water layers that may not be visible to the sonar sensors. To tackle this issue, this project develops a novel algorithm that combines sonar data with elevation information to create a detailed, dynamic map of the environment. This map is then used to generate a optimal navigation path for the robot, taking into consideration both its physical dimensions and the unknown water layers. As new sensor data becomes available, the map and path are updated in real-time to ensure the robot's continued safe operation. Key components of the project include a sonar-based flow field that captures the dynamics of water layers and a motion validator function that ensures the robot's motion is physically feasible. The effectiveness of the integrated system is demonstrated through a series of simulation and real-world test runs.

The prevalence of false news is not only harming the dissemination of accurate information but also poses a threat to society. To combat this issue, effective detection methods are urgently needed. Recent advances in deep learning, particularly transformer-based models, have shown remarkable success in related tasks. Nonetheless, the performance of these methods often regressives when confronted with limited amounts of labeled data necessary for model training. In response to this challenge, we propose a novel false news identification framework that leverages automated text condensation to combine multiple models and utilize a relatively small labeled dataset. By condensing the most discriminative information from vast amounts of unpaid data, our framework achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods in accordance with metrics such as accuracy, F1-score, and AUC.

This research investigates how changes in mean curvature affect Gaussian random fields on submanifolds, particularly focusing on the effects of this change on the probability density function and associated functionals. By leveraging Gaussian features and the properties of submanifolds, we derive an explicit formula for the Laplace operator on embedded submanifolds in terms of the ambient manifold's curvature. This derivation allows us to analyze the impact of curvature on Gaussian random fields on both linear and nonlinear submanifolds. To demonstrate the practical utility of our results, we explore Gaussian distribution validation for data represented as low-dimensional linear embeddings, building on the theoretical framework developed here.

This research targets addressing security concerns in Non-Orthogonal Multiple Access (NOMA) networks by applying quantum cryptography. Specifically, a quantum code named Peres-Mermin box (PMB) is proposed to safeguard information transmission between a central controller and quantum users sharing the same unlicensed frequency band. The code's functionality is then demonstrated in a scenario where users employ NOMA to receive encoded signals, and an unauthorized user launches an attack. Our results show that the proposed code can prevent unauthorized access and ensure reliable communication in the presence of noise, thus providing a foundation for the development of quantum secure NOMA networks. Furthermore, our study assumes that a pre-agreed classical code has already been implemented to address issues such as synchronization and phase error correction.

We introduce an iterative algorithm to identify the principal component in data that exhibits rotational symmetry, specifically suited for data with anomalous outliers. The method converges linearly to the optimal solution and can be applied to high-dimensional, real-time signal processing scenarios. Furthermore, we develop a specialized variant for compactly represented data, demonstrating that the algorithm meets strong convergence criteria. To facilitate computation, we explore an efficient, feedforward neural network representation of our approach. Nevertheless, our primary focus remains on the theoretical aspects of the algorithm.

The deployment of voice assistants like Siri, Google Assistant, and Alexa has increased the need for automatic sentiment identification. These systems' ability to efficiently learn and apply knowledge of emotions could lead to better user experience. BERT-based models have shown impressive results in various sentiment analysis tasks due to their pre-trained capacity for general language understanding. However, traditional approaches rely on pre-defined schema and data patterns, which can limit their effectiveness. By leveraging a BERT-based model, we enhanced the sentiment classification of pre-trained networks through semantic adjustment. Our approach's effectiveness was validated on the SICK dataset, and the results showed that a BERT-based model can efficiently learn key emotion-connected questions through semantic adjustment. Our method's efficiency was further highlighted when compared to the BERT-based model without semantic adjustment, particularly in models trained with limited data.

We investigate an extension of preeminent power association games to groups with a comprehensive ordering, establishing key properties and corollaries. Our analysis also reveals a connection to decision-making frameworks that incorporate dynamic ordering of players' powers.

The classification of polars into synchronous and asynchronous magnetic accretion disks has significant implications, yet their exact categories remain unclear due to the limited understanding of these objects caused by their distant location and faint signal. To better differentiate between these classifications, researchers are turning to the inherent properties of polar materials, such as X-ray tolerance ratios. This study takes a multi-observable approach, utilizing data from the XMM-Newton and Chandra observatories, along with spectral and time-domain observations, to identify patterns in X-ray tolerance ratios in both asynchronous and non-synchronous polars. Although our results show similar distribution patterns for both types of magnets, an difference in the mean values was found, indicating that X-ray tolerance ratios may serve as a distinguishing feature between asynchronous and non-synchronous polars. Furthermore, a link between X-ray tolerance and the temperature of the accretion disk has been established, with a unique characteristic visible in the spectral energy distribution of non-synchronous polars.

This project's primary goal is to offer a simplified method for addressing a complex issue: when a fluid's movement affects the movement of a rigid structure, and the structure's shape is altered by the fluid's flow. To cater to various problem presentations, a unified and a segmented Reduced Basis Method will be introduced. The unified strategy is designed for problems where the fluid and the structure share the same initial geometry. In contrast, the segmented approach is tailored for situations where the two components have distinct geometries. Both methods will be demonstrated using a scenario where air flows through a moving blade in a turbine.

For individuals with visual impairments or those who need assistance navigating, having access to precise and user-friendly mapping information is vital. Present methods primarily focus on creating maps for able-bodied users, which can navigate with visual cues, but often overlook the needs of others who rely on other senses. Unfortunately, existing mapping techniques often miss critical aspects of an environment's layout, particularly when they go untested against a diverse range of users. As a result, there's a lack of effective navigation tools for those who don't rely on visual maps. Traditional cartographic approaches usually represent a building's interior as a two-dimensional surface, but this can lead to significant inaccuracies in their constructed maps, especially when measuring distances. Current research offers a solution using 3D models, but these are usually created with able-bodied users in mind and often don't account for the unique sensory experiences of others. At the heart of HiTMap is a new concept called the Hierarchical Topological Diagram (HTD), a way to represent a space's layout that prioritizes navigational clarity over precise metric measurements. By testing HiTMap with visually impaired users in real-world settings, we show that users can efficiently navigate unfamiliar environments using this system.

The UM-IU@LING system for the 2019 SemEval OffensEval Task is the subject of this paper. We adopted a dual-strategy to identify and categorize hate speech in social media posts. For subtask A, a BERT-based classifier was adapted and achieved a high macro F1 score of 0.8136 in evaluating test data, thereby ranking 3rd among 103 competitors. Meanwhile, our simple yet effective SVM-based approach for subtask B specifically identified tweets containing explicit abuse with a high degree of accuracy, earning us the top rank.

The precise measurement of magnetic field fluctuations around atoms is essential for developing quantum technologies. To achieve this, we propose an atomic interferometry test bed based on superconducting materials, which can generate extremely uniform magnetic fields. By leveraging the Meissner effect, this setup is capable of efficiently eliminating unwanted atomic scheduling, resulting in a significant improvement of atomic interferometry visibility (>10%). Furthermore, we demonstrate that this system can accurately measure very small magnetic field alterations (∼10^-13 G) and show that it is robust against vibrations and temperature variations. This development is expected to contribute to the creation of reliable atomic clocks and quantum computers by facilitating the precise measurement of magnetic field fluctuations.

We investigate the interplay between spin and heat in monolayer MoSe2, MoS2, WS2, and WSe2 using the first-principles calculations. Our analysis reveals that changing the chemical potential has a significant effect on the thermal conductivity and carrier density near the K point in these materials. By examining the thermal conductivity, carrier density, and magnetic moment across the band gap, we identify critical values of chemical potential that mark the transition from high to low thermal conductivity and from small to large magnetic moment. These transitions are accompanied by a significant change in the carrier density. Furthermore, we demonstrate that applying a magnetic field can modulate the thermal conductivity and magnetic moment by controlling the orbital coupling. Our theoretical framework is applicable to other 2D semiconductors, and our results suggest that the magnetic properties of these materials can be evaluated through thermal transport measurements.

We investigate how the electron outflow and nonlocal effects influence the behavior of gap plasmons in a specific interval that shrinks to zero. To accurately assess this, we use a hydrodynamic model that takes into account both electron outflow and nonlocality. Our analysis shows that both factors cause a significant shift in the energy and current velocity of gap plasmons. However, when considering a narrow gap that approaches zero, both outflow and nonlocal effects have an analogous impact on gap plasmons. Furthermore, we demonstrate that both effects lead to an increase in the energy and a decrease in the velocity of gap plons as the gap narrows. Additionally, we find that the electron outflow results in an imaginary part in the gap plasmon's self-energy, which originates from the interaction between gap plasmons and plicas (plasmons in the adjacent interval).

Type theory based on intuitionistic, piecemeal construction of mathematical proofs has a long-standing association with normalization. However, the introduction of dependent types compromises the normalizing property of type theory. This complication arose with the development of the Calculus of Constructions, a foundational theory that incorporates advanced type constructs such as universes with positive equality proof requirements. To address this issue, we adapt a robust normalization approach that accommodates partial and flawed type isomorphisms during the reduction process. This strategy enables the efficient elimination of unsatisfiable types, even with the presence of non-normalizable types and circular references in type definitions. As a result, this approach facilitates the development of reliable and certifiable code generation for the core types of the Calculus of Constructions.

A fundamental understanding of topological quantum states relies on the concept of symmetry-protected edges in models like the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger. This model features two distinct object representations - either atomic sites or lattice sites - which correspond to different universes of description. In our investigation, we switch between these representations, considering both their physical and matricular aspects. When we use the site description, the model includes a specific symmetry-breaking term that explains the edge state within the framework of topology. Conversely, the atomic description views the edge state as a localized defect, separate from topological classifications. Our research demonstrates that both interpretations are equally valid, yet they yield distinct results regarding topological properties. Ultimately, our findings emphasize the importance of clear language in describing physical systems and the caution against mixing physical and matricular languages.

In our analysis, we demonstrate that standard mixture models can be interpreted through a geometric perspective, utilizing the framework of stochastic geometry in a general setting, and we show that finite mixture models can be viewed as a special case of this interpretation. This special case is closely related to a specific type of geometric structure known as a polytope. We then explore how this perspective can be applied to a broad category of models, including hidden Markov models, and we discuss the implications of our findings for model selection and estimation.

We derived a two-loop amplitude formula for N=8 supergravity in the AdS$_5\times$S$^5$ space string theory, which is equivalent to a specific subset of four-dimensional N=4 Yang-Mills amplitudes calculated using the CFT approach. This Yang-Mills amplitudes are then used to predict gravity amplitudes for positive gravity, which differ from the standard N=8 supergravity amplitudes by power-like terms. These power-like terms are shown to come from the AdS$_5$ component and do not agree with certain degree of corruptions in the massless graviton amplitudes obtained from the gravity dual of the AdS$_5\times$S$^5$ supergravity. Moreover, our formula provides an indirect proof of the weakened Graßmann degree conjecture, which would allow the extension of the CFT-based Yang-Mills amplitude calculations to higher loop orders. This is achieved by comparing the BPS (Bose-Fermi saturation) amplitudes at the ten-dimensional S$^5$ space, which remain unchanged under the conversion between type IIB string theory and N=4 Yang-Mills theory. Our analysis extends to three-loop order for BPS amplitudes, which exhibit distinct behaviors compared to the non-BPS amplitudes. Our approach also enables the exploration of simple spin amplitudes, which can be linked to the non-BPS amplitudes through the BPS amplit

Concurrent memory allocation on GPUs is increasingly essential due to the growing use of object-based programming and high-performance numerical applications, as it can significantly improve program performance and efficiency. However, the current gap between parallel program structures and serial memory allocation techniques leads to suboptimal memory fragmentation and slow allocation times. To address this challenge, this research presents a novel, concurrent memory allocator called dynaSOAr, specifically designed for object-based memory allocation on GPUs. By incorporating a binary search method and unique object identifiers, dynaSOAr achieves faster allocation times or reduced memory fragmentation compared to existing techniques. Furthermore, dynaSOAr exhibits better performance in programs with a mix of large and small memory allocations. The source code of dynaSOAr is openly available, and the research includes a comprehensive analysis of memory allocation strategies as well as experimental performance evaluations on various applications.

This paper investigates the boundedness of a diverse set of operators, including those generated by the Calderón-Zygmund operators and the fractional integral operator, on generalized mixed Morrey spaces. Additionally, the article examines the boundedness of the commutators of these operators on the same space. Furthermore, specific applications are considered for operators like the Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator, the Calderón-Zygmund singular integral operators, and the Calderón-Zygmund operators with weights, demonstrating their boundedness or failure of boundedness.

A new theoretical approach is presented that enables the description of superconducting proximitized local magnetic impurities and their dimers within the framework of a real-space, spin-polarized Keldysh technique. By incorporating the YSR states and interacting with a superconducting host metal, the formalism includes the effects of both spin exchange and asymmetry. With explicit applications to manganese adatoms and dimers on the Nb(110) surface, the theoretical framework is put to the test. The findings are compared with experimental data, and the sensitivity of the calculated quantities is examined in relation to the accuracy of the atomic and molecular magnetic exchange interactions. The developed approach is particularly useful for analyzing magnetic monomer and dimer molecules in proximity to superconducting hosts, involving strong hybridization with host electrons, and requiring a precise understanding of proximate spin exchange and asymmetry interactions.

Our proposal, FourierMask, integrates the Fourier series with implicit neural architectures to create instance segmentation masks. FourierMask uses a Fourier transformation on the coordinate positions and feeds the mapped features to an implicit function, allowing for the generation of specific masks. By leveraging the uniqueness of the Fourier spectrum for each instance and taking advantage of the Fourier transformation's orthogonality, FourierMask offers a data-driven approach that supersedes the need for preset grid sizes. This architecture, trained end-to-end, yields compelling results for instance segmentation, as evidenced by our FourierMask-SAR dataset-specific agent, which achieves impressive performance without relying on mask IoU or auxiliary segmentation tasks during training.

This note provides a proof for thefulness of locally area-increasing mappings from a bounded domain in R^n to R^m, where n and m satisfy the condition m >= 2n-1. Furthermore, the proof extends to certain non-locally area-increasing mappings under certain volume constraints, demonstrating the possibility of these mappings to R^m having a full range.

The proposed hypothesis is that the core of thick convective clouds, which these clouds form around, may not be fully visible due to being completely enveloped by water droplets larger than 50 microns in diameter, which could render it opaque even when the surrounding areas are not. To test this hypothesis, we'll use data from the most advanced space-based imaging systems, MISR and MODIS, to take vertical cross-sections of these clouds and look for the cloud core. Since we can't directly observe the core using visible and near-infrared light, we'll use cloud optical thickness and water droplet size as indicators of its location. If the hypothesis is correct, the core's presence should be indicated by a sudden decrease in observed reflectivity compared to surrounding areas, which would be a significant finding in cloud research. To validate our method, we'll use numerical models of water droplet size and optical thickness to simulate the imaging systems' output. If the core is identified in a significant number of cases, it would have implications for the use of radiative transfer models in cloud research and the interpretation of space-based imaging system data.

This research paper suggests a novel approach to ion propulsion efficiency enhancement, utilizing a self-generated electrostatic "chirp" field that forms during the interaction of an extremely fast and narrow electron beam with a stationary propellant target. As this field is exactly 90 degrees out of phase with the electric field of the propellant, it creates a situation of destructive interference, effectively making the propellant target "transparent" to the electron beam. This results in an unusually high and stable amount of beam energy transmission (up to 90%) as the field's time-varying nature causes the neutral atoms to temporarily become quasi-ionic, facilitating this high transmission rate. Computer simulations indicate that this phenomenon occurs not just with fast, low-mass propellants like hydrogen but also with heavier elements like carbon and oxygen. This previously unknown effect could potentially boost the efficiency of ion propulsion by 5-10 times.

The NASA $TESS$ mission's comprehensive sky survey allows the detection of rarest transiting planetary systems. In a new discovery, we found a young star called TOI-712, hosting a system of four planets orbiting it. By analyzing $TESS$ data, the team established that the star rotates in about 12.48 days and has an age ranging from approximately $500$ million to 1.1 billion years. Observations from $TESS$ revealed three mini-Neptune-sized planets with distinct periods of $9.531$ days, $51.699$ days, and $84.839$ days. Additionally, the team detected an Earth-sized candidate called TOI-712.05 with a short orbital period of $4.32$ days. By calculating the habitable zone for this system, TOI-712 d appears to be just $20\%$ more massive than the most minimal world capable of sustaining life. Researchers also studied the star's properties and found it to have active regions and a strong magnetic field, which may reduce the detection probability of additional planets by as much as $30\%$. Furthermore, analysis of the system suggested the possibility of further undiscovered transiting planets with substantial masses.

We performed a comprehensive investigation into the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO2 using a reliable hybrid density functional theory method. By modeling a 2$\times$2$\times$2 supercell and varying the position and bonding of the dopant atom, we evaluated how they affect the arrangement of atoms, energy levels, and magnetic characteristics. The calculations indicated that carbon defects tend to prefer an isolated configuration and have energy levels located in the middle of the bandgap, while also exhibiting ferromagnetic stability. In contrast, nitrogen defects preferably form bonds with oxygen atoms, have energy levels that aren't in the middle of the bandgap, and can have either diamagnetic or magnetic properties, dependent on the placement. Furthermore, our analysis suggests that both carbon and nitrogen defects can enhance the photocatalytic activity of TiO2 when reducing oxides.

The proposed strategy for identifying top quark creation through elastic dijet production involves a detailed theoretical understanding and a complicated experimental analysis process due to fake signal creation. We suggest an alternative method to pinpoint top quark creation directly, by examining the properties of elastic dijet events themselves. This approach allows for a cleaner experimental analysis as fake signal creation does not apply and the method is independent of the theoretical models used to create top quarks. Furthermore, it can provide a direct observation of the Large Hadron Collider's energy range and improve the accuracy of top quark forward scattering amplitude measurements.

Previous research revealed the complexity of the intra-cluster medium's structure function. However, determining the scaling of this complexity using semi-analytical models is challenging due to the lack of accurate measurements for key parameters, particularly their temporal and spatial derivatives. This study utilizes numerical simulations of radiative transfer, solving the radiative transport equation, to assess the impact of measurement inaccuracies on the reconstruction of the intra-cluster medium's complexity. The comparison between simulated observations and actual measurements shows the influence of radiative transfer on the structure function's scaling characteristics. The findings indicate that when assuming collisional excitation as the primary energy source, the intrinsic scatter in observations is significantly reduced, aligning with the expectations from collisional excitation models. Conversely, when considering radiative recombination as the primary energy source, the situation is reversed, with the scatter increasing to match the predictions of recombination models. The results also highlight the significance of radiative transfer in modifying the scaling of the structure function, with specific variations depending on the wavelength and the characteristics of the intra-cluster medium. This study provides a theoretical framework that can be tested against actual observations, offering a pathway for distinguishing between different energy sources and understanding the physical mechanisms driving the complexity observed in the intra-cluster medium.

In this paper, we establish a high degree of variety within an arbitrarily large subset of an infinite random binary graph, G, that is composed of isolated 4-vertices. This is achieved by determining the ramsey number R_K within a dense portion, D, of G. Specifically, we prove that R_K is finite for any fixed K, where K represents a complete subgraph on a small number of vertices, and that the ramsey number R_K increases at a sublinear rate in relation to the number of vertices in K. To facilitate this finding, we first establish a method for identifying small, isolated 4-vertices within an arbitrarily large subset of G. Then, we develop a strategy for applying this approach in conjunction with the dense structure of G to identify large, monochromatic subgraphs defined by K.

Located within the heart of the Milky Way lies the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ), a distinct ring-like formation of molecular activity that has captivated astronomers for decades. By analyzing 12 chemical species in the CMZ, Gu et al. employed a 2D correlation analysis to gain insight into the overall mass distribution of this complex region. The data revealed a prominent axis of chemical symmetry in the CMZ, centered at l ~ 0.5", with a minor axis at b ~ 0.2". When compared to previous estimates, this analysis produced a more accurate measurement of the CMZ's total mass, ranging between 3.4 x 10^4 M_?. Additionally, 2D correlation analysis allowed the identification of two notable mass aggregations within the CMZ -- a large, irregularly shaped mass concentration known as the Super-Skeleton (SS), with a mass of approximately 1.4 x 10^4 M_?; and a smaller, ring-like formation called the Skeleton (ST), with a mass of about 1.0 x 10^4 M_?. By examining the spectral characteristics of various molecules in the CMZ, the authors propose that these mass arrangements in the CMZ are associated with the presence of two distinct star formation episodes in the Milky Way's history.

This research focuses on quickly identifying Bell's Palsy through video analysis, leveraging a neural network called a multi-task convolutional neural network (MT-CNN). We utilized a pre-trained eye-detection system to automatically pinpoint the center of the subject's left eye within each video frame. This eye-centered approach allowed us to accurately determine the side of the subject's face experiencing the paralysis. Furthermore, we developed a straightforward algorithm to pinpoint the area of the face affected by paralysis. Combining these methods resulted in a highly effective Bell's Palsy predictor, revealing a notable side effect - the model's ability to detect hemifacial spasms. As a result, a new spasm-detection module was integrated into the framework, giving rise to the concept of a comprehensive hemifacial disorder detector.

The quantum electrodynamics in su(2) invariant space, known as sQED, is a highly regarded model for studying spin phenomena using quantum simulations. Researchers have previously outlined the basic setup for quantum simulations of sQED using the Husimi Q-function, which effectively maps the complex Hilbert space into a real one, but only at the zero-photon state. However, this approach has a significant drawback in that it destroys the quantum nature of light. In our work, we deviate from this method and propose the use of multilevel qutrits with laser driving to improve the sound detection in quantum simulations of sQED. By adopting the Poincaré section method, which utilizes simplified, quasi-classical descriptions of quantum systems, we are able to accurately model this system despite only having partial knowledge of its quantum state. Furthermore, we demonstrate the versatility of this system by successfully retrieving sQED's physical phenomena, including both stable and unstable photon dynamics, as well as the emission spectra of excited spin states.

The concept of generating highly polarized positron beams through the interaction of intense laser and particle physics is not new, however realizing this in a thick positron source poses significant challenges. A numerical simulation model has been developed to analyze the interaction of an ultra-thin, pulsed electron beam (10.6 MeV, 1.5 kA, 100 fs) with an intense linearly polarized laser (800 nm, 5.5 x 10^22 W/cm^2, 50 fs) in the quantum electrodynamics regime. The simulation includes the impact of classical and quantum effects on the electron beam and demonstrates that even if the electron beam is initially unpolarized, a highly polarized positron source (up to 96.3%) can be achieved, with positron polarization dependent on the electron beam's energy and polarization. Additionally, the relationship between positron polarization and the angle between the electron beam's polarization and the linear polarization of the laser has been explored and a threshold for positron production, influenced by the electron beam's energy and polarization, is identified.

A set of elements is considered 'high-dimensional' if its dimension exceeds the number of its elements, indicating a presence of more coordinate axes required for its representation compared to its scalar count. In the context of this study, the goal is to identify the fewest possible elements needed to describe all possible high-dimensional constructs within a specific framework. By applying certain constraints and a specific mathematical structure, the study successfully determines the smallest number of elements required in such cases. Furthermore, it demonstrates that similar achievements made in an earlier related study are accurate.

This research develops a fully-integrated temperature sensing circuit capable of functioning across a broad voltage range from 0.6V to 1.8V. The design employs a sub-threshold PMOS network to sense temperature, relying on the Nernst effect and the mirror action to produce a precise and reliable temperature reading. Comprehensive mathematical modeling analyzes the device's performance, indicating that the temperature sensor achieves accurate readings with a precision of 0.24°C and an error of 1.4°C within the operating range. The design's energy consumption per transformation is as low as 1.06nj, making it suitable for energy-conscious applications. Furthermore, the design's minimal footprint makes it suitable for integration in memory and logic circuits as a built-in temperature monitoring system.

Long-lasting stability in the magnetic fields of Ap-stars, white dwarfs, and neutron stars has been observed but the exact stellar interior conditions responsible are still the focus of ongoing research. Excluding the effects of stellar p-modes and other unstable oscillations, current studies suggest that magnetic fields in these stars must withstand significant nonlinear interactions with any present convection or shear flows. This work addresses this issue by investigating the stability of axially symmetric magnetic fields in stars using a vector perturbation approach. By applying this method to both nonrotating and rotating stars, we derived a discriminant function determining field stability. This function relies on two key parameters: the Alfven ratio characterizing magnetic field strength and the ratio of stellar rotation to the local sound speed. With these parameters, we establish conditions for linear stability in both rigidly rotating stars and in stars experiencing shear flows.

Using the functional renormalization group (FRG), researchers study the changes in a quantum field theory as a parameter is varied. The FRG flow equations resemble those found in the renormalization group within perturbative QCD. A notable difference exists, however, as the former can be applied to interacting fermions beyond perturbation theory. Despite this capability, the accuracy of the FRG approach for describing physical phenomena has not been thoroughly validated, particularly in regions far from the physical parameters used in its development. In this study, we evaluate the precision of the FRG method for renormalization group flows in a simple, zero-dimensional quantum field theory known as the O(N) model, in which a single type of fermion interacts with itself in a variety of ways. By comparing the predictions made using the FRG flow equations and exact mathematical solutions for this model, we determine the errors associated with the use of the Wilsonian flow equations. These errors are shown to decrease with an increase in certain large numbers, which are essential properties of physical systems and often serve as scales in the theory. These large numbers include the number of symmetry generators (N), the number of fermion components (2S + 1), and the ratio of the fermion mass to its characteristic infrared value, denoted by $m/M$. In the case of the O(N) model, the precision of the Wilsonian approach is accurate to within 1% for values of these parameters that are relevant to physical

Music search applications are extremely popular, with nearly every AGR (Audio Search Gateway) providing comprehensive music databases searchable by melody. Nonetheless, current approaches fall short in effectively leveraging the vast amounts of user-generated content available on social media platforms, which are rich in expressive musical expressions waiting to be analyzed. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel retrieval framework called Pied Piper, which harnesses the power of machine learning to analyze this user-generated data. By utilizing a large, diverse dataset containing annotated musical structures, Pied Piper is capable of learning to identify patterns within music datasets from just a single example - without requiring extensive fine-tuning. As a result, this framework can efficiently handle a wide range of music styles and embeds search queries in a high-dimensional pattern space that retains valuable structural information. Through our approach, we've developed a pioneering method for searching music based on melody, which outperforms existing techniques by a significant margin and showcases its versatility in efficiently handling complex search queries.

This thesis explores the integration process of locally faithful, reduction-preserving subgroupoids on a smooth stack, particularly those with a distinguished base groupoid. It establishes a relationship between these subgroupoids and a diverse range of geometric structures, including a broad category of partial group actions, bundle reductions, and a type of category that arises from symplectic geometry known as Lagrangian foliations. Building on earlier work by the authors, it is demonstrated that smooth stacks equipped with a distinguished base groupoid structure are equivalent to a broad category of non-transitive, reduction-preserving subgroupoids. A key concept known as'reduction' is a crucial component in both the integration and the base groupoid approaches. It plays a pivotal role in non-commutative geometry through the use of partial algebraic structures and is essential for defining the base groupoid structure on a smooth stack.

A massive, infrared dark cloud, referred to as the Dragon, is being considered for a potential pathway to massive star formation. Core expansion within this cloud is being influenced by the contraction of a central protostar and a growing, rotating disk. However, there is also evidence suggesting that core expansion may be driven by the gravitational forces of a highly massive protostar that is no longer visible. If this latter scenario is accurate, it may indicate a critical point at which the formation of massive stars through gravitational collapse is impeded due to the effects of H2 dissociation by the protostar's radiation.

Godel's incompleteness theorem rules out the existence of a complete and consistent formal system that can answer all possible arithmetic questions. However, we can still explore extensions of Godel's theorem through the lens of modal logic, particularly for transitive systems. This study delves into two such extensions featuring agential modal logics, namely Godel's propositional logic and a variant of first-order logic with identity, and proves them complete and consistent with respect to models that incorporate a form of supertransitivity. Furthermore, this research demonstrates several relationships between these modal logics and their corresponding relational structures, including proofs of several transfer theorems for satisfiability and validity.

LiDAR technology enables the creation of detailed 3D environments in various settings, including autonomous navigation, culture heritage preservation, and forestry management. Researchers often extract valuable information from these datasets for subsequent tasks. Nonetheless, the scalability and practical applications of such methodologies are hindered by their reliance on labeled training data. In this work, we investigate the potential of leveraging machine learning tools to uncover meaningful relationships within 3D point clouds, thereby enabling the prediction of target variables without the need for explicit labeling. Specifically, we utilized U-Net, a popular semantic segmentation model, to predict target variables (e.g., forest species, ages, and densities) directly from 3D LiDAR data. In our experiments, we demonstrated that this approach outperformed baseline methods using traditional feature extraction techniques. Furthermore, our results indicated that deep learning architectures can effectively capture relevant information from 3D LiDAR data, leading to accurate predictions of the target variables.

This paper proposes a novel approach to analyzing random functions on the sphere, 
which we refer to as the "one-step" method. Unlike other approaches, this method 
does not rely on the use of local approximation techniques. Instead, we use a 
geodesic partition of the sphere to directly establish an integral equation 
relating the expected values of geodesic mean values to the underlying field's 
properties. Our proposed method is more flexible and can be applied to a wider 
range of scenarios. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we examine a specific 
type of random field defined in terms of its Fourier coefficients and show that 
it meets the criteria we established. Our analysis takes the theoretical 
foundations established here and applies them to the specific type of random 
fields described in the Fourier coefficient paper, verifying that they meet the 
criteria established here.

The source of ultra-high-energy cosmic particles, which exceed $10^{19}$ GeV in energy, remains unknown. To shed light on this enigma, researchers are exploring a potential link between high-energy cosmic rays and neutrino emissions. The acquisition of directional information about neutrino sources could facilitate the correlation of neutrino flux with cosmic ray energy spectra and anisotropies, thereby providing crucial insights. Based on public data from ice neutrino detectors (ARDOR, PINGU, and Neutrino Observatory), we outline a statistical approach to uncover spatial connections between neutrino flux and ultra-high-energy cosmic particle observations. If a significant correlation exists, it would imply a $10^{-2}$ probability and a suitable statistical model would estimate the parameters characterizing the neutrino source distribution.

The flow of liquids through narrow channels is influenced by two opposing effects: surface tension and flow-induced changes to the liquid surface. Flow accelerates the liquid in some areas and slows it down in others, creating both stretching and folding movements within the liquid. As the liquid flows, its surface becomes wrinkled, with ridges and valleys that form at a range of scales, from very small indeed. The flow-induced changes to the liquid's surface can persist for a considerable time after the initial flow has ceased. 

In this study, we examine the long-term consequences of flow-induced changes to the liquid's surface for its flow resistance. We used a combination of physical experiments and numerical simulations to investigate how the flow resistance varies with time and the scale of the roughness. The results show that flow resistance is maximized when the roughness has a medium-scale effect, neither very small nor very large. This phenomenon arises because the largest roughness scales create the greatest local blockage, reducing flow speed and increasing pressure, while the smallest roughness scales have little effect except when the fluid flows quickly. 

These findings may be applicable to a wide range of fluids and could be relevant to the understanding of flow resistance in various situations, such as the resistance faced by a liquid flow as it tries to traverse through another layer of the same liquid, or the movement of a liquid over rough surfaces.

This study proposes an advanced approach to identify outlier tissue samples with abnormal DNA mutation patterns, specifically in the context of skin carcinoma, using a deep learning technique. The method leverages a deep neural network called the Autoencoder, which pinpoints and excludes atypical tissue samples from the training dataset. The proposed framework consists of two main components. Firstly, a deep neural network called the Disorder-to-Order Network is utilized to classify cancer types from histopathological images. Secondly, the technique known as Anomaly-to-Cluster Mapping is employed to identify outlier samples with abnormal DNA mutation patterns. The proposed approach is tested on two datasets: the human genome mutation annotation dataset and the human protein atlas dataset. The results show that the proposed framework outperforms the state-of-the-art approach in accuracy when identifying outlier tissue samples with abnormal DNA mutation patterns.

The interplay between surface tension and rotation in a confined cell, where the inner wall is inclined at an angle $\phi$, leads to an intriguing phenomenon when a foreign liquid with lower viscosity and surface tension than the filled liquid is introduced through a hole in the center. This results in the formation of a mix of radial and circular folds in the foreign liquid, which can accommodate a much larger amount of liquid than would be possible if the cell were not rotated. This difference highlights the effect of rotation on instability modes, with (f/Im)_{\text{crit}} decreasing by approximately half when the angle $\phi$ shifts from $90^\circ$ to $45^\circ$. A similar reduction in (Ga/Im)_{\text{crit}} is observed as the angle $\phi$ changes from $90^\circ$ to $45^\circ$. Furthermore, we have the relationship $\beta \propto \text{Co}^{-0.4}$, and the fact that the curvature of the finger at its tip is determined by the viscosity ratio rather than the ratio of curvatures in the nonrotating situation. This means that the tip of the finger is more closely aligned with the inner wall of the cell as the rate of rotation increases. This alignment can be used as a nondestructive method to determine whether a particular configuration is producing radial or circular instability.

In this work, we address the constraint on the speed of light in vacuum through an innovative approach that overcomes the limitation of constant light speed in vacuo. This is achieved by allowing light speed to vary in line with the changes in phase space volume in a varying scale factor. However, this variation is bounded by certain conditions to avoid instability in hamiltonian dynamics. As a result, light follows non-linear pathways, referred to as hamiltonian pathways, in a constantly transforming phase space. Ultimately, our theory has the potential to expand upon and refine previous ideas on quantum gravity, potentially leading to a more comprehensive framework.

We have been observing the chemical composition of the interstellar medium towards the source TMC-1 for nearly five decades. Our analysis of recent measurements in the 1mm band, specifically towards TMC-1, has yielded an unprecedented level of detail. By employing a nonlinear least-squares method to fit spectra, we obtained precise assessments of column densities for various molecules along this line of sight. Focusing on the ethynyl cyclopentadiene (CCHC5H4) system within this spectrum, we identified two distinct isomers, para and meta, with estimated column densities of 1.4 x 10^11 cm^-2 for the para isomer and 4.6 x 10^10 cm^-2 for the meta isomer. These results demonstrate that the ratio of the para and meta isomers in TMC-1 is approximately 3:1, consistent with a similar ratio found for the cyano cyclopentadiene system. By calculating the total column density of CCH cycles and comparing it to the total column density of CN cycles, we determined the ratio to be approximately 1.4, indicating that CCH cycles are more abundant by a factor of about 1.4 in TMC-1. This difference may arise from an insufficient path length of our current observations or varying excitation conditions. Further research is needed to fully understand these variations.

Our proposed approach, look-ahead focus for creation in neural machine interpretation (LFC-NMİ), is an innovative method for task-oriented interpretation that delves deeper into understanding through neural networks. LFC-NMİ builds upon existing work by incorporating a self-attention mechanism within a encoder-decoder framework, allowing our model to achieve exceptional performance on various understanding tasks while providing insightful visualizations of how the model allocates attention across multiple objects. Furthermore, our approach has demonstrated the ability to successfully learn generation of descriptive phrases for object descriptions, setting a new benchmark in performance.

The concept of translational research has long been recognized in fields like medicine and social sciences, where complex problems require collaboration between distinct disciplines. Unfortunately, the term "translational research" is often misunderstood, leading to unnecessary obstacles in projects that inherently bridge academic and practical domains. The authors of this paper believe that a specific methodological approach, which they call translational, can help break down these hurdles by providing a clear, step-by-step process for developing practical solutions from theoretical foundations. Originally designed for solving complex social problems, this approach has also shown potential in addressing technical challenges, as demonstrated through the authors' experience applying it to resolve a scalability issue in grid computing.

A combined dark substance model is proposed to investigate the behavior of a cosmological system through a variational principle, considering the interaction between dark matter and dark energy as a linked, dissipative, irreversible process. The model's dynamics are described using a Hamiltonian constraint and a dissipation constraint, leading to the derivation of conservation laws, including the conservation of Noether charge and dissipation inequalities. The model's equations of state for dark matter and dark energy are derived as $\rho+3p_\text{dm}=-3\rho_\text{diss}=-\rho_\text{dm}-\rho_\text{de}$ and $w_\text{dm}=\frac{\rho_\text{dm}}{\rho_\text{de}}-1$, $w_\text{de}=\frac{\rho_\text{de}}{\rho_\text{dm}}-1$. Furthermore, a solution for the Hubble parameter is obtained as $H(a)=\sqrt{\rho_0a^{-3\beta}+H_0^2a^{-2}}$, where $\beta$ characterizes the dissipation ratio between dark matter and dark energy.

In educational settings, curiosity is a crucial skill that fosters creativity, a passion for learning, and a vital preparation for a future where lifelong learning and skill acquisition will be increasingly essential.  Unfortunately, many school systems are undermining curiosity by focusing solely on test-taking.  However, educators are seeking innovative ways to spark curiosity in their students, as our traditional teaching methods have shown limited success.  One promising approach involves the use of artificial intelligence, machine learning, and multimedia technologies to create interactive learning environments that can effectively gauge students' curiosity levels.  Previous studies have shown that these technologies can facilitate more engaging and personalized learning experiences, as well as provide valuable insights into students' emotional and cognitive states.  In our study, we combined physiological and self-report data to develop a comprehensive understanding of curiosity in small group learning settings, as well as proposed a novel theory on the dynamics of curiosity, which we tested with a small group of students.  Our results revealed that curiosity exhibits complex dynamics, shifting between three distinct states (stable, sudden change, and gradual transition), and is influenced by internal factors (such as motivation and prior knowledge), external factors (such as instruction and environment), as well as their interplay.  Our research has implications for the design of learning environments and the development of adaptive learning systems that can recognize and respond to the curious states of students in group learning settings.

In our research, we explore how Mat\'ern Gaussian functions can be applied to
estimate data on complex networks by using matrix-based representations of
these functions. This approach enables us to create flexible and interpretable
models for analyzing complex data, especially in cases where other methods
have difficulty predicting certain key features.

The rising popularity of ridesharing services, particularly those that operate on a large scale, offers opportunities for public transportation systems to be detected and characterized through data analysis. Due to the large amount of location updates generated, designing efficient detection algorithms is crucial. Building on previous work using Euclidean distance-based algorithms, we have developed and integrated an optimal detection method utilizing the H3 hexagonal grid system's inherent properties. The new approach demonstrates a significant reduction in computational complexity and a substantial increase in system capacity, enabling the characterization of metropolitan road systems through data collection. The theoretical analysis is supported by experimental results, showcasing the method's superiority. The proposed technique's effectiveness is further highlighted by the inherent resilience to noise and misclassification, ensuring its practical viability.

Our research delves into the implications of the $J/\psi$ decay into invisible particles on a system consisting of a neutrino and a dark sector, with a mass gap. The efficient field theory approach is utilized to investigate the impact of this decay on the neutrino and dark energy sectors. By leveraging the $N_{\rm eff}$ parameter, we assess the conformity of the standard model of particle physics together with its neutrino component with the data from Baryon Acoustic Oscillations and Large Scale Structure at different scales. Furthermore, we explore the conformity of the model with cosmological observations for varying levels of invisible decays in the $J/\psi$ spectrum and establish a lower bound on the parameter $\Gamma_{J/\psi\to {\rm invisible}}$ based on BAO and LSS observations. Specifically, we find $\Gamma_{J/\psi\to {\rm invisible}}\geq 0.4\times 10^{-8}{\rm GeV}$. If this contribution is attributed to the dark sector, we derive a lower limit on the dark photon mass, $m_{A}\geq 17m_{e}$.

The variable timestep Second Difference Integral Mildly Stochastic Differential Equation Method (VSIDMSDEM) is a computational technique recently introduced in relation to stochastic differential equations. This new method uses finite difference approximations for spatiotally homogeneous SDEs, yielding a VSIDMSDEM that employs a variable timestep when solving these equations. In our paper, we demonstrate that the variance of the error term remains bounded by a constant independent of the size of the timestep, under specific conditions. In practice, this allows for significantly larger timesteps to be employed, leading to a significant reduction in computational costs. To illustrate the benefits of VSIDMSDEMs, we compare the results of traditional and variable timestep implementations in relation to the Merton model for pricing credit default swaps.

This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) for analyzing multivariate functional time series data, integrating the singular spectrum analysis (SSA) method with the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a covariance operator. We demonstrate the asymptotic properties of the eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and and establish the connection to traditional SSA methods. Additionally, we explore generalizations of MFSSA to vector-valued and tensor-valued functional time series, and illustrate the methodology through a simulation example and real-world data applications.

Tokenized partial knowledge of target models has significantly contributed to their security, notably with the introduction of token-based methods for cryptanalysis. Research into token-generated ensembles of models, or AESs, through token-based mixed-protocol training, offers an intriguing new pathway. However, our research reveals that AESs possess an unwarranted reliance on the stability of models, along with an unexpected sensitivity to hyperparameters. This complex interplay hampers our understanding of how token-generated ensemble performances can be optimized. Our analysis highlights the detrimental effects of both excessive stability and sudden sensitivity on ensemble performance, identifying key metrics that indicate the occurrence of these phenomena. Ultimately, our research offers a novel strategy for mitigating the adverse effects of this behavior, which can be employed to ensure the reliability of ensemble performance.

This study focuses on a random walk model with a specific duration condition in one dimension. The requirement that the walk last for at least some local minimum duration $m$ before terminating induces a probability distribution on duration $T$ that fulfills the global survival criterion. Our analysis proves that the longer the minimum duration $m$, the smaller the probability of the walk ending within that time frame. This result implies that under the constraint of a longer minimum duration, the walk can potentially last infinitely long. To demonstrate this, we use a method of transforming the problem into an embedded distribution at an arbitrary time $t$, which can be further linked to a geometric distribution. By doing so, we establish a connection between the local and global properties of the walk. Finally, we explore extensions of this model, considering multiple stochastic walks and discussing the effects of changing the starting point or location.

The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to study plasma interactions and probe plasma characteristics. A high-frequency plasma generator is used for plasma creation, operating in two modes: an RF mode and a helicon mode. This study focuses on the helicon mode, which produces a linearly polarized electromagnetic wave at 27.5 MHz to generate plasma via an RF antenna. To verify the effectiveness of this plasma generator, researchers utilized a range of diagnostic tools, including interferometry, a flux probe, and a Langmuir probe. Their findings show that in the helicon mode, a 1 A current results in 300 A of electron tube current and a 13 A/m^2 plasma density at a 0.58 V tongue potential. Additionally, a 1.36 m long plasma column with a 0.1 m diameter is observed.

The model presented in this work simulates the interaction between a microbial insect control system and plant hosts, incorporating the suppression impact on the pathogen. The system consists of two main components: pathogen (microbial agent) and plant (host), with the aim of developing an effective biological control method. A holistic approach is used, with the Gross-Tankow method applying to the human-readable form of the AT-Model. A numerical solution to the resulting system of nonlinear differential equations is found using the Runge-Kutta method. A case study is presented for the nucleopolyhedrovirus (NPV) pathogen in cabbage, with the goal of maintaining a stable, low-pathogen equilibrium that prevents the pest population from recovering. Strategies for activating the suppression mechanism are identified through bifurcation analysis, with the result that only sudden changes can disrupt the system into a state where the low-pathogen equilibrium is unstable, allowing the pest population to flourish.

In this work, we address the challenge of identifying cell nuclei within histology images. Our solution is a novel W-Net, a two-stage network that combines a coarse filter to pinpoint potential nucleus locations, followed by refinement of the outputs through nested networks to achieve precise nucleus segmentation. The potential targets are initially shortlisted based on the W-Net's initial assessments, which are then used to inform the nested networks' architecture. Through this dual-stage approach, W-Net significantly outperforms the current state-of-the-art models, specifically a U-Net, in both precision and recall when evaluated on the Task Force for Image Guided Absorption Measurement (TIGAR) dataset.

Let's consider a global Galois extension $K$ that satisfies certain conditions and is built from a base field $F$. Furthermore, let's establish that the characteristic of $F$ is not $2$. Within this framework, we aim to prove a converse class field theory for specific groups – namely, $SO_{2n+1}(D)$ and $Sp_{2n}(D)$ – where $D$ represents a quaternion division algebra over $F$. To begin this proof, we can leverage Hilbert's reciprocity law to link the arithmetic data represented by a pair of local global functions to the idelic product formula. Ultimately, our argument will involve demonstrating that a specific algebraic group, $G$, meets the condition for the reciprocity law to apply, effectively allowing us to identify the maximal compact subgroup of $N_F(K)$. Building on this understanding, we can then establish that $N_F(K)$ fulfills the requirements for a maximal compact open subgroup. Additionally, we can utilize this analysis to demonstrate that $K$ satisfies an important criterion, thereby providing a key component for our upcoming proof of the CFT.

A graph G is considered to have an "nth line graph within reach" if its nth iteration, denoted as G^(n), can detect all edges in G. The "hamiltonian pathway index" of a graph G, labeled as h(G), is defined as the smallest number n, such that G^(n) is hamiltonian and has an edge detection ability for G. This note aims to provide a proof for the statement that h(G) is greater than or equal to 3, and examples of graphs where h(G) equals 3. Furthermore, upper and lower bounds for the hamiltonian pathway index of certain types of graphs will be determined and discussed.

Cell death via pyroptosis, characterized by inflammation, can contribute to SARS-CoV-2 transmission and the worsening of COVID-19. Pyroptosis is primarily induced by the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation, which can be triggered by various mechanisms, including the interaction between SARS-CoV-2's spike protein and host NRP3. This interaction can occur at multiple stages of infection, allowing for interventions aimed at disrupting the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation. By modeling NRP3's conversion to the active form and the resulting IL-1β secretion, our mathematical framework presents potential targets for anti-inflammatory treatment to curb COVID-19's severity.

External state variables and reinforcement learning models are often used together to handle complex internal dynamics and optimize performance. However, relying on external state variables for rewards can lead to over-reliance on them, making the system vulnerable to their inaccuracy or manipulation. Additionally, learning from reinforcement might not effectively utilize the provided information, potentially hindering progress towards optimal performance. To address these limitations, we explore an alternative approach that eliminates the need for external state variables and learns optimal policy using only natural consequences of internal actions. Within a simple gridworld environment, we demonstrate this approach achieves similar performance improvements and proves robust against action observation, suggesting it is a more direct and reliable means of achieving desired outcomes.

A blockchain-based smart contract platform like Tezos can be seen as an advanced version of traditional digital ledgers, offering more sophisticated digital agreements whose workings mirror intricate biological processes. To ensure the accuracy of these complex contracts, a thorough validation process is crucial. By integrating refined types into the development process, programmers can pinpoint and address potential issues in their code before it's deployed on the network. This enables efficient and reliable collaboration between developers and the community in identifying and fixing errors in the code. Ultimately, this technique facilitates the seamless deployment of high-quality contracts on the Tezos network.

Deep Neural Networks have achieved remarkable performance in various image recognition tasks. Recent advancements like Graph Convolutional Neural Networks have provided a new perspective by modifying the standard CNN framework to accommodate data with non-Euclidean properties. In this research, GCNs are treated as Extended Spatially Invariant Filters that leverage matched filtering concepts to capture local feature patterns. By analyzing the filter structure, we uncover the underlying mathematics and demonstrate the equivalence to standard CNNs. Furthermore, we show how extra information is effectively combined through GCNs by exploring their relationship with CNNs. Through our insights, we pave the way for the development of more efficient GCN models.

We take Einstein's gravity theory and modify it to include a scalar field with an anti-Semantic property, which allows for the addition of Chern-Simons terms. This results in the formation of hairy black holes and solitons when a specific gauge field is present. By analyzing the structure of these objects, we demonstrate that they possess spinning characteristics and distinct thermal properties. Furthermore, the relationship between the mass of the solitons and the charge of the scalar field is non-linear. This modification of general relativity also enables the existence of stable, rotating black holes with large masses when the gauge field meets specific criteria.

The proposed concept of branes in the context of gravity is analogous to objecting surfaces within a curved manifold of higher dimensions. Branes can exist across various dimensions and are associated with spaces that have distinct properties, such as the capacity to compress and release energy. Unlike traditional theoretical objects, branes exhibit irreversible behaviors when interacting with each other, which can result in non-reversible changes in their motion. This study aims to illustrate how incorporating time-reversal constraints into braney systems leads to the discovery of new non-reversible symmetries, which can emerge from combining time-reversal and spatial rotation symmetries. A specific mathematical formula representing the energy exchanged between two branes under collision has been developed, demonstrating how the time-reversal constraint can lead to the emergence of a non-reversible force, which is connected to the force of gravity. Furthermore, it is proposed that the energy exchanged between colliding branes could give rise to particle production, which is influenced by the properties of the branes involved and can vary depending on the direction of travel.

Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the mechanical properties of tissues. Lateral displacement estimation plays a key role in elastography, yet the method's precision is hindered by the limited resolution of B-mode images and assumptions about the image formation process. The Virtual Origin Synthetic Aperture (VOSA) technique, a model-based approach, is an innovative solution that takes into account real-world ultrasound transducers and their non-ideal behaviour. By incorporating a physical model of the transducer, VOSA can determine the actual position of the virtual source, accurately estimating lateral shifts. Numerical simulations demonstrate that VOSA-enhanced elastography yields more precise estimates than conventional methods, while experimental results show that VOSA outperforms electrical source positioning (ESP) in phantom tests and rivals photon momentum transfer (PMT) on soft tissue.

Reasoning about and efficiently navigating through complex data structures is an essential skill for any computer science professional. As a result, teaching students abstract data types and associated algorithms is a fundamental educational goal.
